**Summary.** This paper analyzes how best to discriminate between two noisy qubit processes undergoing amplitude damping by optimizing both the input probe state and the measurement time. It rigorously proves that using an entangled probe can yield a significantly lower error rate at any finite time compared to the best unassisted strategy, which only approaches this limit asymptotically.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous quantitative bounds on the resource utility of quantum entanglement in practical open-system measurements, distinguishing between static vs. time-dependent advantages for characterizing decoherence channels.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on determining the minimum error probability for discriminating between two distinct qubit dynamical processes governed by phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians.

**Main result.** Entanglement assistance allows for a strictly lower minimum error probability at finite interrogation times compared to the best achievable unassisted strategy, which only approaches this value asymptotically.

**Method.** The authors use quantum information theory tools, including trace-norm and diamond-norm distinguishability measures, optimizing over both the input probe state (including entanglement) and the interrogation time $t$.

**Model / system.** The system involves two qubits undergoing dynamics described by a master equation representing phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians. The analysis is performed in a single-use scenario.

**Key observables.** Minimum error probability ($p_E, e_p$), optimal trace-norm distinguishability ($D_{	ext{sep}}(t)$), and entanglement-assisted distinguishability ($D_{	ext{ent}}(t)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The damping rates ($\gamma_+$, $\gamma_-$, $\gamma_z$) define the dynamics, and time $t$ is a crucial optimization variable.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the underlying dynamics are phase-covariant amplitude-damping semigroups; for entanglement assistance, it leverages common U(1) phase covariance to simplify the optimization.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison of minimum error probabilities versus time, demonstrating finite-time advantages achieved by entangled probes over unassisted ones, and show threshold behavior for this advantage.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem setup using distinguishability measures. It then analyzes the unassisted case, deriving closed forms for optimal strategies on different branches. The core contribution involves showing how entanglement reduces the optimization to a one-parameter Schmidt family, leading to fixed-time and time-optimized advantage criteria.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We analyze minimum-error discrimination of two qubit dynamical processes generated by phase-covariant amplitude-damping Lindbladians in a single-use scenario. The optimization involves both the input probe, possibly entangled with an isolated ancilla, and the interrogation time. For unassisted probes we obtain a closed expression for the optimal trace-norm distinguishability at fixed time, with distinct interior and boundary branches. For entanglement-assisted probes, the common phase covariance of the two channels reduces the diamond-norm optimization to a one-parameter Schmidt family. The resulting formula gives transparent sufficient conditions for fixed-time entanglement advantage and separates this local advantage from advantage after global optimization over time. We exhibit examples in which the best unassisted strategy is approached only asymptotically, whereas an entangled probe achieves a strictly smaller error probability at finite time.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a novel fixed-point tensor network approach to describe irrational Conformal Field Theories, using the compactified boson model as a test case. By constructing tensors from boundary data and analyzing them via Tensor Complex Renormalization, the authors successfully reproduce known physical spectra and map out continuous flow paths in the theory's moduli space.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on CFT, the core methodology—using tensor networks (TCR) to simulate complex quantum field theory dynamics and RG flows—is a powerful numerical technique applicable to strongly correlated systems or open quantum systems where exact diagonalization is impossible.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is extending fixed-point tensor network constructions from rational CFTs to irrational theories, specifically using the 2D compactified boson model.

**Main result.** The framework successfully generates a discrete lattice description for the irrational CFT, accurately reproducing the closed-string spectrum and identifying controllable exactly marginal deformations along the c=1 moduli space.

**Method.** The authors employ Fixed-Point (FP) tensor networks, utilizing boundary data to construct tensors that are then analyzed using the Tensor Complex Renormalization (TCR) algorithm for RG flow analysis.

**Model / system.** The system studied is the 2D compactified boson conformal field theory, which serves as an archetypal irrational CFT. The construction relies on mapping correlation functions onto tensor network contractions involving boundary conditions.

**Key observables.** Closed-string spectrum (conformal dimensions $\Delta$), central charge ($c$), and scaling dimensions ($\Delta$) extracted via RG flow analysis.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The compactification radius $R$, the deformation parameter $	au$ or $r$, and the finite grid size $\Lambda$ used for numerical approximation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method requires replacing continuous boundary conditions with a finite, discretized lattice representation, which introduces necessary approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the construction of rank-3 and rank-4 FP tensors, show the recovered closed-string spectrum via transfer matrix methods at various radii, and depict RG spectra derived from these tensor structures.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically builds the tensor network representation for correlation functions (rank-4 tensors), applies the TCR algorithm to analyze the resulting spectrum, and demonstrates how tuning parameters within the tensor structure generates continuous marginal deformations along moduli spaces.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Fixed-point (FP) tensor networks provide a discrete spacetime representation of conformal field theories (CFTs), offering a new route toward understanding holographic duality, generalized symmetries, and even quantum gravity. In this work, we construct FP tensors for the 2D compactified boson theory at a generic compactification radius, an archetypal irrational CFT, using boundary (open-string) data with conformal boundary conditions. We show that the resulting tensors reproduce the closed-string spectrum with high accuracy and generate stable renormalization-group (RG) flows under the tensor complex renormalization algorithm. Moreover, we identify a controllable exactly marginal deformation at the level of a single tensor, enabling flows that move continuously along the $c=1$ moduli space. This framework establishes a concrete lattice-level route toward describing a broad class of 2D irrational CFTs.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously determines the fundamental boundaries on what states can be prepared in an open qubit system under coherent control. It characterizes this boundary as a specific surface of revolution within the Bloch ball using advanced geometric control theory. The results provide essential, constructive bounds for quantum state preparation fidelity in dissipative quantum computing architectures.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a complete, rigorous geometric description of controllability for open quantum systems, which is foundational knowledge for designing robust quantum gates and state preparation routines in realistic noisy environments.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to analytically determine the ultimate geometric limits of state preparation (the reachable set) for an open qubit subjected to coherent control.

**Main result.** It proves that the boundary of the reachable set is a surface of revolution around the $r_x$-axis, which is analytic except for two conical singularities. Furthermore, it provides explicit control protocols to approach any state on this boundary asymptotically.

**Method.** The analysis uses geometric control theory applied to the Bloch sphere dynamics governed by a GKSL master equation, involving techniques like analyzing separatrices and constructing specific time-optimal control protocols.

**Model / system.** The system is an open two-level quantum system (qubit) whose evolution is described by a Lindblad/GKSL master equation incorporating free Hamiltonian ($\mathrm{H}_0$), coherent driving ($V$), and dissipation rates ($\gamma$).

**Key observables.** Bloch coordinates $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ describing the state $ho$, and the boundary surface $\partial R$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio $\alpha = \gamma/\omega$ (dissipation rate to frequency) is a key parameter governing the geometry of the reachable set.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Boundary points are only asymptotically reachable in finite time, and the analysis relies on local hyperbolic dynamics near equilibrium points.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the boundary curve $\Gamma$ defining the reachable set's boundary, its intersection with specific planes (like $r_y=0$), and projections of separatrices onto various coordinate planes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the dynamics in Bloch coordinates, then characterizing the boundary using geometric control theory concepts like separatrices, culminating in the derivation of explicit protocols to approach these fundamental limits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We analytically determine the ultimate limits of state preparation in two-level open quantum systems driven by coherent control. For a dissipative qubit governed by a GKSL master equation, we give an exact characterization of the reachable set in the Bloch ball. Dissipation excludes a region of states in the Bloch ball which cannot be approached even under arbitrarily strong coherent driving, and we prove that this region has a nontrivial geometry whose boundary is a surface of revolution around the $x$-axis which is analytic except for two conical singularities. We derive a closed-form control protocol for moving on this boundary, and construct an explicit protocol that steers the system arbitrarily close to any prescribed boundary state. These results provide a complete geometric constructive description of reachable qubit states in the standard dissipative environment, establishing fundamental bounds on controllability and state-preparation fidelity for open two-level quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper details the use of advanced magnetic traps, generated by higher-order multipoles, to confine levitated superconducting microparticles. This confinement creates anharmonic potentials necessary for inducing nonclassical quantum motion in the particle's center-of-mass. The research paves the way for fundamental experiments testing the boundary between classical and quantum mechanics using massive mechanical oscillators.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges quantum mechanics (quantum interference, non-Gaussian states) with macroscopic mechanical systems and superconducting materials, making it highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum sensing in AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central goal is generating and observing macroscopic quantum interference effects in the center-of-mass motion of levitated superconducting microparticles.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that using higher-order multipole magnetic traps allows for the creation of anharmonic potentials capable of realizing non-Gaussian motional states, opening a path to study the quantum-to-classical transition with massive objects.

**Method.** The analysis involves solving the dynamics of the center-of-mass motion in phase space, utilizing Wigner function representations and analyzing specific nonlinear potential forms like Duffing or double-well potentials.

**Model / system.** The system is a superconducting microparticle levitated and trapped by static magnetic fields generated via higher-order multipole coils. The dynamics are governed by the particle's interaction with an anharmonic potential $U(r)$ derived from the applied field $\mathbf{B}_a$.

**Key observables.** Non-Gaussian motional states, measurement of particle position to distinguish classical vs. quantum behavior.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The nonlinearity scale is set below nanometers (hundred times the zero-point motion); trap potentials are defined by magnetic field coefficients ($b_1, b_2, b_3$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** It is assumed that the superconducting particle remains in a state where its dynamics can be effectively modeled by these anharmonic potentials, and that rapid switching of fields is possible.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates various magnetic traps (harmonic/anharmonic) generated by coil configurations. Figure 2 shows classical trajectory solutions for different nonlinear potential types (DP, DWP).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical platform and the role of higher-order traps in creating anharmonic potentials. It then analyzes the resulting dynamics using phase space methods, deriving specific protocols to generate nonclassical states before concluding with implications for fundamental physics tests.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show how magnetostatic higher-order multipole traps can be used to generate macroscopic quantum interference of the motion of levitated superconducting microparticles. An appropriate combination of multipolar magnetic fields offers great versatility in constructing various trap potentials, including anharmonic trap potentials such as Duffing or double-well types. Crucially, the anharmonic trap potentials realize a nonlinearity on the order of hundred times the zero-point motion, i.e., on a length scale below nanometers. These anharmonic potentials allow for the generation of quantum features of the center-of-mass motion of a magnetically levitated superconducting microparticle. Importantly, they can be easily generated with a static arrangement of coils, requiring only that the current running through them is tunable. We propose protocols exploiting the versatility of the magnetic trap landscape to generate non-Gaussian motional states. We solve the dynamics of the center-of-mass motion of the particle in phase space and analyze its parameter dependence. Furthermore, we give a recipe to distinguish classical from quantum behavior in a statistically meaningful way through measurement of the position of the particle. Our results open a path to accessing the quantum regime of the center-of-mass motion of objects with masses larger than picogram, i.e., $10^{13}$ atomic mass units. This will enable fundamental physics experiments for studying the transition between quantum and classical behavior, exploring the intersection between quantum physics and gravity as well as probing of certain types of dark matter.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically investigates the anomalous Hall effect in $f$-electron antiferromagnets by developing an effective Hamiltonian derived from strong correlation physics. It concludes that the AHE is fundamentally driven by nonlocal spin-dependent hopping mediated by Kondo exchange coupling, rather than local magnetic fields or itinerant electron behavior alone.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed many-body theoretical framework connecting magnetic order (AFM) to transport phenomena (AHE) in strongly correlated materials using concepts like Kondo exchange, which are central to understanding complex electronic states beyond simple band theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to elucidate the microscopic origin of the intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in antiferromagnetic $f$-electron metals, particularly where localized magnetic moments interact with itinerant conduction electrons.

**Main result.** The AHE is found to originate from nonlocal spin-dependent intersite hopping induced by Kondo exchange coupling, rather than a simple local Zeeman field or canting magnetization effect. The $	ext{Ge } 4p$ orbitals provide the dominant contribution to this effect.

**Method.** The authors developed a theoretical framework using Green's function techniques and derived an effective Hamiltonian analogous to the Kondo lattice model, incorporating strong correlation effects via approximations like Hubbard-I.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a localized-$4f$ antiferromagnetic metal ($	ext{Ce}_2	ext{CuGe}_6$), described by a tight-binding Hamiltonian coupling conduction ($c$) and $f$ electrons. The strong correlations are treated using DMFT/Hubbard-I approximations.

**Key observables.** Intrinsic Anomalous Hall Conductivity ($\sigma_{DC}^{xy}$), spin splitting of energy bands, and the dependence of $\sigma_{DC}^{xy}$ on canting magnetization ($m_z$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Kondo temperature ($T_K \simeq 1 	ext{ K}$); hybridization terms ($\hat{V}(\mathbf{k})$); molecular field strengths controlling AFM order.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on deriving an effective Hamiltonian that captures the physics of $c-f$ hybridization, often simplifying by neglecting orbital degeneracy or assuming specific magnetic ordering patterns.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison between local vs. nonlocal contributions to AHE (Figure 1), plot $\sigma_{DC}^{xy}$ dependence on canting magnetization ($m_z$) showing robustness against $m_z$ changes (Figure 2), and show band structure polarization related to spin splitting (Figure 3).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical necessity of an effective Hamiltonian for correlated systems, deriving this model from a full Green's function approach incorporating strong correlations, and finally applying it to calculate $\sigma_{DC}^{xy}$ while decomposing contributions to pinpoint the nonlocal hopping mechanism.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The anomalous Hall effect in antiferromagnetic metals has attracted considerable attention. Most known realizations involve itinerant $d$ electrons that simultaneously mediate charge transport and magnetic order. Here, we focus on $f$-electron materials, where localized magnetic moments and conduction electrons are hosted in different orbitals. We develop a theoretical framework to describe the impact of localized antiferromagnetic order on itinerant electrons. Applying this approach to the recently discovered $4f$ antiferromagnetic metal $\mathrm{Ce}_{2}\mathrm{Cu}\mathrm{Ge}_{6}$, we identify the origin of both the intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity and the spin splitting of the energy bands as spin-dependent intersite hopping induced by nonlocal Kondo exchange coupling, rather than a Zeeman-type effective field acting locally on the conduction electrons.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper develops the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus ($\delta$ZX) to overcome the limitations of standard diagrams when modeling infinitely repeating quantum structures like lattice codes. By introducing a 'delay' generator and defining two formal semantics, it provides a complete algebraic framework for representing and simplifying these infinite processes into unique canonical forms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful mathematical tool for analyzing large-scale quantum systems, such as those found in solid-state or photonic implementations of QEC codes, by providing a rigorous way to handle infinite periodic boundary conditions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams are insufficient for modeling quantum processes that exhibit infinite, translation-invariant structures across space or time.

**Main result.** The authors introduce the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus ($\delta$ZX), establishing a unique normal form and proving soundness, universality, and completeness for its generating tableau semantics.

**Method.** The calculus extends the standard ZX-diagram formalism with a 'delay' generator ($\delta$), allowing the representation of infinite processes via formal variables encoding generating functions.

**Model / system.** The theory models stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes and general translation-invariant quantum circuits, originally formulated for qudits based on an odd prime $p$. The formalism relates these physical systems to algebraic structures like affine Lagrangian subspaces.

**Key observables.** Infinite stabilizer groups; equivalence classes of sequences of quantum channels; generating functions encoding Pauli operators.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The delay parameter ($\delta$); the dimension related to an odd prime $p$; matrix entries in the field $\mathbb{F}_p(\delta)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that infinite, translation-invariant processes can be captured by extending the finite ZX calculus with a formal delay variable.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate axioms of the standard ZX calculus encoding Pauli operators ($Z^z X^x$) and provide examples for various quantum states (e.g., Bell states).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the foundational equivalence between stabilizer mechanics, symplectic linear algebra, and the standard ZX-calculus. It then develops the delayed calculus by introducing $\delta$, providing two semantics (channel sequences and generating functions), and finally proving a complete reduction to a unique normal form via matrix algebra techniques.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Many stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes are built from a finite pattern repeated across space or time, such as lattice codes, translation-invariant graph states, and quantum convolutional codes. Ordinary stabilizer ZX-diagrams capture only finite truncations of such systems, obscuring the repeated structure that defines them. We introduce the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, a finite graphical language for these infinite, translation-invariant processes. It extends the odd-prime-dimensional stabilizer ZX-calculus with a single new generator, the delay, which feeds data from one time step to the next. We equip the calculus with two semantics. In the first semantics, we interpret the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram as an equivalence class of sequences of quantum channels; where two sequences are identified if they have the same information content. We show that the behaviour of a delayed ZX-diagram uniquely determines an infinite stabilizer group. In the second semantics, we interpret the delay as a formal variable, encoding the translation-invariant families of Pauli operators as generating functions. This allows us to represent a delayed ZX-diagram in terms of a tableau of generating functions, from which the infinite stabilizer group can be recovered. Finally, we give a complete axiomatization of the delayed stabilizer ZX-calculus, featuring generalised Euler decomposition and colour change rules. Using generalised forms of local complementation and pivoting, we reduce every diagram to a unique normal form. This establishes soundness, universality, and completeness for the generating tableau semantics.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically explores how combining mechanical strain and electrostatic potentials can precisely control spin and valley polarization in monolayer MoS2. By analyzing quantum transport through engineered potential barriers, the authors predict a dual-knob control scheme that allows for independent tuning of conductance oscillations using these two external fields. This offers a powerful platform for realizing advanced spintronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work demonstrates highly tunable control over fundamental quantum degrees of freedom (spin and valley) in a 2D material using external fields, which is central to developing next-generation spintronic and valleytronic devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates spin- and valley-resolved quantum transport in monolayer MoS2 when subjected to the simultaneous influence of mechanical strain and an external scalar potential, a combination previously unexplored.

**Main result.** The interplay between strain and electrostatic potential allows for orthogonal control over both valley and spin polarization, enabling phenomena like 'electrostatic spin inversion' purely via gate tuning.

**Method.** Theoretical analysis using an effective massive Dirac Hamiltonian incorporating intrinsic spin-orbit coupling to model electron transmission through a barrier region.

**Model / system.** The system is monolayer MoS2 modeled by an effective Hamiltonian that includes terms for Fermi velocity, band gap, spin-orbit coupling, and strain. The transport calculation involves solving coupled differential equations across regions defined by the potential barrier and strain field.

**Key observables.** Spin polarization ($P_s$), valley polarization ($P_v$), resonant transmission probability ($T_{	au s_z}$), and total conductance ($G$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mechanical strain ($\epsilon$), electrostatic potential barrier height ($V_0$), barrier width ($L$), and incident energy ($E$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a continuum effective Dirac Hamiltonian, neglects higher-band corrections or intervalley scattering, and ignores disorder effects.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates the MoS2 sheet under uniaxial strain and an external scalar electrostatic potential. Figure 11 shows spin polarization vs. strain for various barrier widths and energies.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the Hamiltonian incorporating strain and potential, derives transmission coefficients using boundary matching conditions across three distinct regions (outside/inside/outside the barrier), and analyzes how varying parameters controls spin/valley polarization via quantum interference effects.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a theoretical study of spin- and valley-resolved quantum transport in monolayer MoS$_2$ under the combined influence of mechanical strain and an external scalar potential, a combination whose simultaneous unexplored. Within an effective massive Dirac Hamiltonian that incorporates intrinsic spin--orbit coupling, strain induces valley-dependent momentum shifts that lift the degeneracy between the $K$ and $K'$ valleys and strongly modify the transport characteristics. The scalar potential modifies the tunneling spectrum, leading to pronounced changes in resonant transmission, Fabry--Pérot interference, and conductance. We show that the interplay between strain and electrostatic potential enables efficient control of both valley and spin polarization of the transmitted current. In particular, we identify a dual-knob control scheme in which the barrier width governs the frequency of conductance oscillations while strain independently controls their phase and amplitude. Furthermore, we predict electrostatic spin inversion -- a sign reversal of spin polarization achievable purely by gate tuning at finite strain, requiring no geometric reconfiguration. Depending on the strain orientation, the transmission probability and conductance can be selectively suppressed or enhanced, resulting in highly tunable valley- and spin-polarized transport. These findings demonstrate that strain and potential engineering provide orthogonal and independently operable mechanisms for controlling conductance as well as spin and valley degrees of freedom in monolayer MoS$_2$, offering promising prospects for spintronic and valleytronic device applications.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To describe an alternative laser trap for cooling and trapping neutral atoms that operates without relying on a magnetic field, overcoming limitations of traditional Magneto-Optical Traps (MOTs).

**Main result.** The Super-Molasses Trap (SMT) successfully traps and cools cold atoms to microkelvin temperatures with high density, achieving performance comparable to MOTs but using only optical fields.

**Method.** Experimental implementation of the SMT using a simple geometry of collimated laser beams in a tripod configuration, combined with theoretical analysis of dipole trapping potentials.

**Model / system.** The system involves cooling and trapping neutral atoms (e.g., $^{87}	ext{Rb}$) from background vapor using near-resonance laser fields that create a velocity and position-dependent restoring force without external magnetic gradients.

**Key observables.** Atom number ($>10^6$), density ($\sim 10^{10}/	ext{cm}^3$), and temperature (down to $\mu	ext{K}$ range).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Laser detuning ($\Delta$), laser power, background vapor pressure ($10^{-11}$ to $10^{-10} 	ext{ mbar}$).

**Figures summary.** Figures show the laser beam geometry (tripod), dependence of atom number on detuning/power, and temperature measurements demonstrating cooling down to $\mu	ext{K}$ levels after an 'optical molasses' stage.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the SMT as an alternative to MOTs, details experimental measurements showing high performance metrics (density, temperature), discusses the underlying physics via comparison with established techniques, and concludes by highlighting the potential for quantum applications while acknowledging theoretical gaps.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Laser cooled and trapped atoms have been the workhorse of atomic physics for the past four decades. The predominant method has been the highly versatile Magneto-Optical Trap. We describe an alternative laser trap involving a simple geometry of collimated laser beams that provides both a velocity and position dependent restoring force such that a dense cloud of cold atoms is formed. This technique produces similar atom number ($>10^6$) and density ($10^{10}$\,atoms/cm$^{3}$) to the Magneto-Optical Trap, albeit with \emph{no magnetic field}. The beam geometry is compatible with conventional sub-Doppler cooling techniques, allowing the trapped cloud to be cooled to $< 10~μ$K. We demonstrate the validity and robustness of the trap by capturing $^{87}$Rb atoms directly from the background vapor and provide a theoretical discussion of the underlying principles. This trap has many unique properties that make it highly suitable for quantum sensing, timing, and computing applications as well as a new tool in fundamental science and metrology.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces an efficient Multi-band Localization Landscape (LL) model to simulate carrier transport and emission in AlGaN UVC LEDs. By replacing computationally intensive k.p eigenvalue problems with the LL formalism, the authors achieve significant speedups while maintaining accuracy. The method successfully models complex physics like strain effects and polarization switching crucial for optimizing high-efficiency deep-UV light sources.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of a computationally tractable quantum mechanical framework (LL model) that successfully replaces complex eigenvalue solvers for semiconductor device simulation is highly relevant to modeling open quantum systems in solid-state devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to efficiently analyze carrier transport and determine TM-TE emission characteristics in AlGaN UVC LEDs, overcoming the computational expense of conventional k.p models.

**Main result.** A novel multi-band Localization Landscape (LL) model significantly reduces simulation time while accurately reproducing spectral trends and polarization ratios compared to full 3D k.p calculations.

**Method.** The authors employ a hybrid approach combining the LL model with the Wigner–Weyl formalism, solving it within a 3D drift-diffusion framework on a Finite Element Mesh (FEM).

**Model / system.** The system is AlGaN UVC LEDs. The methodology involves coupling the LL theory to solve for carrier localization and band structure changes induced by strain and alloy fluctuations, which are then fed into a 3D drift-diffusion solver.

**Key observables.** Emission/absorption spectra trends, polarization ratio (TE/TM), band structure, hole/electron current densities ($J_p, J_n$), and quantum efficiency (EQE).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Al composition ($	ext{Al}_x	ext{Ga}_{1-x}	ext{N}$), strain tensor components, operating wavelength (220–300 nm), and doping profiles.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The LL theory is assumed to provide an accurate approximation of the full Schrödinger eigenvalue problem, allowing for computational efficiency gains. Strain effects are incorporated via deformation-potential terms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate band structure transitions based on polarization/strain, local strain variation causing band switching, and comparisons of carrier current density maps with and without including the crucial strain-induced deformation term.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the physical problem (UVC LEDs), details the limitations of existing k.p methods, proposes the LL model as an efficient alternative, validates it by comparing results to known physics (strain effects on hole transport), and concludes with analysis of device performance metrics like IQE.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

AlGaN-based UVC LEDs (220-250 nm) suffer from poor hole confinement and strain-induced |Z>-band dominance at high Al content (>60%), leading to increased TM emission and reduced external quantum efficiency (EQE). While conventional k.p models combined with Schrodinger, Poisson, and drift-diffusion solvers are widely used to study optical transitions, they are computationally expensive. In this work, we apply the multiband Localization Landscape (LL) model, including the effect of strain, as an alternative that replaces the eigenvalue problem to efficiently capture quantum effects and carrier localization. Using the 3D multi-band LL model with the Wigner-Weyl formalism, we reproduce emission and absorption spectra trends similar to the results in 3D k.p calculations, but with significantly reduced simulation time. The polarization ratio also agrees well with published experimental results across a wide spectral range. Furthermore, we analyze electrical characteristics such as band structure, polarization switching, and carrier confinement under alloy fluctuations and strain. This multi-band LL-based approach provides a fast and reliable solution for understanding and optimizing UVC LED performance.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a powerful generalization of classical $f$-divergences to the setting of general von Neumann algebras, using 'hockeystick divergences' as the core mathematical tool. It rigorously analyzes the properties of these quantum state distinguishability measures and aims to prove their equivalence with the relative entropy, providing deeper mathematical foundations for quantum hypothesis testing in complex physical systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental mathematical tools for quantifying distinguishability between quantum states in highly general settings (infinite dimensions), which is crucial for developing rigorous theories in quantum field theory or open quantum systems where standard measure theory fails.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper defines and analyzes $f$-divergences and hockeystick divergences for normal positive functionals on general von Neumann algebras, aiming to generalize classical probability measures to quantum settings.

**Main result.** It establishes that the properties of these generalized $f$-divergences (like monotonicity and convexity) can be derived from structural properties of the underlying algebra via hockeystick divergence representations. Furthermore, it aims to prove the equivalence between this generalized $f_0$-divergence and Araki's relative entropy for general von Neumann algebras.

**Method.** The methodology involves defining divergences using operator norms on positive functionals (hockeystick divergences) and utilizing advanced tools from functional analysis, including spectral theory, trace identities, and convergence theorems applied to unbounded operators in the context of operator algebras.

**Model / system.** The mathematical framework is built upon general von Neumann algebras ($M$), which serve as a generalization of classical measure spaces. The physical states are represented by normal positive functionals ($\phi$) on $M$, relevant for quantum statistical mechanics and QFT.

**Key observables.** State distinguishability measures, specifically $f$-divergences and hockeystick divergences; the relative entropy ($D_{f_0}$ when $f(t)=t\ln t$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The structure of the von Neumann algebra (Type I, II, or III), and limits involving regularization parameters ($\epsilon 	o 0$) used to approach infinite-dimensional structures.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the existence of normal positive functionals on general von Neumann algebras and relies heavily on advanced theorems regarding traces and operator convergence in these non-commutative settings.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by first defining hockeystick divergences as a generalization tool, then analyzing the properties of $f$-divergences derived from them. It then tackles the difficult task of proving the equivalence between these generalized divergences and established quantum information measures like relative entropy via multi-shot regularization techniques.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We define and analyze hockeystick divergences and $f$-divergences for normal positive functionals on general von Neumann algebras, generalizing and unifying previous work in classical probability and finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras. All the main properties of these state distinguishability measures (including in particular monotonicity, convexity, semicontinuity, bounds, state discrimination, data processing inequality) are derived from properties of the Jordan decomposition of selfadjoint normal functionals. This is done by representing the $f$-divergences as integrals over hockeystick divergences, and their significance in quantum hypothesis testing is reviewed. The $f_0$-divergence given by the information function $f_0(t) = t \ln t$ is shown to coincide with Araki's relative entropy, extending results of Frenkel to general von Neumann algebras.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces a Lie-Jordan geometric framework to provide a universal algebraic interpretation of dissipative evolution in open quantum systems. By decomposing the GKLS master equation into universal structural tensors and model-specific terms, it cleanly separates the underlying mathematical structure from the physics. This offers a powerful, systematic tool for analyzing any system undergoing Markovian dissipation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This provides a deep algebraic and geometric underpinning for open quantum dynamics, offering tools to analyze the structure of dissipation independent of the specific physical Hamiltonian or Lindblad operators used.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a Lie-Jordan geometric formulation to systematically analyze the algebraic structure underlying open quantum dynamics governed by the Lindblad equation.

**Main result.** It successfully separates the universal, basis-independent algebraic structure of dissipation from the model-dependent physical parameters (Lindblad operators and Kossakowski matrix).

**Method.** The authors endow the Hilbert-Schmidt operator space with an orthonormal basis and encode quantum commutators/anticommutators using Lie and Jordan structure tensors to derive a universal trilinear dissipative map.

**Model / system.** The focus is on finite-dimensional open quantum systems whose evolution is described by the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) master equation. The formalism is tested using qubit examples exhibiting pure dephasing and amplitude damping.

**Key observables.** The component representation of the dissipator, $\dot{ho}_\lambda$, and the resulting Bloch vector dynamics ($\dot{\mathbf{r}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Lindblad operators ($L_\alpha$), Kossakowski matrix ($\gamma_{\alphaeta}$), and the Lie/Jordan structure tensors ($C$ and $B$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system evolution is assumed to be Markovian, completely positive, and trace-preserving.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes; the focus is on algebraic derivations and component equations rather than visual figure summaries.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general geometric framework using structure tensors for commutators/anticommutators to deriving a universal dissipative map. It then applies this formalism to verify known results (like trace preservation) and illustrates it with specific qubit channels, concluding by showing equivalence to standard ordered-product derivations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a Lie-Jordan geometric formulation of finite-dimensional open quantum dynamics, building on the algebraic framework introduced in our previous work (arXiv:2606.26477). The Hilbert-Schmidt operator space is endowed with an orthonormal Hermitian basis, in which the commutator and anticommutator are encoded by the structure tensors \(C_{μν}{}^λ\) and \(B_{μν}{}^λ\). Within this formulation, the von Neumann and Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan equations admit a direct component representation. Our central result is the identification of a basis-independent universal trilinear dissipative map, \( \mathcal D(X,Y)Z=XZY-\frac12\{YX,Z\}, \) whose components define a universal operator-space tensor depending only on the Lie-Jordan structure tensors. The physical dissipator is obtained by contracting this tensor with the expansion coefficients of the Lindblad operators and the Kossakowski matrix, thereby separating the universal algebraic structure from the model-dependent physical information. We further show that the combinations \((B+C)\) and \((B-C)\) generate internal left and right transports, allowing the elementary dissipative map to be expressed as a left-right bimodule action corrected by an ordered Jordan contribution. The universal map satisfies basis-independent trace and Hermitian-conjugation identities, from which trace preservation, Hermiticity preservation of the complete dissipator, and the reality of its component representation in a Hermitian Hilbert-Schmidt basis follow. We also derive its Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint and illustrate the formalism for a qubit with pure dephasing and amplitude-damping channels. This construction provides a tensorial and affine-geometric interpretation of the universal superoperator structure derived in arXiv:2606.26477 while keeping the algebraic and model-dependent sectors explicitly separated.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenge of determining the Hamiltonian of large multi-qubit quantum systems by framing it as a sparse signal recovery problem solvable via compressed sensing. To overcome the inherent mathematical difficulty—the failure of standard sampling conditions at high qubit numbers—the authors introduce a novel 'scale transformation' technique. This method ensures that accurate estimation remains possible even for dozens of qubits, significantly advancing the feasibility of characterizing complex quantum dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial algorithmic breakthrough for characterizing complex quantum dynamics in large systems where full characterization is impossible. The focus on overcoming fundamental mathematical limitations (RIP failure) makes it highly relevant for scaling up quantum simulations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Estimating a sparse Hamiltonian for large multi-qubit quantum systems is computationally difficult due to the exponential growth of parameters.

**Main result.** The authors propose a 'scale transformation' technique that restores the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) required for compressed sensing, allowing accurate estimation using only $O(k \log(4^N/k))$ measurements.

**Method.** The problem is formulated as solving an $\ell_1$-minimization problem ($\min \|h\|_1$ s.t. $\|ar{y} - \Phi h\|^2 \le \epsilon$) using compressed sensing principles, augmented by the scale transformation to handle ill-conditioning.

**Model / system.** The system is an N-qubit quantum processor whose dynamics are governed by a sparse Hamiltonian $H$. The estimation relies on measuring expectation values of observables derived from Pauli matrices acting on initial states.

**Key observables.** Measured expectation values $ar{y}_{ij} = \langle M_j angle_{ho_i}$, and the measurement matrix $\Phi$ constructed from these measurements.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of qubits ($N$), the sparsity level of the Hamiltonian ($k$), and the condition number ($\kappa$) of the measurement matrix's Gramian, which must remain below a critical threshold.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the unknown Hamiltonian $h$ is sparse. A major technical challenge addressed is the 'scalability-induced ill-conditioning,' where standard CS fails for large N.

**Figures summary.** Figures demonstrate the method's effectiveness by showing successful Hamiltonian estimation in 6- and 30-qubit systems, with error decreasing as measurement shots increase (though non-statistical errors persist).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the linear system $ar{y} = \Phi h$, identifies the failure of standard CS due to increasing condition numbers ($\kappa$), and then introduces the scale transformation method to diagonalize the effective matrix, enabling robust reconstruction.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hamiltonian estimation is an effective approach in studying the structure and dynamical evolution of quantum systems. The difficulty in estimating the Hamiltonian is that an $N$-qubit Hamiltonian has $4^N-1$ unknown parameters, requiring exponentially many equations for information extraction. In this paper we develop a method based on compressed sensing to estimate the Hamiltonian of a multi-qubit system. We identify a problem where as $N$ increases, the common sufficient condition (Restricted Isometry Property) for compressed sensing often fails, obstructing the application of compressed sensing in ($N\geq 3$)-qubit Hamiltonian estimation. To solve this problem, we propose a ``scale transformation" technique to restore RIP and ensure a compressive estimation of a $k$-sparse Hamiltonian using only $O(k\log(4^N/k))$ equations. In the numerical examples, we estimate the Hamiltonians of two 6- and 30-qubit systems, demonstrating the effectiveness of the method.

</details>

**Summary.** This work theoretically explains the anomalous sign reversal in the Hall coefficient observed in nickelate superconductors. By combining correlated electron theory with detailed scattering calculations, the authors pinpoint that the effect is due to oxygen vacancies selectively disrupting the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital's contribution to transport. This provides a crucial link between material stoichiometry and macroscopic electronic properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on strongly correlated materials, the detailed treatment of transport coefficients (like R_H) using advanced many-body techniques provides a rigorous framework for understanding how local disorder (vacancies) selectively perturbs orbital character and electronic transport channels.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to determine the microscopic origin of Hall coefficient (R_H) sign reversals observed in superconducting bilayer nickelate films.

**Main result.** The sign reversal is attributed to orbital-selective scattering caused by oxygen vacancies, specifically showing that in-plane vacancies selectively suppress the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital contribution, driving R_H through zero.

**Method.** A correlated multi-orbital quasiparticle model derived from DFT+CDMFT is combined with a T-matrix treatment of scattering potentials within a semiclassical Boltzmann transport framework.

**Model / system.** The system is superconducting bilayer nickelate films containing oxygen vacancies. The theoretical framework involves calculating transport properties using pocket-resolved contributions and modeling the vacancy potential via first-principles DFT calculations.

**Key observables.** Hall coefficient (R_H), longitudinal conductivity ($\sigma_{aa}$), and orbital-selective Hall contributions ($R_r^H$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Oxygen-vacancy concentration ($n_{	ext{vac}}$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the specific type/location of vacancies (in-plane vs. inner-apical).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a dilute-vacancy limit, uses the scalar relaxation-time approximation for scattering rates, and separates rigid-band doping effects from vacancy-induced changes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate quasiparticle Fermi surfaces showing multiple pockets ($\alpha, eta, \gamma$) and plot R_H vs. $n_{	ext{vac}}$, demonstrating how different vacancy distributions cause the sign reversal through orbital suppression.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes that doping alone fails to explain the sign reversal. It then develops a comprehensive model incorporating orbital selectivity via DFT+CDMFT and T-matrix scattering theory, culminating in quantitative predictions showing the specific role of in-plane vacancies.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hall measurements in superconducting bilayer nickelate films show sign reversals that cannot be explained by rigid-band electron doping alone. We combine a DFT+CDMFT-derived correlated multi-orbital quasiparticle model with a $T$-matrix treatment of oxygen-vacancy scattering in a semiclassical Boltzmann transport framework. We find that multiband compensation is insufficient by itself: in-plane vacancies selectively suppress the transport channel dominated by the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital and drive $R_H$ through zero, whereas inner-apical vacancies make $R_H$ more negative. These results identify pocket-resolved and orbital-selective oxygen-vacancy scattering as the microscopic origin of the Hall coefficient sign reversal and provide a framework for oxygen-stoichiometry-dependent transport in nickelate films.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents an integrated theoretical framework connecting the electrostatics of complex CMOS quantum devices to their correlated electronic structure. By developing the accurate PK-GF model, the authors can calculate the confinement potential and then use advanced many-body techniques (UHF/CASCI) to predict spin filling and charge localization in silicon quantum dots. This establishes a vital tool for designing next-generation solid-state qubits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it bridges solid-state device physics (CMOS lithography) directly into advanced quantum many-body theory, providing a crucial, auditable computational pipeline for designing qubits based on semiconductor platforms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is developing a unified, end-to-end modeling framework that connects lithographic CMOS gate geometry electrostatics to the resulting many-electron spin and charge filling in quantum dots.

**Main result.** The authors successfully developed the Poisson-kernel coupled-interface Green-function (PK-GF) model, which accurately predicts device electrostatics at millivolt scales. Furthermore, they showed that the system operates in an interaction-dominated, Wigner-molecule-like regime, supporting low-spin ground states consistent with experiments.

**Method.** The methodology combines advanced analytical electrostatics (PK-GF) to determine the confinement potential, which is then fed into correlated many-body quantum calculations using Unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) and Complete Active-Space Configuration Interaction (CASCI).

**Model / system.** The system modeled is an asymmetric multi-gate silicon quantum dot fabricated within a CMOS architecture. The Hamiltonian incorporates Coulomb interactions, spin, and valley degrees of freedom, treating the gate potential as derived directly from device electrostatics.

**Key observables.** Spin density maps, charge localization (Wigner-molecule tendencies), ground state spin ($S=0$ support), addition energy spectrum, and the interaction-to-level-spacing ratio ($R$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electron number ($N = 2-17$), magnetic field ($B = 5 	ext{ T}$), and electrostatic potential derived from gate voltages.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The PK-GF model assumes a specific coupling between interfaces, and while UHF is used for calculation, the authors note it may overestimate spin polarization compared to CASCI results. The convergence of the singlet-triplet gap is noted as potentially incomplete.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the analytical PK-GF potential against independent Finite Volume (FV) solutions at millivolt scales; they also show charge density lobe profiles, pair correlation functions, and energy level comparisons between UHF and CASCI for different electron numbers.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the electrostatics by introducing and validating the PK-GF model against FV solvers. It then passes this derived potential into a spin-valley many-body calculation using UHF/CASCI to determine correlated electronic properties, culminating in an end-to-end workflow demonstration.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In advanced complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) quantum chips, compact gate stacks make it difficult to connect lithographic geometry, electrostatic confinement and many-electron spin filling in one transparent model. This connection is central to design-technology co-optimization (DTCO). Here we develop a reduced-order analytical framework for asymmetric multigate silicon quantum-dot devices. Its electrostatic core, the Poisson-kernel coupled-interface Green-function (PK-GF) model, agrees with an independent finite-volume solution at the millivolt scale for the matched two-dimensional problem, without fitting to that solution. We then pass the gate-derived confinement, rather than a harmonic or fitted potential, to a spin-valley many-body calculation for a jellybean quantum dot with N = 2-17 electrons at B = 5 T. The unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) solution supports occupation-dependent, Wigner-molecule-like charge localization but likely overestimates spin polarization. Complete active-space configuration interaction (CASCI) supports a low-spin branch within the tested active spaces, which aligns with the experiments. The workflow therefore connects CMOS layout, device electrostatics, and potential-determined quantum observables, providing an auditable modelling layer for CMOS-based qubit design and DTCO.

</details>

**Authors:** Emmanuel Giner  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** other · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.03909v1>

**Summary.** This paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework to derive the core structures of quantum mechanics—including Klein-Gordon dynamics and Poincaré symmetry—entirely from a classical phonon model using Poisson brackets. It achieves this by demonstrating that a specific complex change of variables maps classical Poisson brackets directly onto fundamental quantum commutators, establishing deep formal equivalence between classical and quantum descriptions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly abstract and fundamental theoretical bridge between classical Hamiltonian mechanics (Poisson brackets) and quantum field theory (commutators), which is valuable for understanding quantization procedures beyond standard canonical methods.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to derive the full algebra of quantum mechanics, including Klein-Gordon dynamics and the Poincaré group structure, starting purely from a classical framework.

**Main result.** The paper establishes a strict mathematical equivalence between the Heisenberg formalism (quantum commutators) and the continuous Poisson bracket formalism by utilizing a non-local complex change of variables.

**Method.** It employs the classical phonon model to define continuous Poisson brackets, which are then systematically related to quantum commutators via functional analysis and canonical quantization procedures.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using a classical phonon lattice (related to the Frenkel-Kontorova model) whose continuum limit yields dynamics governed by equations leading to the Klein-Gordon equation. The formalism progresses from real-valued classical observables to complex quantum operators.

**Key observables.** Klein-Gordon fields, Poisson brackets $\{F, G\}$, commutators $[\hat{O}_F, \hat{O}_G]$, and Poincaré group generators ($H, X, P$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The continuum limit parameters (e.g., $N	o\infty, a	o 0$) and the scaling factors used to connect classical variables to quantum operators are crucial.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on assuming that a non-local complex change of variables can bridge the gap between real-valued classical dynamics and complex quantum field theory structures.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical lattice model (Frenkel-Kontorova) and later show abstract mathematical representations of group transformations using matrix forms for the Poincaré algebra generators.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a progression: first establishing classical dynamics via phonons; then introducing Poisson brackets to derive Ehrenfest relations; next, performing a complex change of variables to link $\{., .\}$ to $[\cdot, \cdot]$; finally, applying this structure to recover the full Poincaré algebra in 1+1 dimensions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the first part of this series we have shown how the Schrodinger equation for a single particle and the corresponding non relativistic quantum observables can be obtained from a purely classical phonon model through the Newtonian equations of motion. In this work we focus instead on how the classical Hamiltonian formalism applied to the same phonon system allows to recover the feature of relativistic quantum mechanics for a single spinless particle. Using the classical nature of the phonon model, we naturally define continuous Poisson brackets between classical observables, which allows to recover the dynamics of such observables, i.e. the Ehrenfest relations associated to real-valued Klein-Gordon fields. The Poisson brackets also permits to obtain the generic form of constants of motions, thus generalizing the concept of inner products and momentum on Klein-Gordon fields. We then connect the formalism of real-valued classical functionals with that of hermitian operators and complex-valued wave functions. This is done through the introduction of a non-local complex-valued change of variables which allows to rewrite the real-valued Klein-Gordon equation in a form akin to the Schrodinger equation, and the classical observables as quantum expectation values. Then, we show how this change of variables allows to rewrite the classical Poisson brackets as commutators of hermitian operators. This points out the strict equivalence between the Heisenberg formalism and the formalism of classical Poisson bracket. Eventually, we illustrate how the Poisson brackets allows to recover the transformations of Poincaré group in 1+1 dimension together with its algebra. The latter makes the link between the Lorentz invariant inner product of Mostafazadeh and the Casimir invariant associated to the mass of particle.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper compares bosonic pairing theory against standard Bogoliubov theory for two-component Bose gases approaching the droplet regime. By analyzing observables like the grand potential and static structure factors, the authors show that bosonic pairing predicts distinct correlation signatures not captured by Bogoliubov theory. This suggests that low-momentum measurements in trapped atomic systems can experimentally validate alternative microscopic descriptions of quantum matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous theoretical tool to distinguish between competing descriptions of quantum many-body physics near phase transitions, offering concrete predictions for experimental measurements like Bragg spectroscopy on ultracold atomic gases.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper compares two theoretical frameworks, Bogoliubov theory and bosonic pairing theory, to describe two-component Bose gases across the crossover from a weakly interacting gas to the droplet regime.

**Main result.** Bosonic pairing theory predicts lower grand potentials and distinct correlation signatures—such as enhanced low-momentum interspecies correlations—compared to Bogoliubov theory. These differences suggest that structure factor measurements can experimentally distinguish between the two descriptions.

**Method.** The authors reformulate bosonic pairing theory using an operator formalism and compare its predictions for various observables against those derived from standard Bogoliubov mean-field theory, including fluctuation corrections.

**Model / system.** The system is a homogeneous binary Bose mixture with tunable interactions. The comparison focuses on how the theories handle quantum fluctuations when attractive interspecies interactions lead to droplet formation.

**Key observables.** Grand potential ($\Omega$), excitation spectrum, species-resolved static structure factors ($S_{ij}(q)$), and two-body correlation functions ($G^{(2)}_{12}(r)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction strengths (especially attractive interspecies coupling $g_{12}$), particle density, and momentum transfer ($q$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Bogoliubov theory is compared to bosonic pairing theory in regimes where both possess real excitation spectra. The comparison highlights the limitations of Bogoliubov theory when dealing with spectral instabilities (soft modes).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate $G^{(2)}_{12}(r)$ showing differences in antibunching, and species-resolved static structure factors $S_{ij}(q)$, which show a measurable contrast ratio between the two theories at low momentum.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the theoretical frameworks by deriving key quantities (like the grand potential and correlation functions) using both methods, culminating in a direct comparison of observable signatures across the gas-to-droplet crossover.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Two-component bosonic droplets are commonly described within Bogoliubov theory, where beyond-mean-field quantum fluctuations stabilize the system against mean-field collapse. In the interaction regime where droplets form, however, the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum contains an imaginary branch associated with the underlying instability, which is typically omitted when evaluating the beyond-mean-field energy. Bosonic pairing theory provides an alternative description with a fully real excitation spectrum. In this work, we reformulate bosonic pairing theory within an operator formalism, making its underlying approximations transparent, and compare its predictions with those of Bogoliubov theory for a homonuclear binary Bose mixture across the crossover from a weakly interacting gas to the droplet regime. Working at fixed particle density, we determine the variational parameters of bosonic pairing theory self-consistently and focus on the regime in which both theories possess real excitation spectra, allowing a direct comparison. We find that bosonic pairing theory yields a lower grand potential than Bogoliubov theory and predicts qualitatively distinct correlation signatures, including enhanced long-wavelength interspecies momentum-space correlations and a finite density static structure factor at experimentally accessible low momenta. These differences persist over a broad range of interaction strengths and suggest that correlation and structure-factor measurements can provide direct experimental tests of bosonic pairing across the gas-to-droplet crossover.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main result.** The authors propose and prove a novel framework showing that an arbitrary N-qubit pure state can be uniquely parameterized using exactly 2N-1 spheres, providing a strict bijection to the standard state vector representation.

**Method.** The methodology involves generalizing the geometric concept of the Bloch sphere by deriving parameterizations for two and three qubits based on controlled rotation gates. This leads to establishing a unique normal form for the state vector through sequential phase elimination and amplitude setting using unitary transformations.

**Model / system.** The system under study is an N-qubit quantum state, $|	ext{Q}angle$, whose representation is mapped onto a geometric structure involving multiple interconnected spheres. <details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Bloch sphere is an elegant tool for representing single-qubit states. However, a widely accepted generalization for multi-qubit systems with entanglement remains absent. We propose a novel geometric model extending the Bloch sphere representation to arbitrary $N$-qubit systems using $2^N-1$ spheres. We demonstrate that any pure 2-qubit state is uniquely described by three spheres: two for individual qubits and a third encapsulating bipartite entanglement. Generalizing this, we establish an $N$-qubit parameterization through the hierarchical application of controlled rotation gates along the $Z$ and $Y$ axes. We formally prove a strict bijection between the standard state vector representation and our model's angular parameters. This framework provides an intuitive visualization of multiple entanglement, offering potential computational advantages for quantum simulators and new analytical perspectives on quantum gates.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analytically characterizes cross-click operators used in analyzing photodetection processes for quantum key distribution. By showing these operators are related to symmetric tensor powers, the authors derive exact formulas for spectral properties like monotonicity and convergence rates. This breakthrough replaces complex Fock-space numerics with general, closed-form bounds essential for rigorous QKD security proofs.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous analytical tools to quantify security loopholes in QKD protocols caused by detector imperfections, moving beyond computationally intensive numerical simulations into closed-form physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To provide a sharp analytic characterization of the spectral behavior of cross-click operators in passive multi-basis photodetection for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security proofs.

**Main result.** The work establishes monotonicity, two-sided exponential bounds, and exact factorization formulas for these operators, replacing finite-sector numerical calculations with closed-form analytical results.

**Method.** The analysis leverages the structural property that silence operators are second quantizations of explicit single-photon contractions, allowing properties to be derived from tensor algebra and operator inequalities.

**Model / system.** The system models passive linear-optical analyzers using threshold single-photon detectors, applicable to polarization, time-bin, or spatial-mode qubits in QKD setups.

**Key observables.** The minimum eigenvalue of the cross-click operator on the n-photon subspace, $f^{(n)}$, and related quantities like $1 - f(n)$ for the no-cross-click operator.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Detector efficiencies ($\eta_d$), dark-count probabilities ($\epsilon_d$), and the photon number ($n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results hold for arbitrary passive analyzers with specified parameters, assuming independent dark counts and uncorrelated efficiencies; afterpulsing breaks the product structure.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate a running example (six-state polarization analyzer) showing cross-click probability $f(n)$ versus photon number, tracking the closed-form convergence rate $\max_b \|A_b\|$, and visualizing joint operator factorization $f(n_A, n_B)$.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops its findings by first establishing the structural lemma for silence operators, then proving monotonicity (Theorem 1), deriving two-sided exponential bounds (Theorem 2) to find the exact convergence rate, and finally presenting special cases like ideal detectors and joint operator factorization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Cross-click operators, the POVM elements for simultaneous clicks in detectors assigned to different measurement bases, are used in QKD and entanglement-verification analyses with realistic threshold detectors to bound multiphoton contributions. Earlier applications verified the needed growth of the minimum eigenvalue $f^{(n)}$ on the $n$-photon subspace only numerically over finite sectors. This work gives an analytic characterization for passive linear-optical analyzers with arbitrary efficiency mismatch and dark counts. The key observation is that every silence operator is the second quantization $Γ(A)$ of an explicit single-photon contraction $A$, whose $n$-photon restriction is $A^{\otimes n}$ on $\mathrm{Sym}^n$. This yields: (i) monotonicity $f^{(n+1)}\ge f^{(n)}$; (ii) two-sided exponential bounds $\max_b γ_b|A_b|^n \le 1-f^{(n)} \le \sum_b γ_b|A_b|^n$, which determine the exact asymptotic convergence rate from single-photon spectral data; (iii) for ideal detectors and $n\ge1$, the exact formula $f^{(n)}=1-\sum_b p_b^n$; and (iv) an exact factorization $1-f^{(n_A,n_B)}=(1-f_A^{(n_A)})(1-f_B^{(n_B)})$ for the two-party cross-click operator. The results apply to polarization, time-bin, and spatial-mode analyzers within the stated threshold-detector model. As an application, we obtain closed-form photon-number weight bounds used in detection-efficiency-mismatch analyses, replacing finite-sector Fock-space numerics by formulas valid for all photon numbers.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper establishes a highly general mathematical framework for analyzing Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) using commuting operators. It overcomes limitations in previous work by employing advanced tools from operator algebras to handle arbitrary environments. The result provides rigorous security bounds by casting the key rate calculation into a solvable Non-Commutative Polynomial Optimization problem.

**Why it may be interesting.** It pushes the boundaries of quantum information theory by providing security proofs that are robust against uncharacterized devices and complex environmental interactions, which is crucial for realizing practical quantum technologies.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a maximally general mathematical framework for analyzing Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) security that avoids restrictive assumptions on the underlying Hilbert space structure.

**Main result.** The authors provide a representation-independent route to derive AEP-based security statements by utilizing the commuting operator framework, proving key results like the projectivity of measurements w.l.o.g.

**Method.** The work employs advanced tools from operator algebras (C*-algebras, von Neumann algebras) and casts the key rate computation as a Non-Commutative Polynomial Optimization (NPO) problem solvable via the NPA hierarchy.

**Model / system.** The system is DIQKD involving two parties (Alice and Bob). The mathematical model uses universal C*-algebras to represent local measurements, allowing for rigorous analysis of security even when Eve's side information requires general von Neumann algebras.

**Key observables.** Key rates, conditional von Neumann entropy, observed input-output statistics ($ho_{AB}$)

**Important parameters / regimes.** The framework is designed to be general regarding the structure of the underlying Hilbert space and environment description (e.g., type-III algebra for Eve).

**Assumptions / limitations.** It addresses and overcomes limitations in existing proofs that rely on specific tensor product structures or assume measurements are always projective.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the general DIQKD experimental setup involving local Random Number Generators (RNGs) used by Alice and Bob to generate output statistics.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from reviewing necessary algebraic concepts (C*-algebras, states, traces) before detailing the DIQKD formulation in Section 5. It introduces technical tools like generalized relative entropy formulas for von Neumann algebras and applies these to the NPO problem.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) is arguably the gold standard for secure quantum communication, as it aims to rely only on observed input-output statistics of an uncharacterized device which is only assumption to obey the laws of quantum physics. A corresponding security analysis hence demands a description of a quantum experiment from a most general perspective. Under close inspection, existing proof techniques do not always meet this goal as they tend to rely on subtile assumptions on a tensor product structure of the underlying Hilbert space and a 'hidden but finite' dimensionality. In this work, we collect the tools needed for a full analysis of DIQKD in the commuting operator framework, which avoids these subtilities and provides the arguably most general view on a quantum experiment. We rigorously proof the common assumption that in DIQKD measurements can be w.l.o.g. assumed to be projective. Furthermore, we show that task of computing key rates can be casted as a non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problem to which the Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy gives a correct and converging relaxation.   As a tool, we generalize the integral representation for the relative entropy by Frenkel [Quantum 7, 1102 (2023)] to general von Neumann algebras and apply techniques from Kossmann and Schwonnek [arXiv: 2411.04858] for the approximation in an NPO program.

</details>
