**Summary.** This paper develops a framework to analyze how quantum subspaces evolve over time by factoring the Schrödinger equation into dynamical and geometric parts. The authors demonstrate that this separation fails because the resulting 'quasi-connection' retains a history-dependent term, proving that geometry and dynamics are fundamentally intertwined in this setting. This offers a deep gauge-theoretic understanding of non-adiabatic subspace evolution.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous geometric/gauge-theoretic perspective on open quantum systems dynamics, directly addressing the fundamental question of separability in time evolution that is crucial for understanding decoherence or adiabatic approximations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is investigating whether the quantum time evolution of subspaces can be cleanly separated into purely geometric (holonomic) and dynamical components.

**Main result.** The authors show that this separation fails in general because the effective quasi-connection depends explicitly on the history of the dynamical propagator, indicating an inherent intertwining of geometric and dynamic effects.

**Method.** They develop a framework by factoring the Schrödinger evolution into dynamical and connection-induced parts using a moving basis along paths in the complex Grassmannian.

**Model / system.** The model concerns the time evolution of $M$-dimensional subspaces within an $N$-dimensional Hilbert space, mathematically described as paths on the complex Grassmannian $	ext{Gr}(N; M)$ governed by a matrix differential equation.

**Key observables.** The quasi-connection $	ext{AD}(t)$, which is used to diagnose the failure of separation from standard connection forms.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cyclic evolution (loops) and the time dependence of the Hamiltonian/generators $K(t)$ and $A(t)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on factoring the propagator using a moving basis, but the core limitation is the history-dependence of the resulting quasi-connection.

**Figures summary.** Not specified by the notes.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem via the Schrödinger equation factorization, derives the quasi-holonomy generator $	ext{AD}(t)$, proves it fails to be a true connection due to history dependence, and discusses conditions under which separation might occur (e.g., commutativity).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a framework for quasi-holonomy in non-adiabatic quantum time evolution of subspaces along loops in a complex Grassmannian. By factoring the Schrödinger evolution into dynamical and connection-induced contributions in a moving basis, we obtain an effective geometric generator that depends explicitly on the dynamical propagator. This quasi-connection does not define a genuine connection on the original Grassmann bundle, since its gauge transformation law acquires a history-dependent, nonlocal term. Other ways of factoring the Schrödinger evolution are briefly discussed. All these approaches suffer from the same type of history-dependence, thereby defining transport of subspaces in which geometric and dynamical effects are generally intertwined, just as in the case of the quasi-holonomy. Our work sheds light on the issue of separating quantum evolution of subspaces into holonomic and dynamical parts from an essentially gauge-theoretic perspective.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports the first experimental evidence for a thermodynamically equilibrated Supercritical Fluid (SCF) phase at the Mott transition in superconducting fullerides. By simultaneously analyzing electrical conductivity and magnetic susceptibility, the authors establish two distinct but converging MIT lines meeting at a Mott endpoint. This dual-probe approach provides a unified picture of the correlated electron physics underlying high-$T_c$ superconductivity.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous combination of transport ($\sigma$) and magnetic ($\chi$) probes to characterize a single quantum critical point provides a powerful methodology for studying strongly correlated electron physics that transcends limitations of single-observable analyses.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the elusive supercritical fluid (SCF) phase of quantum electrons at the Mott metal-insulator transition (MIT) in strongly correlated systems without symmetry breaking.

**Main result.** The authors report the first experimental identification of a thermodynamically equilibrated SCF phase and its associated Mott endpoint using superconducting fullerides, unifying insights from both electrical conductivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements.

**Method.** A dual-probe approach combining independent measurements of electrical conductivity ($\sigma$) and magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$), along with hypothesis-free two-particle analysis (Widom line) and scaling analysis, was employed.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the three-dimensional superconducting fulleride $	ext{Cs}_x	ext{Rb}_{3-x}	ext{C}_{60}$. Theoretical modeling involves effective spin Hamiltonians and analyzing electronic state degeneracies related to $t_{1u}$-orbitals.

**Key observables.** Electrical conductivity ($\sigma$), magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$), critical exponents ($z
u$), Mott endpoint (MEP), and the superconducting $	ext{T}_c$-dome structure.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Stoichiometry ($x$ in $	ext{Cs}_x	ext{Rb}_{3-x}	ext{C}_{60}$), temperature ($T$), pressure ($P$), and unit cell volume ($V_{	ext{cell}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the existence of a thermodynamically equilibrated SCF phase, which is characterized by maximizing two-phase mixing entropy in magnetic susceptibility measurements.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the convergence of distinct MIT lines from $\sigma$ and $\chi$ at an MEP, mapping out the SCF zone on T-V diagrams, and comparing theoretical models to experimental data across various stoichiometries.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the physical problem (SCF at Mott transition), then presenting the dual-probe methodology using fullerides, analyzing both $\sigma$ and $\chi$ measurements independently, and finally synthesizing these results into a unified microscopic picture of the M-I coexisting SCF phase.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The supercritical fluid (SCF) of quantum electrons at the Mott metal-insulator transition without symmetry breaking is one of the most elusive phenomena in strongly correlated electron physics. Prior studies of Cr-doped V2O3 and organic Mott systems reported discrepant critical exponents. A key limitation is that the scaling analysis relies on a single experimental observable, leaving the roles of phase coexistence, inhomogeneity, and percolation unaddressed. Here we report the first experimental identification of a thermodynamically equilibrated SCF phase and its associated Mott endpoint in the three-dimensional superconducting fullerides CsxRb3-xC60, using two independent probes of electrical conductivity and magnetic susceptibility, which reveal two distinct metal-insulator transition lines converging at a single Mott endpoint. A hypothesis-free two-particle analysis of magnetic susceptibilities yields a metal-insulator coexisting SCF by exhibiting the maximum two-phase mixing entropy, in agreement with a picture of a thermodynamically equilibrated Widom line. Simultaneously, conductivity scaling yields a critical exponent in the regime of quantum critical predictions. Our new dual-probe approach provides a unified microscopic picture of the Mott SCF with a characteristic length scale below current diffraction resolution, in addition to a new interpretation on the origin of superconducting Tc-dome.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates that while 1D quantum walks can mimic gapless Dirac physics with preserved symmetries, their 2D counterparts are fundamentally unstable. The authors prove that generic potential scattering terms break the necessary protecting symmetries, leading to the opening of a gap at zero energy for the Dirac cone.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous lattice model framework for understanding how topological protection, robust in continuum models, breaks down when discretized into higher dimensions due to the constraints of locality and symmetry on the underlying quantum walk operator.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether a two-dimensional (2D) Dirac quantum walk, analogous to continuum physics models like graphene, retains topological protection against gapping induced by potential scattering or disorder.

**Main result.** Unlike the 1D case, the 2D Dirac quantum walk is fundamentally fragile; its unpaired $\epsilon=0$ cone can be gapped by generic spatial inhomogeneities or potentials due to symmetry constraints imposed by locality.

**Method.** The authors analyze the system using Floquet theory and examine the symmetries (chiral and time-reversal) of the lattice Hamiltonian. They employ mathematical tools involving Laurent polynomials to constrain the existence of gapless points.

**Model / system.** The model is a local two-band quantum walk implemented on a $(2+1)$-dimensional space-time lattice, whose continuum limit approximates the massless Dirac equation. Specific realizations include Palindromic, Squared, and Ho-Chalker quantum walks.

**Key observables.** Quasi-energies ($\epsilon_n$), gap size ($\Delta$) at $\epsilon=0$, and the preservation/breaking of chiral and time-reversal symmetries.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The strength and periodicity ($\mathbf{Q}$) of applied potentials ($V$ or $M$), which act as disorder terms.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis primarily focuses on local, two-band spin-1/2 implementations and assumes the potential scattering is short-range correlated.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the momentum dependence of quasi-energies showing gap opening for various potentials (e.g., staggered potentials), confirming the gapping effect on the Dirac cone.

**Paper structure.** The paper contrasts the robust 1D case with the fragile 2D case, demonstrating symmetry breakdown under disorder. It systematically tests different quantum walk constructions (Palindromic, Ho-Chalker) against specific potential scattering terms to prove gap opening.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It is known that a one-dimensional (1D) quantum walk gives a local space-time discretization of the massless Dirac equation with a single quasi-energy cone (no fermion doubling at low energies), keeping the fundamental symmetries (chiral and time-reversal) of the continuum theory. We show that the analogous 2D construction is fundamentally more fragile. Local two-band quantum walks can have an unpaired Dirac cone, but the protecting symmetries then cease to be ordinary on-site symmetries: they become non-symmorphic, involving half-lattice translations, and are broken by generic spatial inhomogeneities. In particular, we demonstrate that the 2D Dirac quantum walk based on the Ho-Chalker network model can be gapped by potential scattering.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes the Trace-to-Hilbert-Schmidt Speed Ratio ($\mathcal R$) for evolving quantum states. It derives sharp universal bounds on $\mathcal R$ based on the operator's rank, establishing that this ratio serves as an effective-rank diagnostic for local quantum dynamics. The results provide new constraints on quantum speed limits by linking them to spectral properties like the effective rank and QFI.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental mathematical constraints on the rate of change of quantum states, linking geometric measures (norms) directly to spectral properties (effective rank), which is crucial for understanding measurement precision and dynamical limitations in open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the Trace-to-Hilbert-Schmidt Speed Ratio, $\mathcal R$, for differentiable quantum states to establish universal bounds on local quantum dynamics.

**Main result.** Sharp bounds are established: $\sqrt{2} \le \mathcal R \le \sqrt{r}$ for a tangent operator of rank $r$, with a global maximum bound derived for odd-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The ratio is identified as an effective-rank diagnostic.

**Method.** The analysis relies on bounding the ratio of two norms ($\|\cdot\|_1 / \|\cdot\|_2$) applied to the Hermitian, traceless tangent operator $X = \partial_\phiho$, utilizing spectral properties and elementary inequalities.

**Model / system.** The study concerns a differentiable family of finite-dimensional quantum states $ho(\phi)$ evolving in time or parameter $\phi$. The dynamics are characterized by the tangent operator $X = \partial_\phiho$, which is constrained to be Hermitian and traceless.

**Key observables.** Trace Speed ($\|\cdot\|_1$), Hilbert-Schmidt Speed ($\|\cdot\|_2$), Trace-to-Hilbert-Schmidt Speed Ratio ($\mathcal R$), Effective Rank ($r_{	ext{eff}}$), Quantum Fisher Information (QFI).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension of the Hilbert space ($d$) and the rank ($r$) of the tangent operator are key parameters determining the bounds.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to nonstationary points where the tangent operator $X$ is non-zero, and it heavily leverages the Hermitian and traceless nature of $X$.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining $\mathcal R$, deriving bounds based on the rank $r$ (establishing $\sqrt{2} \le \mathcal R \le \sqrt{r}$), proving a sharper global bound for odd dimensions, and finally interpreting $\mathcal R^2$ as an effective-rank diagnostic linked to QFI and quantum speed limits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the ratio between the trace speed and the Hilbert-Schmidt speed for differentiable finite-dimensional quantum states, $\mathcal R(φ)=\|\partial_φρ(φ)\|_1/\|\partial_φρ(φ)\|_2$. Because $\partial_φρ(φ)$ is always Hermitian and traceless, this ratio is constrained more strongly than for a generic operator. For any nonzero tangent operator $X=\partial_φρ$ of rank $r$, we prove the sharp bounds $\sqrt{2}\le \|X\|_1/\|X\|_2\le \sqrt r$. The lower bound is attained exactly for rank-two tangents, while the upper bound is attained exactly when all nonzero singular values are equal, which in the traceless Hermitian setting requires even rank. At every nonstationary point of a pure-state family, the tangent has rank two, implying $\mathcal R=\sqrt2$. For odd Hilbert-space dimension $d$, we further prove the sharp global maximum $\mathcal R\le \sqrt{d-1/d}$, with equality characterized by full-rank spectra whose positive and negative eigenvalues are separately degenerate and have multiplicities differing by one. We identify $\mathcal R^2$ as the inverse participation ratio of the singular-value distribution of the tangent operator, giving $\mathcal R$ a natural interpretation as an effective-rank diagnostic for local quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we decompose the effective rank into classical (eigenvalue) and quantum (eigenvector) contributions and prove the bound $r_{\mathrm{eff}}\le r_C + r_Q$, with equality guaranteed when either component vanishes. We establish a direct inequality linking the effective rank to the quantum Fisher information (QFI), which forces a large number of active singular modes when the QFI is small relative to the squared trace speed. Finally, we derive a hierarchy of quantum speed limits in which the effective rank controls the tightness of bounds expressed through the Hilbert-Schmidt speed.

</details>

**Summary.** This work applies high-precision ab initio calculations using Bogoliubov Coupled-Cluster theory to determine the binding energies of tin isotopes near the neutron drip line. By incorporating triples correlations, the authors significantly improve theoretical accuracy and map out how nuclear structure predictions conflict with existing Energy Density Functional models regarding exotic nuclei.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on nuclear physics, the use of advanced many-body quantum field theory techniques (like coupled-cluster expansions) to solve complex Hamiltonians shares conceptual overlap with methods used in strongly correlated electron systems or open quantum system dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To perform high-precision ab initio calculations of nuclear binding energies for tin isotopes across the neutron drip line.

**Main result.** The predicted location of the neutron drip line is highly sensitive to the employed nuclear interactions and shows tension with recent Energy Density Functional predictions. The inclusion of triples corrections significantly improves accuracy by reducing uncertainty from tens of MeV to below 3 MeV in key isotopes.

**Method.** Bogoliubov Coupled-Cluster (BCC) theory, specifically utilizing the BCCSD[T] approximation to account for leading three-body correlations beyond standard CCSD calculations.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on even-even Tin (Sn) isotopes ($Z=50$) ranging from $N=50$ up to $N=126$. Calculations are based on realistic chiral Effective Field Theory ($\chi$EFT) two- and three-nucleon interactions.

**Key observables.** Binding energies ($E_0$), two-neutron separation energies ($S_{2n}$), and the predicted location of the neutron drip line.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The calculations use a spherical harmonic oscillator basis ($\hbar\omega = 12$ MeV) and are sensitive to the specific $\chi$EFT Hamiltonian employed (e.g., $1.8/2.0 (	ext{EM})$ vs. $\Delta-	ext{N}2	ext{LOGO}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary approximations involve truncating the cluster expansion at BCCSD[T] and using a specific basis set, leading to residual uncertainties from missing higher-body correlations ($T_{k\ge 4}$) and basis incompleteness.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares ground-state energies calculated with BCCSD vs. BCCSD[T] against experimental values for Sn isotopes; Figure 2 and 3 show $S_{2n}$ around the $N=50$ shell closure and beyond $N=82$, respectively.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical framework of BCC theory, progresses from BCCSD to the improved BCCSD[T] approximation by solving for triples correlations non-iteratively, applies this method to calculate binding energies across the Sn isotopic chain, and discusses the implications for nuclear structure models like EDFs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The location of the neutron drip line in tin isotopes has important consequences for our fundamental understanding of nuclear structure and nuclear forces as well as for astrophysical nucleosynthesis. Performing high-precision ab initio calculations of even-even tin isotopes from $N=50$ to $N=126$ based on chiral two- and three-nucleon interactions, the predicted drip-line location is found to be highly sensitive to the employed nuclear interactions and to exhibit tension with recent energy-density-functional predictions. On the neutron-deficient side, results are consistent with extrapolated two-neutron separation energies constrained by recent Penning-trap mass measurements.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces stellar braid monodromy as a powerful topological invariant for characterizing non-Gaussian bosonic photonic states. It shows that the space of these regular states has a fundamental group isomorphic to the Artin braid group. This invariant captures how the state's defining zeros move along a preparation path, offering a comprehensive tool complementary to existing quantum diagnostics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep geometric and topological tool (braid theory) to classify quantum states beyond simple measures like entanglement or negativity. For AMO/Quantum Optics, understanding how state properties change topologically under parameter variation is crucial for designing robust quantum protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a topological invariant, called stellar braid monodromy, that characterizes regular parameterized families of non-Gaussian bosonic states.

**Main result.** The regular stratum of the finite-rank state space is biholomorphic to the unordered configuration space $	ext{Conf}_r(\mathbb{C})/\mathfrak{S}_r$, meaning its fundamental group is the Artin braid group $B_r$. The resulting monodromy provides a robust, path-dependent invariant complementing scalar measures of non-Gaussianity.

**Method.** The authors map the state space onto the configuration space of the stellar zeros by analyzing the motion of these zeros under continuous deformations (parameter loops). This movement is captured by calculating the braid monodromy homomorphism into the Artin braid group.

**Model / system.** The system involves single-mode bosonic Fock states, whose non-Gaussian structure is encoded by a finite stellar divisor in the Bargmann representation. The analysis is restricted to the regular stratum of these finite-rank states within the truncated Fock subspace $\mathcal{H}_r$.

**Key observables.** Braid monodromy (the full braid invariant), Stellar Rank, Wigner negativity, and the coefficients $(b_0, \dots, b_{r-1})$ defining the state in the finite-Fock chart.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The rank $r$ of the non-Gaussian state; the parameters defining the preparation loop or parameterized family.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is strictly limited to the 'regular' stratum where stellar zeros do not collide and no zero vanishes at infinity. The method does not directly address mixed states or multimode dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the mathematical framework by relating the state space to configuration spaces, deriving that the fundamental group is $B_r$. It then extends this concept to define the braid monodromy invariant for parameterized families of states, comparing it to existing diagnostics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Finite-rank non-Gaussian bosonic states admit a holomorphic description in the Bargmann representation: after a zero-free Gaussian factor is separated off, their non-Gaussian structure is encoded by a finite stellar divisor. This article introduces a topological refinement of stellar rank for regular parameterized families of such states. Rather than only counting the zeros of the stellar divisor, we follow their motion under deformations of the state and record the associated braid monodromy. In the finite-Fock chart, a regular degree-r stellar state is represented by a monic polynomial with r simple zeros. The regular stratum is biholomorphic to the unordered configuration space of r points in the complex plane, and its fundamental group is the Artin braid group on r strands. Thus braid monodromy is an intrinsic invariant of loops in the regular finite-rank stellar state space. We then extend the construction to admissible finite stellar divisors of the form E_tau,mu(z) P(z); the zero-free Gaussian parameters form a contractible fiber over the same configuration-space base. Experimentally motivated finite-Fock families, especially the cubic subspace spanned by the first four Fock states, provide concrete laboratories, while trinomial slices yield explicit discriminants and local half-twists. The resulting invariant is post-tomographic and applies to preparation loops and parameterized families; it complements Wigner negativity, stellar rank, approximate stellar rank, and other scalar diagnostics of non-Gaussianity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a unified diagrammatic framework to calculate the time evolution of moment operators for Brownian motion on orthogonal and symplectic Lie groups. By extending techniques from unitary ensembles, it derives explicit formulas for these moments up to fourth order. This work is vital for analyzing quantum chaos, thermalization, and transport in systems with particle-hole symmetry.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides powerful mathematical tools derived from random matrix theory that describe quantum dynamics in systems possessing specific symmetries (orthogonal/symplectic), which is crucial for understanding transport and chaos.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a unified diagrammatic framework to characterize Brownian ensembles for orthogonal and symplectic random matrices.

**Main result.** Explicit, complex formulas are derived for the time evolution of moment operators ($U_k(t)$) and their corresponding trace moments ($	ext{Tr}(V^k)$) up to fourth order.

**Method.** The calculation uses diagrammatic techniques based on extending methods from unitary ensembles to orthogonal and symplectic cases, involving tensor algebra and matrix exponentiation.

**Model / system.** The study concerns Brownian motion on the orthogonal $O(q)$ and symplectic $	ext{Sp}(q)$ groups. The dynamics are governed by moment operators derived from random matrices constrained by an antiunitary involution Z.

**Key observables.** Moment operators ($U_k(t)$), trace moments ($	ext{Tr}(V^k)$), spectral form factor, and frame potential.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension parameter $q$, the time variable $t$, and the order of the moment $k$ (up to 4).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on treating the problem using an antiunitary involution Z to unify the orthogonal and symplectic cases, and involves advanced tensor algebra related to the Brauer algebra.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows diagrammatic representations and multiplication rules for basis tensors in the orthogonal case; Figure 2 does the same for the symplectic case.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds systematically by calculating moment operators $U_k(t)$ and trace moments recursively, first establishing the general framework (k=1, 2) and then providing explicit, highly complex formulas for higher orders (k=3, k=4).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Matrix Brownian motion provides a powerful framework for studying crossover ensembles in quantum chaos and quantum transport, as well as thermalization and information scrambling in many-body dynamics. Here, we develop a unified diagrammatic framework to characterize Brownian ensembles for orthogonal and symplectic random matrices, which describe systems with particle-hole symmetry. We compute polynomial averages up to fourth order and construct an orthogonally invariant interpolation for the disconnected $\mathrm{SO}^-(q)$ sector of the orthogonal group. We consider applications relating to the fields of quantum information, quantum chaos, and quantum transport.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes integrating circuit design considerations, specifically using Hadamard Test constraints, into adaptive variational quantum algorithms. By doing so, it significantly reduces the measurement overhead required to build expressive ansätze for solving problems like the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. This systematic approach enhances the practical feasibility of running complex quantum simulations on current NISQ hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses practical limitations in quantum computation by providing algorithmic guidelines (circuit-aware ansatz construction) that improve resource scaling for simulating physical systems like those modeled by the NLSE.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing resource-efficient variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) suitable for the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era.

**Main result.** Incorporating circuit design constraints, such as those derived from the Hadamard Test architecture, can systematically reduce measurement overhead in adaptive VQA frameworks by 25% to 55%.

**Method.** The authors employ an adaptive variational framework that iteratively constructs hardware-aware ansätze while enforcing structural constraints on the candidate gate pool.

**Model / system.** The study applies these techniques to find the ground state of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE), which is discretized using a finite-difference method.

**Key observables.** State fidelity ($F' = 1 - |\langle\Psi_{	ext{target}}|\Psi_{	ext{var}}angle|^2$) and measurement overhead/required measurement resources.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nonlinearity strength ($g$), system size ($n$), and the depth of the variational ansatz layers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that incorporating constraints from hardware connectivity, HT structure, and non-redundancy is sufficient to guide the construction of expressive ansätze.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Hadamard test circuit, the scaling reduction of the gate pool size due to constraints, and comparisons showing adaptive ansätze achieving higher state fidelities than simple layered ones for the NLSE ground state.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for resource efficiency in NISQ devices. It then details the use of adaptive VQA frameworks applied to the NLSE ground state problem. The core contribution is demonstrating how circuit design constraints prune the gate pool, leading to significant overhead reduction while maintaining high fidelity compared to unconstrained or purely layered approaches.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Resource-efficient computation is of central importance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, where decoherence, gate errors, and restricted qubit connectivity severely limit the reliable execution of quantum algorithms. In this work, we demonstrate that incorporating circuit design considerations is crucial for developing resource-efficient variational quantum algorithms. By focusing on the Hadamard test circuit architecture, hardware-aware qubit connectivity, and problem-specific adaptive framework, we analyze how circuit design constraints can systematically reduce the measurement overhead associated with repeated evaluations of the candidate gate pool in adaptive algorithms. Specifically, we demonstrate reductions in the required measurement resources ranging from at least 25% to as high as 50% - 55%. To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we investigate the ground state problem of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Overall, our work contributes to resource-friendly strategies for quantum computation and underscores that algorithmic frameworks should systematically integrate circuit design constraints with hardware-aware and problem-specific structures to enhance the practical feasibility of quantum devices in the NISQ era.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper develops an effective field theory for noncritical M-theory by applying bosonization techniques to its microscopic description as a free fermion system. The authors validate this derived bosonic action by calculating correlation functions and showing they match predictions from the exact fermionic model in appropriate limits, advancing the understanding of spacetime gravity connections.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on string theory, the core methodology—bosonizing excitations around a Fermi surface (the coadjoint orbit approach)—is directly applicable to strongly correlated electron systems where low-energy physics is governed by collective modes near the Fermi level.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is constructing an effective spacetime gravity description for noncritical M-theory by relating it to its known microscopic definition as a free fermion system.

**Main result.** The authors derive an effective field theory using bosonization that successfully reproduces established results in lower dimensions (like the Das-Jevicki theory) and matches correlation functions calculated from the exact Fermi liquid description in the semiclassical limit.

**Method.** They extend the coadjoint orbit approach to bosonization, systematically comparing the resulting bosonic effective action with predictions derived from the underlying integrable structure of noncritical M-theory.

**Model / system.** The model is Noncritical M-theory, which is treated as a double-scaled $(2+1)$-dimensional nonrelativistic Fermi liquid. This system serves as a lower-dimensional analog for understanding string theory vacua and quantum gravity.

**Key observables.** Fermion density correlation functions (one-, two-, and three-point functions) are used to test the consistency between the effective field theory and the exact fermionic description.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis focuses on different dimensions ($1+1$d and $2+1$d), the semiclassical limit, and the underlying parameters defining the Fermi surface/potential.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key steps involve applying approximations like the stationary phase approximation to calculate resolvents and assuming suitability of gauge choices for dimensional reduction.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the double scaling limit zooming in on the quadratic maximum potential, showing the filled Fermi sea boundary corresponding to the static Fermi surface. Other figures compare exact resolvents with saddle point approximations.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically applies the coadjoint-orbit method to derive an effective bosonic action for bosonization of the Fermi surface. It then rigorously tests this action by calculating and comparing its correlation functions against known results from the exact fermionic theory, culminating in discussions about gravitational interpretations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We extend the coadjoint orbit approach to bosonization systematized by Delacretaz-Du-Mehta-Son to double-scaled non-relativistic Fermi liquids with central inverted harmonic oscillator potential. In 1+1d, this reproduces the Das-Jevicki collective field theory describing quasiparticle excitations of the $c=1$ matrix model. In 2+1d, this yields an effective field theory for noncritical M-theory, namely the 2+1d Fermi liquid proposed by Hořava and Keeler as a unified framework for characterizing noncritical string vacua. With a suitable gauge choice this theory reduces to a continuous family of 1+1d chiral bosons resembling Das-Jevicki collective fields coupled by additional interactions. Utilizing the underlying integrability of noncritical M-theory, we compute select fermion density correlation functions order-by-order in perturbation theory, and provide evidence that they agree with their Fermi liquid counterparts in a suitable semiclassical limit. This represents a step toward an effective spacetime gravity description of noncritical M-theory, which we expect to shed light on both the landscape of 2d noncritical strings and 3d quantum gravity in general.

**Summary.** This work develops a general fluctuation theory for competitive exploration processes by analyzing the fraction of first discoveries secured by one searcher. The key finding links the persistence of early advantages to the spectral dimension ($d_s$) of the underlying random walk, establishing a critical threshold at $d_s=2$ that dictates whether fluctuations are persistent or self-averaging.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of 'spectral dimension' controlling macroscopic fluctuation behavior is highly relevant to understanding anomalous transport in complex media, which has parallels in quantum many-body systems exhibiting fractal or disordered dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is determining whether early competitive advantages, measured by the 'discovery share' ($X_n$), persist or are erased over long exploration histories in a setting where multiple searchers compete for resources.

**Main result.** Self-averaging (convergence to $1/2$) occurs if and only if the spectral dimension $d_s$ of the underlying random walk is greater than or equal to 2, with specific power laws governing the variance decay in different regimes defined by $d_s$.

**Method.** The analysis involves deriving asymptotic fluctuation laws for the discovery share using tools from probability theory, specifically analyzing two-point correlations and scaling functions.

**Model / system.** The model is competitive exploration involving multiple searchers discovering sites on a lattice or space whose dynamics are characterized by the spectral dimension $d_s$. This framework is generalizable to various random walk types (e.g., Brownian motion, Lévy walks) and geometries.

**Key observables.** Discovery share ($X_n$), asymptotic variance ($	ext{Var}(X_n)$), two-point label correlations $	ext{Cov}(I_k, I_{k+\ell})$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Spectral dimension ($d_s$): controls the fluctuation regime; $d_s < 2$ (persistent randomness) vs. $d_s \ge 2$ (self-averaging).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a general symmetric jump law for the searchers, allowing the results to be generalized across different geometries and memory effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram based on $d_s$, showing variance decay tests confirming derived power laws, and demonstrate covariance collapse onto universal scaling functions for various random walk types.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the diagnostic observable ($X_n$), links its fluctuation behavior to the spectral dimension ($d_s$) of the underlying diffusion process, derives asymptotic variance formulas across different $d_s$ regimes, and validates these results by testing multiple physical models (e.g., Lévy walks, unequal mobilities).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Random exploration is usually quantified by how fast new space is found, from   the range of a single walker to the territory collectively covered by many   walkers. In competitive exploration, first arrival secures an exclusive resource, as when foragers compete for food items or agents capture distributed targets. It is then no longer enough to know which sites have been discovered: one must determine, for each discovered site, which searcher reached it first. We introduce the discovery   share $X_n$, the fraction of the first $n$ collective discoveries secured by   a tagged searcher. For two identical competitors, exchange symmetry fixes   $\langle X_n\rangle=1/2$, but the central question is whether this equal   split emerges in each long exploration history or only on average, \emph{i.e.} whether early   competitive advantages are erased or persist. Here we show that the answer is   controlled by the spectral dimension $d_s$, defined by the large-time decay of the probability that a single searcher is at   its starting point after $t$ steps, $p_0(t)\sim t^{-d_s/2}$.   Across ordinary diffusion, long-range superdiffusion and subdiffusion induced   by crowding or memory, $d_s$ separates persistent randomness in   recurrent exploration $(d_s<2)$, anomalously slow non-Gaussian concentration   for $2\le d_s<3$, and Gaussian concentration, logarithmically corrected at   $d_s=3$, for $d_s\ge3$. For $d_s\ge2$, we derive exact asymptotic   variances, including prefactors, and the discovery scale on which competitive   imbalances are erased. Two-point correlations of first-discovery labels identify the memory mechanism behind these regimes.   The same phase structure persists under changes in geometry, competitor   heterogeneity, number of competitors and memory, revealing a general fluctuation   theory of first-arrival inequalities.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces HamQASBench, a novel benchmark that evaluates Quantum Architecture Search methods by analyzing the underlying Hamiltonian structure rather than just the final energy value. By deriving fingerprints from Pauli operators and entanglement, it categorizes molecular problems into five distinct structural tiers. This allows researchers to diagnose specific failures in QAS algorithms, such as over-parameterization or representation bottlenecks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous framework for testing the fundamental capabilities of quantum machine learning algorithms (QAS) in simulating chemistry, moving the field past simple 'energy matching' to structural validation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a diagnostic benchmark for Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) that evaluates circuit design beyond simple energy accuracy by diagnosing underlying structural failures.

**Main result.** The proposed HamQASBench successfully reveals five distinct failure modes in QAS methods, including over-parameterization and representation bottlenecks, which are invisible to conventional energy metrics.

**Method.** The authors introduce a Hamiltonian-informed benchmark that uses fingerprints derived from Pauli operator bases, computational basis representations, and entanglement structure to categorize molecular Hamiltonians into structural tiers. They complement this with a critical-structure extraction procedure using gate ablation.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on simulating the ground-state energy of small molecules (e.g., H2, BeH2) governed by their qubit Hamiltonian ($H$), which is analyzed across five structural tiers based on its mathematical properties.

**Key observables.** Per-qubit von Neumann entropy, pairwise state fidelity, redundancy ratio ($ho$), Mean Absolute Entropy Difference (MAES), and success rates at chemical accuracy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The benchmark defines five structural tiers: Minimalism, Degeneracy, Strong Correlation, Topology Constraints, and Scalability/Growth. The analysis uses an error tolerance budget ($\epsilon_{	ext{allow}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** It is assumed that the required circuit complexity can be isolated by pruning redundant gates while maintaining energy performance, allowing structural comparison against theoretical fingerprints.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the fingerprinting process for small molecules (H2, H3), and tables summarize QAS results across the five diagnostic tiers and scaling ladders.

**Paper structure.** The paper first critiques existing benchmarks based only on molecular identity. It then details HamQASBench, defining structural fingerprints from three Hamiltonian views to create 5 structural tiers. The core methodology involves a post-hoc critical-structure extraction layer that moves beyond energy evaluation by analyzing entanglement and gate necessity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) automates the design of parameterized quantum circuits for variational quantum algorithms, yet existing benchmarks organize instances by molecular identity or qubit count -- criteria agnostic to Hamiltonian structure -- and rely solely on energy accuracy, which cannot detect structural failures such as over-parameterization on near-product ground states. We introduce HamQASBench, a Hamiltonian-informed diagnostic benchmark organizing 11 molecules into five structural tiers via fingerprints derived from the Pauli operator basis, computational basis representation, and ground-state entanglement. A post-hoc critical-structure extraction procedure identifies minimal circuits consistent with each tier's requirements, complementing energy-based evaluation with per-qubit entanglement analysis and pairwise state fidelity. Benchmarking five QAS methods across four paradigms reveals failure modes invisible to conventional metrics: over-parameterization in the minimalism regime, eigenstate commitment under degeneracy, a representation bottleneck in strongly correlated systems, topology-induced routing failure, and circuit search space growth as a scalability bottleneck.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a unified analytical framework to estimate logical error rates for advanced Quantum Error Correction codes. By modeling contributions from code structure and gate overhead, it allows researchers to compare performance across diverse physical platforms like superconducting circuits and trapped ions. The work helps identify optimal design regions for building large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides quantitative tools for comparing the resource overheads of different fault-tolerance schemes on realistic hardware constraints, which is crucial for designing next-generation quantum processors.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing scalable quantum computers is hindered by physical noise and limited qubit counts, necessitating efficient Quantum Error Correction (QEC).

**Main result.** The authors present a unified analytical framework to estimate logical error rates for various advanced QEC codes across different hardware platforms.

**Method.** They use an analytical framework that models logical failure based on the accumulation of physical errors from code structure and two-qubit gate overheads.

**Model / system.** The analysis considers multiple leading hardware platforms (superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral atoms) and advanced codes like topological, qLDPC, and Floquet codes. The framework separates intra-QPU and inter-QPU error sources for distributed systems.

**Key observables.** Logical error rates ($p_L$), code parameters ($[[n, k, d]]$), and the identification of dominant error contributors (e.g., routing overhead).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical error rate ($p_{loc}$), effective number of fault locations ($N_{loc}$), circuit volume, and connectivity constraints.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework simplifies complex simulations by focusing on key circuit-level parameters; it assumes certain noise models (e.g., depolarizing) and may neglect correlated errors or full compilation overheads.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but the paper analyzes various code families and their performance metrics across different hardware architectures.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of scalability via noise, introduces a unified analytical framework to estimate $p_L$, details how platform connectivity affects error accumulation ($N_{loc}, p_{loc}$), and applies this model to compare various QEC codes (Topological, qLDPC, etc.).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The theory of quantum error correction was established decades ago. Yet the limitation of the quantum computing platforms in terms of noise level and available physical qubit count persists, which greatly hinders the development of scalable quantum computing systems. In this paper, we present analytical estimates of logical error rates of advanced QEC codes across leading hardware platforms and distributed quantum computing systems using a simple but unified framework. The analysis captures two dominant contributors to logical error: code structure and two-qubit gate overhead. The framework provides a fast estimate of logical error rates and identification of dominating factors in different hardware platforms, such as circuit volume, routing overhead, inter-QPU operations, or asymmetric noise protection. We show that several qualitative trends observed in larger-scale simulations can be reproduced and interpreted analytically within this framework. We further demonstrate that the framework can be used to find the sweet spot design region of distributed QEC, which is critical for the design of distributed quantum computing systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper develops an exact mathematical framework to study how changing the initial state of a quantum system affects its Krylov complexity. By employing polynomial spectral filters and Christoffel transforms, it derives finite formulas that bypass computationally intensive full Hilbert space calculations. This provides a powerful 'relative calculus' for analyzing complex dynamics in various physical models.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides powerful algebraic tools to analyze spectral properties and complexity measures by decoupling the dependence on the initial state from the underlying Hamiltonian structure, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems or time-dependent perturbations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the 'relative initial-state problem' for Krylov complexity, which quantifies how changing the initial state of a quantum system affects its spectral properties.

**Main result.** It derives an exact relative calculus that allows generating polynomially related initial-state dynamics without needing to recompute the full Lanczos expansion in the original Hilbert space.

**Method.** The core method involves using polynomial spectral filters, $Q(H)$, which transforms the spectral measure via a Christoffel transform into shifted Krylov amplitudes and projected Christoffel–Darboux kernels.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to general quantum evolution governed by a Hamiltonian $H$ (or Liouvillian $\mathcal{L}$) acting on an initial state $|K_0angle$. It tests the formalism on solvable Jacobi chains, including Heisenberg–Weyl/Charlier and SU(2)/Krawtchouk models.

**Key observables.** Krylov complexity, spread complexity ($\Phi[Q]$), filtered spectral measure $	ext{d}
u_Q(E)$, and projected Christoffel–Darboux kernels.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The polynomial filter $Q$, the initial state $|K_0angle$, and temperature/time parameters in generalized extensions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method is exact for polynomial seed jumps, though some interpretations are restricted to fixed low-degree spectral preparation regimes. Generalizations require careful handling of inner products (e.g., thermal vs. zero-temperature).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first establishing the relative initial-state problem using polynomial filters, deriving exact finite sums for amplitudes and kernels via Christoffel transforms. It then generalizes this to operator dynamics (Liouvillians) and discusses extensions to thermal equilibrium.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

State Krylov, or spread, complexity is a property of a pair $(H,\ket{K_0})$ rather than of the Hamiltonian alone. Thus, changing the initial state at fixed $H$ generally changes the Lanczos coefficients and the ordered Krylov basis. We solve this relative initial-state problem for normalized polynomial filters, $\ket{ψ_Q}=Q(H)\ket{K_0}/\sqrt{N_Q}$ with $N_Q=\langle K_0|Q(H)^\dagger Q(H)|K_0\rangle$. The filtered spectral measure is the positive polynomial modification $|Q(E)|^2\mathrm dμ(E)/N_Q$, and orthogonality turns this measure change into a finite-band transfer from reference Fourier-orthogonal-polynomial moments to shifted Krylov amplitudes. We derive exact finite sums for individual amplitudes and projected Christoffel-Darboux kernels for cumulative probabilities and spread complexity. The formulae cover confluent roots, complex seed coefficients, support loss, and terminal quotients in finite dimensions. We evaluate the construction in three canonical Jacobi families, the Heisenberg--Weyl/Charlier oscillator, the compact $SU(2)$/Krawtchouk spin, and the constant-coefficient tight-binding/Chebyshev chain, with a Hermite central-limit scaling of Charlier as a continuous-spectrum check of this Christoffel jump machinery. Finite seed families are organized by a matrix-valued parent measure whose scalar compressions recover the individual shifted problems. The fixed-inner-product construction carries over to operator Krylov complexity after the replacement \(H\mapsto\mathcal L\) and \(\ket{K_0}\mapsto O\); polynomial seeds then become nested-commutator descendants \(Q(\mathcal L)O\). The result is an exact relative calculus in which a solved cyclic problem generates a family of polynomially related initial-state dynamics without repeating Lanczos in the original Hilbert space.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper proposes that describing composite quantum systems requires a 'Noether structure' beyond the standard statistical axioms. The authors demonstrate that this structure is necessary because simple tensor product rules lead to non-unique mathematical descriptions of combined states and operations. Ultimately, they establish that physical reality must select one specific 'quantum orientation' from multiple mathematically possible choices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work tackles foundational issues regarding how quantum theories must be mathematically structured when combining subsystems or defining irreversible processes (operations), which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper argues that quantum theory requires an additional 'Noether structure' beyond its statistical framework to properly describe system composition and define completely positive operations.

**Main result.** The standard statistical structure for composite systems is not unique, requiring the specification of a 'quantum orientation' (a choice between two possible structures) to fully characterize physical reality.

**Method.** The analysis uses axiomatic approaches, comparing the statistical structure $\langle K, L, \mu angle$ with requirements for tensor product mappings and analyzing geometric structures like principal bundles over state spaces.

**Model / system.** The focus is on abstract Quantum Theory (QT) foundations, specifically dealing with observables (Hermitian operators), state spaces ($K$), effect spaces ($L$), and the composition of systems via Hilbert space tensor products in the finite-dimensional limit.

**Key observables.** Observables are Hermitian operators; key diagnostics include the structure of product states and the existence/choice of 'quantum orientation'.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is strictly limited to the finite-dimensional case ($	ext{dim}(H)=N$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the statistical structure alone is insufficient, necessitating the introduction of the Noether structure; the analysis also assumes specific mappings related to tensor products.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but references include geometric structures like principal bundles ($\pi: B 	o F_3$) and algebraic identities derived from operator traces (Appendix C).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the insufficiency of the statistical structure, then investigating composition via tensor products, leading to the discovery of non-uniqueness in composite structures. It concludes with detailed mathematical proofs concerning homeomorphisms between state space descriptions and the characterization of pure operations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this paper we argue that, in addition to the statistical structure of quantum theory, another structure, referred to here as the ``Noether structure," is necessary to describe the composition of systems and to define completely positive operations. A Noether structure reflects the dual role of Hermitian operators as observables on the one hand and as generators of symmetry transformations on the other. This idea has been expressed in a similar form in the works of Alfsen and Shultz, who investigated the conditions under which the Jordan product can be extended to an associative product of operator algebras. Our investigations into the Noether structure and the composition of systems are limited to the finite-dimensional case and establish a connection to completely positive operations. In the case of pure operations, the latter can be characterized as orientation-preserving maps.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes when continuous-time quantum walks on cycle graphs achieve perfect or near-perfect mixing. It proves that specific cycles, like $C_9$ and $C_{15}$, fail to mix uniformly at any time. Conversely, it establishes a positive result by showing that cycles of the form $C_{p^2}$ do admit $\epsilon$-uniform mixing for all primes $p$, using advanced spectral and algebraic methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study of quantum walks' mixing properties is central to understanding quantum transport, decoherence, and the efficiency of quantum computation protocols in graph structures. The distinction between exact (uniform) and approximate ($\epsilon$-uniform) mixing provides deep insights into the underlying symmetries and algebraic structure of the graph.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the mixing properties (uniform and $\epsilon$-uniform) of continuous-time quantum walks evolving on cycle graphs ($C_n$).

**Main result.** The paper proves that $C_9$ and $C_{15}$ do not admit uniform mixing, while demonstrating that $C_{p^2}$ admits $\epsilon$-uniform mixing for any prime $p$.

**Method.** The analysis combines spectral theory (using eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix) with advanced algebraic techniques like Gröbner basis calculations to establish necessary and sufficient conditions for perfect mixing.

**Model / system.** The model is a continuous-time quantum walk on a cycle graph $C_n$, whose evolution is governed by the unitary operator $U(t) = \exp(itA)$, where $A$ is the adjacency matrix.

**Key observables.** Uniform mixing (where $|U(t)_{u,v}|^2 = 1/n$) and $\epsilon$-uniform mixing ($\|U(t) \circ U(t)^{*}-I/n\| < \epsilon$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The cycle length $n$, specifically focusing on $C_9$, $C_{15}$, and $C_{p^2}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies heavily on the spectral decomposition of the evolution operator and algebraic results concerning roots of unity.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes general conditions for uniform mixing using polynomial ideals (demonstrated via Gröbner bases for $C_9$ and $C_{15}$), followed by a separate analysis proving $\epsilon$-uniform mixing on $C_{p^2}$ using spectral approximation techniques.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study continuous-time quantum walks on cycles. We prove two complementary results. Firstly, the cycle $C_9$ does not admit uniform mixing at any time. Using the similar idea and Dickson polynomials, we prove that $C_{15}$ does not admit uniform mixing at any time neither. Secondly, for every prime $p$, we show that the cycle $C_{p^2}$ admits $ε$-uniform mixing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper characterizes the complex, variable channel loss encountered when performing Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution from a satellite to Earth due to atmospheric turbulence and beam spreading. By modeling these physical impairments across different zenith angles, the authors demonstrate that secure quantum key generation remains feasible under specific operational constraints.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous theoretical framework for quantifying decoherence and loss mechanisms (scintillation, wandering) in real-world, dynamic free-space quantum channels. The integration of atmospheric physics into QKD security analysis is key.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing dynamic channel loss for Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution (CV-QKD) when transmitting signals from a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite to a ground station.

**Main result.** It demonstrates that by characterizing variable channel losses due to atmospheric effects like turbulence and beam wandering, it is possible to generate a positive secret key rate under restricted security assumptions for the proposed space-based QKD link.

**Method.** The analysis involves modeling atmospheric propagation using established models (e.g., Hufnagel-Andrew-Phillips) to calculate weighted averages of refractive index structure parameters ($C_N^2$), alongside detailed calculations for scintillation variance and beam spreading loss.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a satellite-to-ground free-space optical link operating at 1550 nm, utilizing the parameters derived from the SPOQC mission concept. The analysis incorporates effects like atmospheric attenuation, turbulence-induced broadening, and pointing inaccuracies.

**Key observables.** Achievable secret key rates, weighted $C_N^2$ profiles vs. zenith angle, scintillation variance ($\sigma^2_{	ext{sci}}(	heta)$), and total loss due to various atmospheric impairments.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Zenith angles between $-30^\circ$ and $+30^\circ$, LEO altitude (550 km), wavelength (1550 nm), and varying turbulence strengths ($C_N^2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on practical assumptions, restricted Eve security assumptions, and models the channel loss based on specific atmospheric propagation equations.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the satellite pass geometry over the ground station. Figure 2 shows profiles of $C_N^2$ versus altitude (top) and weighted $C_N^2$ versus zenith angle (bottom).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the necessity of characterizing dynamic loss in space-based CV-QKD. It then details the physical modeling of atmospheric effects, including turbulence and beam spreading across various zenith angles. Finally, it presents the derived key rate analysis based on these characterized channel parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In space based quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, the quantum channel will be dynamic in nature and the channel loss will change with respect to the zenith angle. In the context of continuous variable (CV)-QKD, this will cause issues with parameter estimation and for a transmitted local oscillator in particular it will also fluctuate the shot noise. Therefore, it is vital to characterise this channel loss and the sources of this loss. In this paper the varying channel loss is characterised under practical assumptions. This is shown for various different scenarios, turbulence strengths, as well as wavelengths. This work shows, for the channel parameters considered, it is possible to generate a positive secret key if restricted Eve security assumptions are made.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates how to effectively use Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) with Ising machines to solve large Vehicle Routing Problems. By comparing two subproblem construction methods, LNS-K and LNS-Q, the authors demonstrate that incorporating the semantic structure of the current solution is crucial for optimization success. The findings suggest that structural information matters more than simply controlling the size of the variables fed into the quantum annealer.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on optimization heuristics, the reliance on mapping complex combinatorial problems onto QUBOs solved by quantum annealers touches upon the practical application of quantum computation for hard constraint satisfaction problems relevant to many-body physics modeling.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses limitations when using Ising machines for large-scale combinatorial optimization problems, specifically QUBO formulations of VRPs.

**Main result.** Subproblem design for sequential optimization must consider the semantic and geometric structure inherited from the current solution, not just the number of binary variables.

**Method.** The authors compare two Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) strategies: LNS-K (based on route structure) and LNS-Q (based on QUBO variables), applied to VRPs solved via Ising machines.

**Model / system.** The model is a Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulated as a QUBO, which is then optimized iteratively using an Ising machine framework. The comparison focuses on how the subproblem is constructed from the current solution state.

**Key observables.** Total distance achieved, position variance (spatial spread of selected customers), and the number of binary variables in the subproblems.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The size of the subproblem ($B_m$), the type of construction rule (LNS-K vs. LNS-Q), and the controlled annealing time budget for quantum annealers.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The comparison is limited by matching either the number of variables or the total annealing time, not end-to-end wall-clock runtime; a causal link between geometric localization and performance improvement is not established.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate that LNS-K yields shorter total distances and shows decreasing position variance during iterations compared to LNS-Q, even when subproblem sizes are matched.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the challenge of large QUBOs for Ising machines, proposes using LNS, and then systematically compares two construction methods (LNS-K vs. LNS-Q) on VRP instances by analyzing performance metrics like distance and spatial variance.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Large-scale quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulations of constrained combinatorial optimization problems often exceed the input-size limit of present Ising machines or suffer from degraded solution quality as the number of binary variables increases. Large neighborhood search (LNS) mitigates this difficulty by sequentially optimizing restricted subproblems, but the structural factors that distinguish subproblems beyond the number of binary variables remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we examine vehicle routing problems and compare a construction based on the vehicle routes of the current solution, denoted by LNS-K, with a construction based on QUBO variables and constraint relations, denoted by LNS-Q, while controlling the number of binary variables in the subproblems. Under the tested conditions, LNS-K obtained shorter total distances than LNS-Q in the matched-size comparisons, and the position variance, a measure of the spatial spread of the selected customers, decreased during the iterations in LNS-K. These observations suggest that subproblem design for sequential optimization with Ising machines should consider not only subproblem size but also semantic and geometric structures inherited from the current solution.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tests Quantum Machine Learning (QML) by applying hybrid QNNs to model cloud microphysics in climate science. Despite significant optimization efforts, the quantum models were outperformed by simpler classical neural networks. The findings underscore that while QML shows potential, substantial theoretical and practical improvements are needed before it can reliably tackle complex physical modeling tasks.

**Why it may be interesting.** Although focused on climate physics, the core challenge—applying quantum models to complex, high-dimensional physical parameterizations—is relevant for developing novel machine learning techniques applicable to open quantum systems or strongly correlated materials simulations where classical methods struggle.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper assesses whether Quantum Machine Learning (QML) can effectively parameterize complex physical processes, specifically cloud microphysics in climate modeling, and identifies the limitations of variational quantum models.

**Main result.** While QNNs benefit from extensive hyperparameter optimization, they were outperformed by simple classical fully-connected neural networks on the benchmark task. This highlights a need to improve VQMs to fill gaps where classical methods fail or are inefficient.

**Method.** A hybrid quantum neural network (QNN) architecture was implemented, combining quantum circuits for data encoding and feature extraction with classical post-processing layers. Performance was rigorously compared against optimized classical FCNN baselines using Mean Squared Error minimization.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is cloud microphysics parameterization, involving phase transitions of water in the atmosphere, derived from large atmospheric datasets (ICON model). The ML models used are hybrid QNNs and standard FCNNs trained to predict changes in state variables like temperature and mass mixing ratios.

**Key observables.** Test $R^2$ score, Mean Squared Error (MSE), basis state probabilities ($p_m$), and various atmospheric tendencies ($\Delta T$, $\Delta qv$, etc.).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hyperparameters optimized included circuit depth ($L$), number of qubits ($M$), learning rates ($\eta$), and polynomial degrees ($P$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation noted is the presence of extreme outliers in the training data, which artificially inflate the loss function and affect performance metrics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the hybrid QNN architecture (quantum circuit $ightarrow$ classical post-processing) and show the convergence of test $R^2$ scores for both QNNs and FCNNs during hyperparameter optimization.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, details the hybrid QNN/FCNN methodology using extensive data preprocessing and HPO routines, presents comparative results showing classical superiority, and concludes by discussing bottlenecks in VQMs.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum machine learning (QML) could have the potential to leverage advantages of quantum over classical computing but still lacks strong evidence of actual improvements and scalability, partly due to phenomena such as barren plateaus. In this paper, we employ a hybrid quantum neural network (QNN) on a dataset on cloud microphysics, containing processes for phase transitions of water in the atmosphere and its related temperature changes, which are highly relevant for accurate climate predictions and projections. To reach optimal performance of our QNNs, we employ a rich and trainable frequency spectrum together with expressivity enhancing classical postprocessing. We find that our QNNs strongly benefit from extensive hyperparameter optimization and thereby demonstrate the feasibility of applying QNNs to complex physical systems. At the same time, the QNNs are outperformed by classical baselines in the form of simple fully-connected neural networks. We discuss identified bottlenecks of this class of quantum models to learn the full complexity of the cloud microphysics dataset to show that there is a need to further understand and improve variational quantum models for machine learning such that they might fill the gap where classical models fail or are inefficient.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes using twin optical PUFs—which derive their randomness from correlated speckle patterns generated by light scattering—to establish a secret key. It develops a rigorous, information-theoretic protocol for key agreement that accounts for environmental noise and fabrication variability. This offers a hardware-based alternative to traditional quantum key distribution methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly about quantum dynamics, the reliance on complex physical phenomena like light scattering in disordered media to generate high-entropy random numbers touches upon open questions at the intersection of condensed matter physics (disorder) and information theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates establishing a shared secret key between two parties using twin optical Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) as a hardware-based platform for cryptography.

**Main result.** An explicit information-theoretic protocol is developed that quantifies the achievable lower bound on the final secret key length, identifying noise regimes where secure agreement is feasible without relying on computational assumptions.

**Method.** The core method involves developing an information-theoretic key-agreement protocol incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification applied to correlated PUF responses.

**Model / system.** The physical platform utilizes twin O-PUFs, where the fingerprint is a speckle pattern generated by coherent light scattering through disordered optical structures. The model mathematically describes the output electric field using linear scattering theory involving transmission matrices.

**Key observables.** Information leakage due to public helper data; lower bounds on the length of the final secret key; Bit Error Rate (BER) between raw keys.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fabrication-induced variability ($\sigma_F$) and environmental noise ($\sigma_E$); the maximum allowed Hamming distance ($t$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes linear scattering theory in the diffusive limit, challenge uniformity, and that the adversary is limited to observing public classical communication.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates the main steps of key agreement using twin PUFs, detailing the flow from raw key generation through sketching, reconciliation, and amplification.

**Paper structure.** The paper first models the physical process using correlated O-PUFs. It then develops the information-theoretic protocol (sketching $ightarrow$ reconciliation $ightarrow$ amplification). Finally, it analyzes the security bounds based on noise regimes and discusses integration into QKD networks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the use of twin optical fingerprints derived from correlated physical unclonable functions (PUFs), as a hardware-based platform for cryptographic key generation and distribution. Each fingerprint is associated with a random, yet reproducible speckle pattern, generated when coherent light is scattered by a disordered optical structure. We consider a pair of correlated optical PUFs, and study the conditions under which two honest parties can establish a common secret key, despite fabrication-induced variability and environmental noise. An explicit information-theoretic key-agreement protocol is developed, incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification. We quantify information leakage due to public helper data, and derive lower bounds on the length of the final secret key. The analysis identifies the noise regimes in which secure key agreement is feasible, and examines the performance of both practical and near-capacity reconciliation schemes. Finally, we discuss how twin optical PUFs could be integrated into quantum key distribution (QKD) networks, as a mechanism for establishing an initial pre-shared secret key between two honest users, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.

</details>
