**Summary.** This paper addresses the challenge of building universal fault-tolerant quantum computation by proposing a hybrid architecture combining two related 3D color codes. By leveraging complementary transversal operations, they achieve an almost-universal gate set, completing it through a complex round-robin construction for the necessary entangling gates. This provides a new pathway to implement hard algorithms while keeping most required operations transversal.

**Why it may be interesting.** While highly theoretical, the focus on resource optimization (concentrating non-transversal gates) and using structured codes like color codes is relevant to designing practical quantum hardware architectures that minimize error correction overhead.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Achieving a universal set of transversal logical gates for fault-tolerant quantum computation, which is restricted by the Eastin–Knill theorem.

**Main result.** The authors propose a hybrid architecture using two complementary color codes (tetrahedral and H-tetrahedral) to realize an almost-universal gate set, completing universality via a complex round-robin construction for the entangling CZ gate.

**Method.** The approach combines bitwise Hadamard transformations between two related quantum error-correcting codes and utilizes pieceable fault-tolerant constructions for necessary non-transversal gates.

**Model / system.** The system is based on the $[[15, 1, 3]]$ tetrahedral three-dimensional color code and its Hadamard-transformed counterpart. The implementation details involve syndrome extraction using auxiliary qubits and constructing logical operations between these two codes.

**Key observables.** Logical state fidelities (e.g., $F_{CZ}|\cdotangle$), effective distances ($d_X, d_Z$), and the existence of transversal non-Clifford gates.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The smallest instance considered is the $[[15, 1, 3]]$ code; resource overhead is concentrated in a few non-transversal Clifford operations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial CNOT realization between codes is one-way (control $	o$ target), and achieving full universality requires complex round-robin constructions for the missing entangling gate.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the $[[15, 1, 3]]$ code structure, transversal operations in the hybrid architecture, and the ordering of physical CZ gates required for fault-tolerant logical gates.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the need for transversal gates, proposes the hybrid tetrahedral/H-tetrahedral architecture to achieve an almost-universal set, details the construction of the full universal gate set via a round-robin process, and analyzes related concepts like syndrome extraction overheads.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Transversal logical gates provide a direct route to fault-tolerant quantum computation, but the Eastin-Knill theorem forbids a universal transversal gate set within a single quantum error-correcting code. We propose a hybrid architecture based on the tetrahedral three-dimensional color code and its Hadamard-transformed counterpart, which we call the H-tetrahedral code. The two encodings support complementary transversal non-Clifford operations. Combined with bitwise Hadamard transformations that switch between the two encodings and a one-way transversal logical CNOT from the tetrahedral code to the H-tetrahedral code, these operations realize an almost-universal transversal logical gate set that enables both the creation of entanglement and logical states with magic. We complete a universal gate set through a pieceably fault-tolerant round-robin construction of a logical controlled-$Z$ gate between two H-tetrahedral codes. This logical entangling gate is interleaved with reduced-overhead Steane-type syndrome extraction using logical two-dimensional color-code auxiliary qubits. Our construction provides a new route toward implementing classically hard-to-simulate quantum algorithms where magic and most entangling operations are transversal while the resource overhead is concentrated in a small number of non-transversal Clifford entangling operations.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates an efficient classical algorithm (frozen-tree sampling) capable of reproducing the exact statistical output distribution of Random Circuit Sampling (RCS). By showing this equivalence, the authors argue that RCS does not constitute a sound standalone benchmark for quantum advantage, as all observable sample statistics can be classically simulated.

**Why it may be interesting.** It directly challenges a cornerstone assumption in quantum computation benchmarking by providing an efficient classical simulation for the underlying probability distribution, suggesting that true advantage must be sought elsewhere than sample statistics alone.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper challenges the widely accepted premise that Random Circuit Sampling (RCS) provides a demonstration of quantum advantage over classical computation.

**Main result.** An efficient classical frozen-tree sampling algorithm can reproduce the exact probability distribution of RCS outputs, meaning no sample-based statistical test can distinguish between the two processes.

**Method.** The authors propose and implement an $O(n)$ classical frozen-tree sampler that exploits the conditional scale invariance property of Haar-random quantum states to generate bitstrings matching the Dirichlet distribution statistics.

**Model / system.** The model involves $n$ qubits whose state is assumed to be random (Haar-random), leading to output bitstring probabilities following a flat Dirichlet distribution. The analysis focuses on the probability vector $p(x) = |\langle x|\psiangle|^2$.

**Key observables.** The output bitstring probability distribution $p(x)$, and diagnostic metrics like the branch-ratio fidelity $\hat{F}_d$ and the exponential law adherence for leaf probabilities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits ($n$), depth of the circuit, and noise parameters (depolarizing, amplitude damping).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The argument relies on exploiting the exact conditional scale invariance property inherent to Haar-random states and assumes that verification must rely only on sample statistics.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the frozen-tree sampler's performance ($\hat{F}_d=1$) against empirical data from quantum hardware (Sycamore), showing perfect fidelity, and validate the reproduction of ideal exponential laws under various noise models.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces RCS as a benchmark, then derives the classical sampling method using frozen-tree techniques based on conditional scale invariance. It systematically compares the resulting statistics against known quantum benchmarks (including noisy channels) to show statistical equivalence.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Random circuit sampling of bitstrings from a Haar-random quantum state is widely believed to be classically intractable, and has therefore been implemented as a primary benchmark for demonstrating quantum advantage. Here, we challenge this premise by proposing an efficient classical frozen-tree sampling algorithm that exploits the conditional scale invariance of Haar-random quantum states [Oh, arXiv:2602.19448]. The frozen-tree sampler draws bitstrings of $n$ qubits in $O(n)$ time per sample. Moreover, its output probability $p_F(x)$ is statistically identical to the probability $p_C(x)$ of a random quantum circuit, since both are independent instances of the same Dirichlet distribution. Consequently, no statistical test acting on samples alone can distinguish the classical frozen-tree sampler from a quantum random circuit. The claimed quantum advantage of random circuit sampling therefore does not withstand scrutiny: its hardness lies not in sampling from the Dirichlet distribution, which is classically efficient, but in identifying a specific circuit realization.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors perform highly accurate relativistic many-body calculations on $^{23}	ext{Na}$ to predict its hyperfine structure constants. They systematically incorporate electron correlation effects up to triple excitations and include QED/Breit corrections. The findings emphasize that achieving experimental accuracy requires the combined inclusion of these higher-order correlation terms alongside fundamental physical interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work exemplifies the state-of-the-art in high-precision atomic structure theory, demonstrating how subtle correlation effects (like triples) are essential for matching spectroscopic measurements in alkali atoms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to accurately determine hyperfine structure constants (HFCs) and ionization potentials for $^{23}	ext{Na}$ by rigorously investigating the role of electron correlation effects, particularly those involving triple excitations.

**Main result.** Accurate theoretical predictions require the inclusion of higher-order correlation terms (like triples), alongside relativistic corrections (Breit, QED, BW) to reconcile discrepancies between theory and experiment for $	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$.

**Method.** The study employs advanced relativistic coupled-cluster theory ($	ext{RCCSDT}$) combined with perturbation theory treatments for various physical interactions.

**Model / system.** The system is the sodium ($^{23}	ext{Na}$) atom. Calculations utilize a Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian and treat electron correlation effects systematically through methods like $	ext{RMBPT}$ and coupled-cluster expansions up to triple excitations.

**Key observables.** Magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants ($	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$), electric quadrupole hyperfine structure constants ($	ext{B}_{	ext{hf}}$), and Ionization Potentials (IPs).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative importance of correlation effects versus Breit, QED, and Bohr-Weisskopf corrections is a key focus.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations rely on approximations inherent to many-body perturbation theory ($	ext{RMBPT}$) or coupled-cluster expansions ($	ext{RCC}$), which systematically treat electron interactions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the systematic inclusion of different physical processes (e.g., correlation effects) and show how triple excitations modify $	ext{A}_{	ext{hf}}$ constants, while tables present numerical comparisons across various theoretical approximations.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares results from lower-order methods ($	ext{RMBPT}(2)$, RPA) against higher-order treatments incorporating explicit triple excitations ($	ext{RCCSDT}$), while also adding external corrections like Breit and QED to achieve convergence toward experimental values.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Accurate determination of hyperfine structure constants in atomic systems provides important insight into the interplay of electron correlation and relativistic effects in the nuclear region. Although sodium (Na) is a relatively light atom, previous all-order relativistic many-body calculations of the magnetic dipole hyperfine constants for the low-lying states of $^{23}$Na show noticeable discrepancies with experiment. To address this, we calculate the ionization potentials and hyperfine structure constants of $^{23}$Na using relativistic coupled-cluster theory with explicit inclusion of triple excitations. We further incorporate corrections from the Breit interaction, quantum electrodynamics, and the Bohr-Weisskopf (BW) effect. Results from lower-order methods are also presented to assess the importance of different physical contributions across states. Our calculations demonstrate that contributions from the lower-order relativistic and BW effects play almost similar roles with the electron correlation effects, including triple excitations, and are essential for reconciling theoretical predictions with experimental observations. This study can also serve as a useful guide for understanding the role of triples in heavier alkali systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces LNS-VT, an advanced technique for solving large combinatorial optimization problems using Ising machines by adaptively controlling the size of subproblems solved at each step. By demonstrating that flexible subproblem sizing is critical—outperforming methods that only guarantee feasibility—it provides a powerful heuristic framework applicable to various complex scheduling and resource allocation tasks.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical optimization, the use of Ising machines connects directly to quantum annealing hardware. The need to manage problem size and complexity in QUBO formulations mirrors challenges in mapping complex physical Hamiltonians onto limited qubit architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Improving solution quality for large-scale combinatorial optimization problems like VRP and QMKP using Ising machine solvers within a Large Neighborhood Search (LNS) framework.

**Main result.** A novel LNS variant, LNS-VT, that flexibly controls the subproblem size significantly outperforms existing methods by achieving up to 10% objective value reduction in VRP compared to fixed-size approaches.

**Method.** The authors propose LNS-VT, which iteratively updates solutions by solving smaller, carefully sized subproblems derived from the original problem structure, ensuring feasibility is maintained while allowing fine control over variables.

**Model / system.** The core model involves mapping combinatorial optimization problems (VRP, QMKP) into QUBO Hamiltonians solved by Ising machines. The system relies on defining and iteratively solving smaller subproblems rather than the entire large-scale problem at once.

**Key observables.** Objective function value reduction ($\approx 10\%$ improvement), total profit maximization for QMKP, and the number of binary variables in the subproblem.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The tunable parameter is the length of consecutive route segments re-optimized per vehicle (for VRP) or the prescribed number of items ($N'$) and selected knapsacks ($K'$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Feasibility preservation alone is insufficient; controlling the subproblem size independently of problem structure is crucial for optimal performance.

**Figures summary.** Figure 8 shows that for QMKP, the total profit increases significantly when the number of binary variables in the subproblem is tuned to an optimal range (100-150), demonstrating the benefit of variable control.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the VRP formulation and LNS framework, contrasts existing methods with the proposed LNS-VT for VRP, applies this principle to QMKP, and concludes by emphasizing that structure-aware subproblem sizing is key.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Ising machines are heuristic solvers for combinatorial optimization, but their solution quality can degrade when large-scale constrained problems are solved directly. Ising-machine-assisted large neighborhood search (LNS) instead repeatedly updates a feasible current solution by solving smaller subproblems. An existing feasibility-preserving method for the vehicle routing problem (VRP) re-optimizes the entire routes of selected vehicles and thus cannot adjust the subproblem size finely. We propose LNS-VT, which introduces the number of consecutive steps re-optimized per vehicle as a parameter to control the subproblem size finely while preserving feasibility. For a 300-site, 5-vehicle VRP, its best setting reduced the objective value by approximately 10\% relative to the existing method after 100 iterations, and the appropriate setting changed with the current solution quality. Applying the same principle to the quadratic multiple knapsack problem, we confirmed that an appropriate subproblem size also exists, indicating that subproblem-size control is important in Ising-machine-assisted LNS.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces 'logical spectroscopy' to solve the problem of constructing usable logical bases for Abelian lifted-product qLDPC codes. By employing the Chinese Remainder Theorem to decompose the underlying group algebra, it replaces failed global row reduction with solvable finite-field computations. This yields a fully addressable and structured basis essential for implementing quantum gates in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful algebraic tool to analyze complex quantum error-correcting codes by translating difficult group algebra problems into manageable finite-field computations, which is crucial for designing scalable fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is developing a systematic method to construct and addressable conjugate logical operators for high-rate Abelian lifted-product quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes.

**Main result.** The authors introduce 'logical spectroscopy,' a spectral construction that successfully replaces failed global row reduction with finite-field computations, yielding complete addressable conjugate logical bases.

**Method.** The method utilizes the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) to decompose the group algebra into Frobenius character packets. Calculations are performed independently in each packet, and results are then lifted back using CRT idempotents.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on Quantum Error-Correcting (QEC) codes, specifically Abelian lifted-product (LP) qLDPC codes, which encode logical qubits for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

**Key observables.** Complete addressable conjugate logical bases; packet ranks showing sector splitting; certified upper bounds on basis width from lifted representatives; and packet-attributed dimensions for erased logicals.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The construction is valid under bounded seed-shape and bounded group-basis-support assumptions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption enabling the spectral method is that the complex problem over the group algebra can be decomposed into independent, solvable finite-field problems via CRT.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the process flow: moving from a module problem over the group algebra to factorization into CRT packets, solving each packet independently, and finally lifting the results back to establish logical sector pairing.

**Paper structure.** The paper first identifies the failure of standard row reduction for Abelian LP codes. It then introduces 'logical spectroscopy' as the spectral replacement, detailing the use of CRT decomposition, computation within individual packets (kernels, quotients), and the final reconstruction/pairing of X and Z logicals.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum LDPC memories can encode many logical qubits, but dimension alone does not make them usable: applications need explicit conjugate logical operators with structured labels and physical representatives. For hypergraph-product (HGP) codes this structure is transparent, since the input matrices are binary and can be row-reduced over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Abelian lifted-product codes are subtler. Their seed entries are shifts, or sparse sums of shifts, in a group-algebra ring rather than a field, so pivot blocks need not be invertible and global row reduction can fail.   We address this with \emph{logical spectroscopy}, a spectral construction that replaces global row reduction by finite-field computations in the Frobenius character packets of the Abelian lift group. The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) decomposes the group algebra into these packets. In each packet, we compute kernels, quotients, and product-complex homology; we then lift the resulting representatives back with CRT idempotents and pair $X$ and $Z$ logicals through reciprocal trace-dual packets. This gives complete addressable conjugate logical bases for finite Abelian lifted products $\mathsf{LP}(A,B)$.   The same packet data also gives design diagnostics. Packet ranks show how logical sectors split, the lifted representatives give certified upper bounds on the width of the constructed conjugate basis, and whole-orbit erasures decompose into packet-attributed erased-logical dimensions. Thus, CRT packets also serve as working coordinates: they label logical sectors, certify the constructed basis width, and attribute structured erasure failures. Under bounded seed-shape and group-basis-support assumptions, this construction gives Abelian lifted-product qLDPC families an HGP-like feature while preserving the layout freedom of group-algebra lifts.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the onset of quantum chaos in hyperbolic billiards by introducing small geometric perturbations to an arithmetic system. The authors demonstrate a measurable crossover in spectral statistics from Poissonian (arithmetic) behavior towards GOE statistics as the perturbation strength changes. This transition is confirmed through both eigenvalue spacing analysis and eigenfunction localization measurements, providing a comprehensive view of chaotic emergence.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a detailed, combined spectral and wave-function picture of quantum chaos transition in non-Euclidean geometry, which is relevant for understanding chaotic dynamics in curved spaces or complex potentials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how generic quantum chaos emerges from an arithmetic billiard system defined on the hyperbolic plane when subjected to small area-preserving geometric perturbations.

**Main result.** The spectral statistics exhibit a clear, perturbation-dependent crossover from Poisson-like arithmetic behavior towards Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) statistics, which is corroborated by eigenfunction localization measurements.

**Method.** The analysis combines spectral analysis of eigenvalues with the study of eigenfunctions using Poincaré–Husimi representations to quantify phase-space localization.

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum billiard defined on a hyperbolic domain (a perturbed Schmit triangle) governed by the Laplace–Beltrami operator. The Hamiltonian is analyzed through its spectral properties and eigenfunction structure.

**Key observables.** Nearest-neighbour spacing distribution, localization width ($\sigma_{	ext{Beta}}$), spectral statistics crossover scale, and Lyapunov exponent.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Perturbation strength ($\epsilon$), wavenumber ($k$), and the hyperbolic geometry parameters defining the billiard domain.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The generalized-gamma fit is used only as a diagnostic tool, not as a universal law; convergence analysis relies on specialized numerical techniques for solving boundary integral equations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the geometric setup (tessellation of the hyperbolic triangle) and show spectral/localization data confirming the crossover behavior across different perturbation strengths.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining the perturbed hyperbolic billiard, calculating eigenvalues via boundary integral methods, analyzing the resulting spectral statistics (Poisson to GOE), and complementing this with eigenfunction localization analysis.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the emergence of generic quantum chaos from an arithmetic billiard in the hyperbolic plane. Starting from an arithmetic triangle, we introduce small area-preserving geometric perturbations and compute long consecutive sequences of eigenvalues and eigenstates. The spectral statistics show a perturbation-dependent crossover from Poisson-like arithmetic behaviour to the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), with the crossover scale moving to higher wavenumbers as the perturbation decreases. To characterize the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution, we compare the data with Brody and generalized-gamma fits. The generalized-gamma form is used only as a two-parameter diagnostic, allowing the small- and intermediate-spacing structure to vary independently from the large-spacing tail, rather than as a universal crossover law. For the weakest perturbation, we also compare the data with an effective block-GOE model, which diagnoses residual block-like structure deep into the computed spectral range. We complement the spectral analysis with Poincaré-Husimi representations of the eigenstates and quantify phase-space localization using an entropy-based measure. Its distribution is well described by Beta distributions whose width decays as a power law in the wavenumber. Before the spectral crossover, the localization statistics retain memory of the near-arithmetic regime. After the GOE regime is reached, the localization-fluctuation widths collapse onto a common decay law, sigma(Beta) ~ k^{-eta}, with eta approximately 0.37--0.38. These results provide a combined spectral and eigenfunction-level picture of the arithmetic-to-GOE crossover in hyperbolic quantum billiards.

</details>

**Summary.** QuTuner is a novel framework designed to automatically tune the sequence and selection of optimization passes within quantum compilers. It overcomes limitations of prior work by incorporating 'optimization-aware pass embeddings' alongside static circuit features. By training machine learning models on a large dataset, QuTuner efficiently retrieves and ranks optimal pass sequences, leading to substantial improvements in compiled circuit quality while drastically cutting down tuning time.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles the practical engineering challenge of optimizing quantum algorithms for near-term hardware by automating complex compiler decisions, which is a critical bottleneck in realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing effective, generalizable methods for 'pass tuning' within quantum compilers to minimize resource costs (like gate count or depth) while improving execution fidelity.

**Main result.** QuTuner significantly improves metric reduction on both Qiskit and PyTKET benchmarks—up to 84.85% improvement on Qiskit—while drastically reducing the required tuning time.

**Method.** The authors propose QuTuner, a feature-guided framework that builds an optimization dataset by characterizing circuits using static features and novel 'optimization-aware pass embeddings' derived from profiling circuit responses to individual passes.

**Model / system.** The system is quantum computation realized through quantum circuits (sequences of 1Q and 2Q gates) compiled for platforms like Qiskit. The optimization process involves multiple compiler passes that transform the initial circuit representation.

**Key observables.** Circuit-level metrics targeted for reduction include two-qubit gate count ($\Delta 2Q$), one-qubit gate count ($\Delta 1Q$), and overall circuit depth ($\Delta 	ext{Depth}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The tuning objective is a weighted combination of metric reductions: $	ext{Objective} = \alpha \cdot \Delta 2Q + eta \cdot \Delta 1Q + \gamma \cdot \Delta 	ext{Depth}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Prior methods are limited because they only search small pass subspaces or rely solely on static features that fail to capture how a circuit reacts dynamically to optimization passes.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates an example quantum circuit and the stages of compilation. Figure 2 details the two-stage QuTuner workflow (offline training $ightarrow$ online retrieval/ranking). Figure 3 shows various feature types used for circuit characterization.

**Paper structure.** The paper first identifies limitations in prior tuning methods, then introduces QuTuner by detailing its dataset construction and dual feature representation (static + embedding). It describes the two-stage learning process (pruning/ranking models) before presenting quantitative results on major quantum toolkits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum compilers play a key role in transforming quantum circuits into lower-cost implementations with improved execution fidelity. This process is commonly guided by circuit-level metrics, such as gate counts and circuit depth. Although compiler pass tuning has been widely studied in classical compilation, directly transferring these techniques to quantum compilers is challenging, because quantum programs are expressed as circuits and exhibit optimization behaviors that are shaped by quantum-specific structures. Prior quantum compiler tuning approaches have begun to use circuit features to guide pass selection, but they remain limited in two aspects: they search only a small portion of the optimization-pass space, and they mainly rely on static features that do not explicitly reflect how a circuit reacts to compiler optimizations.   We present QuTuner, a feature-guided quantum compiler pass tuning framework that generalizes across compilers and tuning objectives. QuTuner first builds a large optimization dataset. It then characterizes each circuit from two complementary views: static circuit features that describe circuit structure, and optimization-aware pass embeddings that summarize the circuit's responses to individual optimization passes. Using these representations, QuTuner trains two offline models to retrieve and rank candidate pass sequences for unseen circuits, followed by lightweight refinement. We evaluate QuTuner on Qiskit and PyTKET using two benchmark suites. On Qiskit, QuTuner improves the evaluation-metric reduction by up to 84.85% over the strongest baseline while reducing tuning time by 73.59%. On PyTKET, it improves metric reduction by up to 18.68% with a 64.49% reduction in tuning time. These results show that QuTuner provides an effective approach to adaptive pass tuning for quantum compilers.

</details>

**Summary.** This study uses muon spin rotation ($\mu$SR) to probe superconductivity in $	ext{Cu}_{1-x}	ext{Zn}_x	ext{Ir}_2	ext{S}_4$, a material near a metal-insulator transition. The results confirm an s-wave superconducting gap, arguing that high levels of electronic disorder force the pairing symmetry into an isotropic form. This suggests that strong scattering can stabilize superconductivity in correlated materials operating near fundamental physical limits.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides experimental evidence on how strong electronic disorder can stabilize an isotropic s-wave superconducting state even when underlying physics suggests complex, anisotropic pairing mechanisms typical of strongly correlated electron systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Investigating superconductivity in Zn-substituted thiospinel $	ext{Cu}_{1-x}	ext{Zn}_x	ext{Ir}_2	ext{S}_4$ and understanding how disorder affects the pairing mechanism near a metal-insulator transition.

**Main result.** The superconducting state is confirmed to be an isotropic, fully gapped s-wave, robustly surviving deep within the dirty limit despite strong electronic correlations suggesting unconventional pairing.

**Method.** Transverse-field muon spin rotation ($\mu$SR) measurements are used to probe the temperature and field dependence of the superfluid density, complemented by normal state resistivity measurements.

**Model / system.** The system is the thiospinel $	ext{CuIr}_2	ext{S}_4$, which undergoes an MI transition. Zn substitution induces superconductivity ($T_c \approx 2-3$ K). The analysis framework incorporates concepts from the dirty limit and proximity to Mott-Ioffe-Regel limits.

**Key observables.** Superfluid density ($\sigma_s$), magnetic penetration depth ($\lambda$), temperature dependence of $\mu$SR linewidth, normal state resistivity ($ho$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Disorder parameter (implied by high $ho$, placing system in dirty limit), coherence length ($\xi_0$), critical temperature ($T_c$), and the degree of electronic disorder.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The superfluid density follows a two-fluid model approximation, and the analysis assumes that strong scattering averages out potential anisotropy expected from unconventional pairing mechanisms.

**Figures summary.** Figures show $\mu$SR time spectra demonstrating temperature-dependent relaxation below $T_c$, and plots analyzing linewidth ($\sigma$) vs. temperature/field, confirming s-wave behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the background (MI transition in $	ext{CuIr}_2	ext{S}_4$), presents $\mu$SR results showing s-wave pairing, discusses the implications of high resistivity placing it in the dirty limit, and proposes a unified framework linking disorder to superconductivity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The thiospinel CuIr$_2$S$_4$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition below $\approx$230 K, which is suppressed by substitution of Cu with Zn (Cu$_{1-x}$Zn$_x$Ir$_2$S$_4$) to induce superconductivity for $0.2\lesssim x\lesssim0.8$. We show that the temperature/field dependence of superfluid density in samples with $x = 0.3$ and 0.4 ($T_{\rm c} \approx 3$ K and 2.5 K) investigated by muon spin rotation and relaxation ($μ$SR) is consistent with a fully gapped $s$-wave pairing. Meanwhile, the relatively high resistivity (10$^{-3}$-10$^{-2}$ $Ω\:$cm) in their normal state suggests that the superconductivity is in the "dirty limit" where the mean free path is much shorter than the coherence length ($\ell \ll ξ_0$). This indicates that the potential anisotropy associated with unconventional pairing mechanisms expected under the strong electron correlations is smeared out by the electron scattering. Based on these observations, we discuss potential link between the Zn substitution-induced superconductivity and that recently discovered in CuIr$_2$S$_4$ under high pressure ($>18$ GPa) where the existence of strong electron scattering is also suggested.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper addresses the challenge of verifying quantum computations performed by untrusted quantum servers using hardware-efficient security protocols. It introduces a modular framework that breaks down verification into manageable primitives like remote state preparation and error detection. The work provides an architectural guide to making these complex security proofs practical for real-world, noisy quantum devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides an architectural roadmap for making quantum security proofs practical by systematically reducing hardware overheads, which is crucial for bridging theory and near-term quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing methods for a classically limited verifier to confirm the output of an untrusted, fully quantum server performing complex computations.

**Main result.** The paper proposes a modular framework that systematically relaxes hardware requirements by decomposing verification into independent primitives like remote state preparation and trap-based deviation detection.

**Method.** It synthesizes various advanced protocols (e.g., Robust VBQC) using concepts from interactive proof systems, composability theorems, and error detection to build practical security guarantees.

**Model / system.** The model involves an interaction between a Verifier (classical/limited quantum resources) and an untrusted Prover (BQP machine). The focus is on abstract protocols rather than a specific physical hardware implementation.

**Key observables.** Statistical soundness, indistinguishability ($\epsilon$-statistical), computational complexity class (e.g., BQP vs. classical limits).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Error tolerance ($\epsilon$), number of qubits/parties in multi-party settings, and the level of fault tolerance required.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The authors assume the existence of underlying cryptographic primitives and focus on architectural principles rather than deriving all technical proofs themselves.

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured conceptually: first, defining the problem space (verification gap); second, introducing a modular framework composed of independent verification primitives; third, showing how these primitives can be combined to address increasingly complex scenarios like multi-party and fault-tolerant computation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

How can a user with limited quantum resources verify the output of an untrusted, fully quantum server? This manuscript provides a conceptual synthesis of some recent developments toward answering this question under statistical (information-theoretic) security. Rather than duplicating the dense technical proofs of the underlying publications, our focus here is on the physical motivations, the structural connections between different protocols, and the path toward hardware-efficient implementation.   We begin by introducing a modular, composable framework that partitions verification into three distinct, independent primitives: remote state preparation, trap-based deviation detection, and error-correcting embedding. Using this framework, we show how the demanding hardware requirements of early protocols can be systematically relaxed. We review schemes that eliminate the spatial overhead, remove the need to prepare computational-basis dummy states, and replace single-photon sources with trusted local rotations or weak coherent pulses. Finally, we examine how these techniques scale, both to asymmetric multi-party settings and to the delegation of fully fault-tolerant computations in the presence of gate-level noise. This document is intended as a guide to the architectural principles of practical quantum verification.

</details>

By applying a rotating electric field, the researchers demonstrate a controllable transfer of bipartite entanglement between different spin pairs. This establishes these molecular magnets as promising platforms for electrically steering and localizing quantum information at the nanoscale.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses electrical control over quantum correlations in solid-state molecular systems, which is highly relevant for developing nanoscale quantum devices where local electric fields can manipulate spin states.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how quantum entanglement can be controlled and transferred between different spin pairs within a molecular magnet using the Katsura-Nagaosa-Balatsky (KNB) magnetoelectric coupling mechanism.

**Main result.** A rotating in-plane electric field allows for the controllable, nearly ideal transfer of bipartite entanglement between spin pairs, establishing these magnets as platforms for electrical quantum state engineering.

**Method.** The analysis involves calculating and mapping various measures of quantum entanglement (bipartite and tripartite negativity) derived from the system's Hamiltonian eigenstates.

**Model / system.** The model is a spin-1/2 Heisenberg trimer with an isosceles triangular geometry, incorporating spin-induced electric polarization via the KNB mechanism. The dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian including exchange couplings ($J_1, J_2$) and an electric field interaction term.

**Key observables.** Bipartite negativity ($N_{ij}$) and tripartite negativity ($N_{ABC}$), which quantify quantum entanglement; also analyzed are the saturation magnetic field ($B_{	ext{sat}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electric field magnitude ($E$), orientation ($\phi$), bond angle ($	heta$), exchange coupling ratios ($J_1/J_2$), and non-uniformity parameter ($\alpha$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system is modeled using a spin-1/2 Heisenberg Hamiltonian for a trinuclear molecule, and the analysis focuses on ground state properties.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how bipartite negativity varies with the electric field angle $\phi$ (showing distinct lines for different pairs) and density plots mapping entanglement extrema over the $(\alpha, E/J_2)$ parameter space.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops by first defining the Hamiltonian incorporating KNB coupling, then analyzing the system's ground states and magnetic saturation field dependence on external fields. The core is dedicated to calculating and demonstrating the controllable transfer of bipartite entanglement using varying electric field parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate quantum entanglement in a spin-1/2 Heisenberg trimer with spin-induced electric polarization described by the Katsura-Nagaosa-Balatsky (KNB) mechanism in the presence of external magnetic and electric fields. The electric field is assumed to lie in the plane of the magnetic ions, allowing its strength and orientation to be tuned independently. We analyze both bipartite and tripartite entanglement and demonstrate that the spin-electric-field coupling provides an efficient mechanism for controlling quantum correlations within the molecular nanomagnet. Depending on the electric-field parameters, the bipartite entanglement can be significantly enhanced or suppressed, while the multipartite entanglement exhibits a rich dependence on the microscopic spin-electric coupling. Most notably, we demonstrate that a rotating in-plane electric field of constant magnitude induces a controllable transfer of bipartite entanglement between different spin pairs. In the symmetric case of homogeneous exchange interactions and uniform KNB coupling, this transfer is found to be nearly ideal, with the bipartite negativity approaching its theoretical maximum for one spin pair while simultaneously vanishing for the remaining pairs. We show that the efficiency of the transfer can be tailored through the exchange interactions, bond geometry, and nonuniform spin-electric coupling. These results establish molecular nanomagnets with KNB spin-electric coupling as a promising platform for the electrical manipulation, steering, and localization of quantum entanglement at the molecular scale.

</details>

**Summary.** This experiment demonstrates precise control over up-conversion luminescence by placing rare-earth nanocrystals near metallic nanowires separated by a polymer spacer. By tuning this separation distance, the emission can be switched between quenching, plasmonically enhanced glowing, or isolated behavior. This offers a powerful tool for designing nanophotonic structures with tailored optical properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a clean experimental platform to study open quantum systems dynamics (energy relaxation) where coupling to an external environment (the plasmonic metal) can be tuned deterministically via geometry. The measurement of decay rate changes directly probes the modification of the local photonic density of states, which is central to cavity QED and open system theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to achieve precise, distance-controlled manipulation of energy decay pathways in up-conversion luminescence by controlling the separation between rare-earth nanocrystals and metallic nanowires.

**Main result.** By tuning the polymer spacer thickness, the emission can be deterministically switched between three regimes: quenching (direct contact), plasmonic enhancement (intermediate distance), and effective decoupling (large distance).

**Method.** The researchers used time-resolved fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy ($\mu$s-FLIM) on single nanostructures to map luminescence intensity and decay times as a function of the emitter-metal separation.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a hybrid nanostructure comprising $	ext{NaYF}_4:	ext{Er}^{3+}/	ext{Yb}^{3+}$ up-conversion nanocrystals placed near silver nanowires, separated by a polymer spacer layer (PVA).

**Key observables.** Luminescence intensity maps and fluorescence decay times ($	au$) measured via $\mu$s-FLIM.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The separation distance ($d$), controlled by the PVA thickness (e.g., $0 	ext{ nm}$, $20 	ext{ nm}$, $65 	ext{ nm}$), is the key tuning parameter.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that eliminating residual polymer layers allows for unambiguous interpretation of distance-dependent effects, and that the observed enhancement/quenching reflects controlled coupling to plasmon modes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic control over geometry using PVA thickness (Fig. 1), show PL intensity maps demonstrating quenching vs. enhancement based on separation (Fig. 4), and map decay times confirming changes in radiative rates (Fig. 5).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically presents sample preparation details, followed by characterization of the three distinct interaction regimes—quenching, enhancement, and decoupling—using PL imaging and time-resolved lifetime measurements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We demonstrate controlled transitions between competing radiative and nonradiative decay channels in the up-conversion luminescence of NaYF4:Er3+/Yb3+ nanocrystals placed in proximity to metallic nanowires. The nanocrystal-nanowire separation is used as a key control parameter governing the optical response. An essential aspect of our approach is the removal of inhomogeneous residual polymer layers from the nanowires, eliminating any compromise on distance control and reproducibility in emitter-metal hybrid nanostructures. Replacing them with a well-defined polymer spacer yields controlled access to three qualitatively distinct interaction regimes: luminescence quenching, plasmonic enhancement, and effective decoupling. Transitions between these regimes are shown to reflect changes in the dominant energy relaxation pathways: from nonradiative losses in direct contact with the metal, through modification of the local photonic density of states and coupling to plasmon-mediated modes, to behavior characteristic of quasi-isolated emitters. The plasmonic origin of the emission enhancement in the intermediate regime is evidenced by an increase in luminescence intensity accompanied by shortened decay times, as revealed by fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy of up-conversion nanocrystals. All experiments were performed on single nanostructures, thereby excluding artefacts arising from aggregation effects and strengthening the interpretation of the observed phenomena. The presented approach provides controlled access to plasmon-modified decay channels and offers a basis for the rational design of functional nanophotonic and sensing structures with tailored optical properties.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a sophisticated Lindblad-based linear response formalism to accurately characterize the electrical response of complex hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots. It moves beyond standard Kubo treatments by incorporating non-unitary effects via 'Hermes' and 'Sisyphus' susceptibilities. The theory is demonstrated on Kitaev chain models, showing how these advanced terms are crucial for correctly interpreting measurements like qubit readout fidelity.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems as it provides advanced tools (Lindblad response theory) to model dissipation and measurement back-action in solid-state quantum devices like superconducting qubits.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the need for a comprehensive theoretical framework to understand the response of complex hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots (SCQDs) to external probes and environmental dissipation.

**Main result.** It demonstrates that a full Lindblad linear response formalism is necessary, showing that contributions like 'Hermes' terms compensate decoherence effects in dispersive readout and provide corrections beyond simple thermalized state approximations.

**Method.** The authors develop and apply a Lindblad-based linear response formalism to calculate the system susceptibility ($\chi$), decomposing it into static, Hamiltonian, Sisyphus, and Hermes contributions.

**Model / system.** The primary model is hybrid SCQD devices, exemplified by quantum dot-based Kitaev chain setups used for Majorana-based parity qubits. Dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation, and the analysis focuses on calculating susceptibility components derived from this formalism.

**Key observables.** Linear-response susceptibility ($\chi(\omega)$), Quantum Capacitance ($C_Q$), static susceptibility ($\chi_{st}$), Hamiltonian contribution ($\chi_H$), Sisyphus susceptibility ($\chi_\Gamma$), and Hermes susceptibility ($\chi_L$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Frequency ($\omega$), temperature ($T$), coupling strength ($\Delta, t$), and detuning parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on the Born-Markov approximations (weakly coupled environment with no memory) and analyzes the system within the linear response regime.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate parameter fluctuations contributing to observables, compare various susceptibility terms ($\chi_{st}, \chi_H, \chi_\Gamma, \chi_L$) against theoretical predictions like band curvature, and show parity state differentiation in common gate spectroscopy.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the general Lindblad linear response formalism for N-level systems. It then applies this theory to minimal Kitaev junctions, deriving specific expressions for the four susceptibility components ($\chi_{st}, \chi_H, \chi_\Gamma, \chi_L$). Finally, it analyzes these contributions in the context of quantum capacitance and parity state spectroscopy.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The field of hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots is advancing toward the development of functional devices that leverage the advantages of both types of materials. However, the inherent complexity of these devices demands a comprehensive theoretical framework for a complete understanding of their responses to external probes, readout and the dissipation arising from environmental coupling. We present a Lindblad-based linear response formalism that captures the multi-level nature of these devices, their probe-readout flexibility, and the non-unitary effects of finite-frequency response, including the so-called Sisyphus and Hermes dynamical susceptibilities. These arise from fluctuations in the rates and jump operators, and are hence absent in standard Kubo linear response treatments. We exemplify the framework using quantum dot-based Kitaev chain setups which are promising candidates for topologically protected Majorana-based parity qubits. Our results shed light onto the validity of the standard curvature-based approximation for fermionic parity and qubit readout, show that Hermes terms compensate decoherence in dispersive readout and implement important corrections beyond thermalized states.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper reports the experimental observation of spin-momentum locking (SML) in polariton edge states within honeycomb lattices. By exploiting the inherent spin-orbit coupling from cavity geometry, they demonstrate that counter-propagating edge modes carry opposite circular polarizations. This effect is leveraged to achieve all-optical control over light directionality via spin-selective lasing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an optical analogue for realizing robust chiral transport phenomena, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and condensed matter physics concerning topological edge states and spin-orbit coupling effects in artificial systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to demonstrate spin-momentum locking (SML) of polariton edge states and achieve ultrafast, all-optical control over their directional propagation without external magnetic fields.

**Main result.** SML is confirmed in the zigzag edge states of honeycomb exciton-polariton lattices via polarization measurements. Furthermore, selective lasing using spin-polarized injection enables switching the direction of light flow by changing the pump helicity.

**Method.** The study combines experimental characterization using micro-photoluminescence with full Stokes polarimetry and theoretical modeling based on effective Hamiltonian descriptions for photonic lattices.

**Model / system.** The system is an exciton-polariton honeycomb lattice realized in GaAs-based semiconductor microcavities. The physics is governed by an effective spin-orbit coupling arising from TE/TM splitting, which dictates the polarization of edge states.

**Key observables.** Circular polarization ($S_3$), degree of elliptical polarization, and directional emission observed via $\sigma^+$ vs $\sigma^-$ pumping in both linear and gapped lattice geometries.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The TE-TM coupling strength ($\Omega_{TE-TM}$), the complex wavevector associated with evanescent fields ($\lambda_y$), and the lasing threshold power ($P_{th}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** SML is shown to be an intrinsic property arising solely from the exponentially localized nature of edge states, independent of external magnetic fields.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate SEM images of zigzag edges, simulated band structures showing opposite spin polarization for counter-propagating modes, and experimental maps demonstrating directional switching of emission based on pump helicity above lasing threshold.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the argument by first establishing the theoretical origin of SML from TE-TM splitting in edge states. It then presents experimental evidence using polarimetry to confirm this locking in both normal and stretched honeycomb lattices, culminating in a demonstration of spin-controlled directional lasing.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Transverse-electric/Transverse-magnetic splitting in dielectric-mirror microcavities introduces an effective spin-orbit coupling for photons. While the bulk states remain linearly polarized, for exponentially localized edge states in a photonic lattice, this coupling induces elliptical polarization whose handedness is locked to the propagation direction, analogous to the transverse spin of evanescent electromagnetic waves. We reveal spin-momentum locking through Stokes polarimetry of zigzag edge states in a honeycomb exciton-polariton lattice. The effect persists in a stretched honeycomb supporting a photonic bandgap, where spin-polarized carrier injection enables selective lasing of either chiral edge states. Our results provide a route toward ultrafast spin-controlled unidirectional propagation in polariton systems without external magnetic fields.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors report achieving tunable nonlinear dynamics in graphene NEMS by exploiting internal resonances induced by a gate voltage. They demonstrate the device's ability to generate controlled frequency combs and undergo predictable period-doubling cascades. This shows that a single, gated solid-state device can act as multiple functional components (multiplier, comb source) on demand.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a solid-state platform to study fundamental nonlinear dynamics (like those seen in classical optics or Josephson junctions) using mechanical resonators, offering an accessible quantum/classical analog system for studying complex bifurcations and energy transfer mechanisms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research demonstrates tunable nonlinear dynamics in a solid-state nanomechanical system, specifically observing high-harmonic generation (HHG) and frequency comb formation.

**Main result.** By tuning the gate voltage to induce an internal resonance, the graphene device can function as a switchable source for integer harmonics, broadband combs, or chaotic signals via controlled period-doubling transitions.

**Method.** The study combines experimental measurements using optical interferometry with theoretical modeling based on coupled nonlinear oscillator equations and harmonic balance techniques.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a suspended monolayer graphene drumhead NEMS resonator. The dynamics are governed by an effective potential incorporating quadratic ($\zeta$) and cubic ($eta$) nonlinear terms, which are tunable via an applied gate voltage ($V_{dc}$).

**Key observables.** Integer harmonics ($n\omega_d$), dense frequency combs, period-doubling cascades, and the measurable nonlinear coefficients $\zeta$ and $eta$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate voltage ($V_{dc}$) used to tune nonlinearity; achieving 1:2 internal resonance ($\omega_2 \approx 2\omega_0$) is critical for strong coupling.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on modeling the system using coupled equations of motion and employing techniques like harmonic balance or steady-state amplitude fitting.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate spectral maps showing transitions from single peaks to combs, followed by period doubling. Resonance dispersion plots show how the fundamental and higher modes couple as a function of gate voltage.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical setup and model potential, then details experimental measurements across varying drive amplitudes and frequencies. The core results demonstrate the sequence: IHG $ightarrow$ Comb Formation $ightarrow$ Reverse Period-Doubling, confirming control over nonlinear regimes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nonlinear nanomechanical resonators give convenient solid-state access to classical analogs of extreme nonlinear optics and to phononic signal processing. Here we report integer high-harmonic generation and phononic frequency combs in a suspended monolayer graphene drum. A gate voltage breaks the out-of-plane symmetry of the membrane and tunes its fundamental flexural mode onto a 1:2 internal resonance with a higher mode at twice the frequency, where the quadratic coupling between the two modes becomes large. A single drive tone then generates phase-locked integer harmonics in sequence, and at larger drive these fill in to a dense frequency comb. Raising the drive further, we find a reverse period-doubling transition: the comb spacing doubles, the line density halves, and energy flows back into the even-order comb lines. The measured spectra yield the quadratic ($ζ$) and cubic ($β$) nonlinear coefficients of the membrane. These results show how the tunable nonlinear landscape of graphene supports distinct dynamical regimes on demand, allowing a single gated device to act in turn as a frequency multiplier, a broadband comb source, and a chaotic generator.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a theory to calculate the finite-frequency magnetic common bath experienced by two spin probes inside a ferromagnetic cavity. By utilizing the retarded magnetic Green tensor, the authors derive key coupling kernels ($\gamma_{12}, \Omega_{12}$) that quantify dynamic interactions. The results provide measurable predictions for linewidth splitting and Lamb shifts in solid-state quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for quantifying dynamic coupling mechanisms between quantum emitters mediated by structured magnetic environments, extending static results into the frequency domain relevant for modern quantum sensing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is formulating and evaluating the finite-frequency magnetic common bath experienced by two spin probes situated within a ferromagnetic planar cavity.

**Main result.** The work successfully derives finite-frequency counterparts for static coupling shifts, yielding measurable off-diagonal linewidth splitting and collective Lamb shift kernels ($\gamma_{12}, \Omega_{12}$).

**Method.** The analysis employs macroscopic Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) by calculating the retarded magnetic Green tensor ($\mathbf{G}_{	ext{BB}}$) projected onto a scalar TE channel.

**Model / system.** The system consists of two spin probes coupled via a common bath mediated by a finite-thickness ferromagnetic film deposited on a nonmagnetic substrate. The coupling is modeled using the transverse diagonal Polder permeability ($\mu_{\perp}(\omega, \mathbf{B})$).

**Key observables.** Common-bath kernels ($\gamma_{12}$ and $\Omega_{12}$), linewidth splitting, and collective Lamb shift.

**Important parameters / regimes.** GHz probe transition frequencies, millikelvin temperatures, film thickness ($t=200\,\mathrm{nm}$), and cavity separation ($ho=3\,\mu\mathrm{m}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model simplifies the full planar response by using a scalar TE channel projection, neglecting TE–TM conversion and nonreciprocal off-diagonal Polder responses.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the geometry of two probes coupled via a ferromagnetic film. Comparisons are made between finite-thickness cavity integrals (e.g., $\delta\gamma_{\perp}^{12}/2\pi$) and static benchmarks derived from image series calculations.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first defining the common bath kernels using the magnetic Green tensor, then deriving the necessary reflection coefficients for a finite slab structure, and finally applying these to calculate observable quantities like linewidth splitting in specific physical regimes (e.g., near-field).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We formulate the finite-frequency magnetic common bath of two spin probes in a ferromagnetic planar cavity. The probes couple to the retarded magnetic Green tensor of the cavity, whose imaginary and real parts determine the collective decay kernel \(γ_{12}\) and the Lamb-shift kernel \(Ω_{12}\). We evaluate these kernels for a finite-thickness scalar TE channel formed by a ferromagnetic film on a nonmagnetic conducting substrate, using the transverse diagonal Polder permeability \(μ_\perp(ω,B)\) as the magnetic input. The normalization is fixed by the free-space magnetic-dipole decay rate. In the \(ω\to0\) limit, the constant-reflection benchmark reproduces the static image-series reference, while the finite slab retains the corresponding static TE reflection amplitude. For a \(t=200\,\mathrm{nm}\) film described by a representative Ni-like parameter set in a micron-scale mid-gap cavity, the GHz probe transition samples the positive-frequency response of the body-assisted magnetic reservoir at millikelvin temperature. On resonance, the off-diagonal linewidth splitting reaches about two thirds of the single-spin scattering linewidth at \(ρ=3\,μ\mathrm m\). The resulting linewidth splitting and collective Lamb shift provide finite-frequency counterparts of the static TE coupling-frequency shift.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the nonlinear sensitivity of phononic frequency combs using a reduced two-mode resonance model. By mapping how observables like amplitude and frequency change with detuning, drive strength, and damping, the authors reveal that sensitivity is highly structured, governed by distinct physical mechanisms like parametric resonance thresholds. This provides a roadmap for engineering these systems for advanced sensing applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed map of nonlinear control parameters for an artificial quantum/classical system (PFCs), offering blueprints for designing sensing platforms where specific physical changes induce predictable, measurable shifts in spectral features.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how the observable properties (amplitude and frequency) of phononic frequency combs respond to variations in physical parameters, quantifying their nonlinear sensitivity.

**Main result.** Sensitivity is highly non-uniform: primary detuning causes smooth shifts, secondary detuning creates sharp transitions near resonance manifolds, and peak sensitivity concentrates near the activation threshold. This points to a common origin in autoparametric resonance and saturation.

**Method.** The authors employed numerical investigation of a reduced two-mode autoparametric resonance model derived from underlying mechanical equations.

**Model / system.** The system is Phononic Frequency Combs (PFCs), modeled by coupled, first-order ordinary differential equations describing the complex envelopes ($\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$) of primary and secondary modes. The dynamics are governed by detunings, drive amplitude, and relative damping.

**Key observables.** Amplitude ($|\psi_i|^2$), frequency ($\omega_{\psi_i}$), mean intensity, peak-to-peak amplitude, and differential sensitivity across parameter space.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Primary detuning ($\Delta_1$), secondary detuning ($\Delta_2$), drive amplitude ($f$), and relative damping ($\gamma_{21}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes slow variation of complex envelopes relative to carrier lines, allowing reduction from second-order to first-order ODEs.

**Figures summary.** Figures map sensitivity across parameter planes (e.g., $\Delta_2$ vs $f$) showing sharp resonance ridges and threshold boundaries; frequency plots show abrupt jumps near critical detuning values.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the response to each perturbation ($\Delta_1$, $\Delta_2$, $\gamma_{21}$, $f$), first examining steady-state amplitudes, then mapping the differential sensitivity of both amplitude and frequency across various parameter combinations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Phononic frequency combs offer a rich platform for nonlinear sensing, yet how their observable properties respond to changes in physical parameters remains poorly understood. Using a reduced two-mode autoparametric resonance model, we investigate how primary and secondary detuning, drive amplitude, and relative damping jointly shape amplitude and frequency sensitivity across the nonlinear parameter space. We find that sensitivity is far from uniform: primary detuning shifts the comb response smoothly, secondary detuning produces sharply localized transitions near resonance manifolds, and drive amplitude concentrates peak sensitivity close to the activation threshold rather than deep within the comb state. The relative damping redistributes energy continuously between modes without introducing discontinuities. The nonlinear sensitivity of amplitude and frequency observables across all parameters points to a common physical origin in autoparametric resonance, nonlinear saturation, and coupling-induced synchronization, offering a coherent basis for designing nonlinear sensing platforms with deliberate, parameter-aware sensitivity engineering.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops an effective field theory for relativistic superfluids carrying spin angular momentum. By incorporating topological terms into the action, the authors derive novel physical consequences such as modified transport relations and anomalous effects. It provides a rigorous framework for understanding how spin dynamics modify the macroscopic energy-momentum tensor of these exotic quantum fluids.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on high-energy/condensed matter theory, the derivation of generalized conserved currents and anomalous response terms (like Hall viscosity) shares mathematical structure with open quantum systems dynamics where dissipation and non-equilibrium responses are key.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper constructs an effective field theory description for relativistic superfluids that possess a non-zero angular momentum density (spinful superfluids). It aims to derive the resulting physical transport properties.

**Main result.** The theory yields several novel effects, including the relativistic Mermin-Ho relation and anomalous transport phenomena like the anomalous Ettingshausen effect. The stress-energy tensor is shown to acquire one-derivative corrections due to spin dynamics.

**Method.** The analysis uses an effective action approach involving topological terms derived from a two-form current $J$. Equations of motion are derived by varying this action with respect to gauge fields and spin components.

**Model / system.** The model is a relativistic superfluid, applicable to systems like quark matter or superfluid Helium-3, characterized by Cooper pairs carrying angular momentum. The theory treats the dynamics using effective field theory techniques in curved spacetime.

**Key observables.** Stress-energy tensor ($T^{\mu
u}$), spin current ($\Sigma^{\mu\alphaeta}$), anomalous Ettingshausen effect coefficient ($q_{AE}$), and magnetization current ($j^\mu$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The topological coefficient $s$ (assumed constant) and the low-energy expansion order (one-derivative corrections).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is limited to one-derivative corrections in the effective Lagrangian, and it assumes a specific form for the superfluid condensate dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from the general construction of the effective action incorporating spin degrees of freedom, derives conservation laws for energy and momentum, analyzes the resulting stress-energy tensor corrections, and finally identifies specific anomalous transport effects.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We construct an effective field theory description of relativistic superfluids with nonzero angular momentum density. At first order in the derivative expansion, the effective action contains a term with a quantized coefficient, which encodes the Berry phase for the angular momentum of the superfluid condensate. From this single term we derive a number of physical effects, including the relativistic Mermin-Ho relation, an anomalous Ettingshausen effect (exchangeable for an anomalous Hall effect), and an anomalous Hall viscosity.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the nonlinear Hall effect in Floquet-driven 1T'-MoS2 to characterize engineered topological phases. The key finding is that a sign reversal in the NHE conductivity provides an unambiguous signature of these transitions, distinguishing them from simple parameter tuning. This establishes the material as a viable platform for all-electrical detection of non-equilibrium topology.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of non-equilibrium optical driving to induce and probe topological phases is highly relevant for AMO physics, particularly concerning how external fields (like light) can engineer quantum states in solid-state systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to establish a universal transport fingerprint for Floquet-engineered topology by investigating the nonlinear Hall effect (NHE) in driven 2D materials.

**Main result.** A sign reversal in the NHE conductivity, which coincides with optically induced band inversions and gap closings, serves as an unambiguous signature of genuine topological phase transitions.

**Method.** The analysis employs a high-frequency Floquet effective Hamiltonian derived from coupling to circularly polarized light and utilizes nonlinear semiclassical transport theory.

**Model / system.** The system is monolayer 1T'-MoS2, modeled as a low-symmetry quantum spin Hall material with intrinsic Berry-curvature dipole moments. The driving mechanism involves off-resonant circularly polarized light applied via minimal coupling.

**Key observables.** Nonlinear Hall conductivity (chi_xyy), Berry-curvature dipole moment (D_y), and the total Chern number of the occupied band.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Floquet drive strength ($\xi$), perpendicular electric field ($E_z$, controlled by $\alpha$), Fermi energy ($E_F$), and temperature ($T$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the off-resonant high-frequency (van Vleck) expansion for the Floquet effective Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate how D_y changes sign only when the gap closes due to driving ($\xi$), contrasting this with monotonic changes observed when tuning band tilt or electric field alone. Temperature dependence shows signal suppression at higher T.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the model and Hamiltonian, then calculates topological invariants (Chern number) under Floquet driving. The core argument links sign reversals in the Berry-curvature dipole moment to these topological phase transitions, demonstrating this link via the NHE measurement, and finally explores control knobs like electric field and temperature.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the nonlinear Hall effect in Floquet-driven monolayer \(1T'\)-MoS\(_2\), a low-symmetry quantum spin Hall material whose tilted Dirac bands sustain an intrinsic Berry-curvature dipole without the need for strain or trigonal warping. We show that off-resonant circularly polarized light offers a way to control both the sign and the magnitude of the nonlinear Hall response through optically induced topological phase transitions using a Floquet effective Hamiltonian and nonlinear semiclassical transport theory. We show that the anisotropic crystal symmetry enforces a selection rule in which the Berry-curvature dipole elements satisfy $D_x\equiv0$, while a finite $D_y$ originates from the intrinsic band tilt. The Berry curvature is recreated in momentum space as the Floquet drive successively inverts individual spin-valley sectors, resulting in an identical sign reversal of the nonlinear Hall conductivity and the Berry-curvature dipole at each bulk gap closing. In contrast, tuning the band tilt modifies only the magnitude of the response without changing its sign, establishing the observed sign reversal as an unambiguous transport signature of genuine Floquet topological phase transitions. We further show that the nonlinear Hall response can be controlled by the driving strength, perpendicular electric field, Fermi energy, and temperature, providing multiple experimental knobs for observation. Our findings establish the sign of the nonlinear Hall response as a universal transport fingerprint of Floquet-engineered topology and point to monolayer \(1T'\)-MoS\(_2\) as a viable platform for all-electrical detection of nonequilibrium topological phases.

</details>
