**Summary.** This work investigates current-driven oscillations in synthetic antiferromagnets using spin-orbit torque. By measuring the spin-rectification voltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{SRE}}$), the authors demonstrated that self-oscillations emerge above a critical DC current threshold, exhibiting characteristic signatures of injection locking. This establishes SAF nanoconstrictions as a viable platform for studying nonlinear spintronic oscillators.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on spintronics, the study of driven, non-equilibrium collective excitations (self-oscillations) in magnetic systems shares conceptual links with open quantum system dynamics and nonlinear response theory relevant to AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to demonstrate and characterize spin-orbit torque (SOT)-driven self-oscillatory dynamics in synthetic antiferromagnets (SAFs) using electrical measurements.

**Main result.** The research successfully identified low-field, current-induced peaks in the spin-rectification voltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{SRE}}$), interpreted as signatures of current-selected chiral self-oscillations and injection locking near the spin-flop transition.

**Method.** The study combines electrical measurements (spin-rectification spectroscopy) with theoretical modeling, utilizing both micromagnetic simulations and macrospin approximations.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a nanoconstriction patterned from a synthetic antiferromagnet (SAF) multilayer stack. The dynamics are governed by exchange coupling, spin-orbit torque (SOT), and applied DC/RF currents.

**Key observables.** Spin-rectification voltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{SRE}}$), acoustic and optical eigenmode resonance frequencies, Power Spectral Density (PSD) features indicating self-oscillation onset and injection locking.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Critical DC current threshold ($J_{above}^{dc}$), applied magnetic field ($\vec{H}$), RF frequency range ($2	ext{ GHz}$ to $12	ext{ GHz}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The observed $	ext{V}_{	ext{SRE}}$ peaks are interpreted as electrical signatures of self-oscillatory dynamics, rather than direct emission detection.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the SAF structure and patterned device; they show distinct resonance peaks for acoustic/optical modes (Fig. 1d); simulation results demonstrate threshold excitation of oscillations in PSDs (Fig. 2b); and $	ext{V}_{	ext{SRE}}$ measurements confirm current-dependent, self-oscillatory signatures (Fig. 3).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the linear eigenmodes via SRE spectroscopy across different angles ($\Phi$). It then investigates nonlinear dynamics by observing that additional peaks appear only when a DC current exceeds a critical threshold, confirming self-oscillation and subsequent injection locking.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Antiferromagnets offer a promising route toward robust spintronic devices because of their compensated magnetic order and exchange-enhanced spin dynamics. Here, we demonstrate a spin-orbit torque (SOT)-driven antiferromagnetic oscillator based on a nanoconstriction patterned from a synthetic antiferromagnet (SAF). Spin-rectification spectroscopy reveals electrical excitation of both acoustic and optical SAF eigenmodes, whose field and frequency dependences are quantitatively described by an antiferromagnetic resonance model. In addition to these linear eigenmodes, we observe low-field spin-rectification peaks that emerge only above a threshold DC current near the spin-flop transition. Their current-polarity-dependent sign and locking to an injected RF frequency provide electrical spin-rectification signatures consistent with current-selected chiral self-oscillatory dynamics. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce the threshold excitation of SOT-driven self-oscillations and injection locking, while macrospin simulations predict stable and chaotic nonlinear dynamics within the same spin-flop region. We interpret the multi-peak, weakly RF-frequency-dependent responses as a qualitative signature of complex nonlinear dynamics. These results establish SAF nanoconstrictions as an experimentally accessible platform for studying current-driven antiferromagnetic-like oscillator dynamics and motivate future work on nonlinear spintronic devices for signal processing and reservoir-computing concepts.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper theoretically investigates the pseudo-superconducting-diode effect in ferroelectric Josephson junctions by coupling superconducting dynamics with ferroelectric polarization switching. Using a coupled dynamical model solved numerically, the authors show that current sweeping induces nonreciprocal supercurrents due to history-dependent polarization changes. This confirms FE-JJs as tunable platforms for field-free nonreciprocal electronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work models a complex interplay between quantum coherence (superconductivity) and classical/emergent order parameters (ferroelectricity), which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where dissipation and environmental coupling drive macroscopic effects.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The authors investigate the pseudo-superconducting-diode effect (SDE) in ferroelectric Josephson junctions, which manifests as nonreciprocal critical and retrapping supercurrents.

**Main result.** They demonstrate that this nonreciprocity is a history-dependent, non-equilibrium phenomenon arising from current-induced polarization switching, confirming FE-JJs as promising field-free devices.

**Method.** The study employs a coupled dynamical model combining the Resistively and Capacitively Shunted Junction (RCSJ) description with Landau-Khalatnikov-Tani ferroelectric dynamics, solved via numerical simulations including thermal noise.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an inversion-asymmetric Ferroelectric Josephson Junction (FE-JJ). The model couples the superconducting phase dynamics ($\phi$) governed by a polarization-dependent RCSJ equation with the ferroelectric polarization ($P$) governed by the LKT equation.

**Key observables.** Asymmetric critical and retrapping supercurrents ($i_{c\pm}, i_{r\pm}$), diode efficiency ($\eta$), time-averaged voltage, and polarization switching dynamics.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Ferroelectric parameters (e.g., $	heta P_0$), temperature ($T$), and the bias current sweep protocol are crucial for tuning the nonreciprocity.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes validity of linear approximations for critical current dependence on polarization in some contexts, and thermal noise is modeled as Gaussian white noise.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic setups, hysteresis loops showing voltage/polarization under sweeps (comparing P-RCSJ to conventional RCSJ), histograms of currents at finite T, and time evolution during switching events.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the coupled dynamical model using Lagrangian formalism, deriving equations of motion for both superconducting and ferroelectric components, simulating current sweeps to observe hysteresis and polarization switching, and finally analyzing the temperature dependence of the resulting nonreciprocity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The superconducting diode effect (SDE), characterized by unequal critical supercurrents in opposite current directions, enables supercurrent rectification. We propose a magnetic-field-free pseudo-superconducting-diode effect in ferroelectric Josephson junctions with broken inversion symmetry. Using a coupled dynamical model that combines a polarization-dependent RCSJ description with Landau-Khalatnikov-Tani ferroelectric dynamics, we show that ferroelectric polarization switching induces asymmetric critical and retrapping currents under current sweeps. The resulting nonreciprocity is highly tunable via ferroelectric parameters and the sweep protocol and remains robust at finite temperatures. Our work identifies ferroelectric Josephson junctions as a promising platform for magnetic-field-free nonreciprocal superconducting devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically demonstrates that OAM dichroism in vortex light is forbidden in uniform crystalline media. By introducing nonuniform strain into a 2D Dirac material, the authors show how transverse momentum transfer can be supplied via a pseudo-gauge field. This allows for a measurable, non-zero OAM-odd optical conductivity, opening a pathway for differential optical measurements of strain effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects topological light properties (OAM) with material strain engineering in 2D electron systems, providing a concrete mechanism for optical detection of subtle symmetry breaking effects relevant to condensed matter physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research investigates the mechanism by which Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) dichroism of vortex light can be generated in condensed matter systems, overcoming theoretical no-go theorems.

**Main result.** Nonuniform strain in a 2D Dirac material bypasses the no-go condition, allowing for a measurable OAM-odd conductivity ($\sim 10^{-3}e^2/\hbar$) through the coupling of vortex phase current with the strain field.

**Method.** The analysis uses theoretical derivations involving nonlocal response functions, factorizing the dichroism into an elasto-optic tensor and a geometric overlap term derived from Green's function techniques.

**Model / system.** The model employs a two-dimensional Dirac material Hamiltonian, specifically incorporating nonuniform strain (modeled as a Gaussian bubble) to break translational symmetry. The analysis considers both interband and intraband contributions to the optical response.

**Key observables.** OAM dichroism ($\Delta\sigma_{OAM}$), nonlocal elasto-optic tensor ($\Lambda^{(s)}_{ab}$), and Geometric Overlap Tensor ($B^{(\ell)}_{ab}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strain amplitude ($\alpha$), beam waist ($w_0$), bubble displacement ($d$), and the ratio of material parameters defining valley inequivalence.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on perturbative expansions in strain/momentum transfer (Q) and assumes specific limits for integrals, such as $k=0$ for intraband calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical setup (vortex light on strained material), show the dependence of the geometric overlap term on displacement, and plot resonant enhancements of material coefficients near resonance.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the no-go theorem for OAM dichroism in translationally invariant systems. It then introduces strain as the necessary symmetry breaker, developing theoretical frameworks to calculate the nonlocal elasto-optic tensor ($\Lambda$) and the geometric overlap ($B$). Finally, it calculates these terms for specific Dirac models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Vortex light carries orbital angular momentum (OAM) in its transverse phase, unlike spin, which is encoded in polarization. We show that this phase cannot produce OAM dichroism in any continuously translation-invariant system, even when optical nonlocality and multipole light--matter coupling are included. Nonuniform strain in a two-dimensional Dirac material bypasses this no-go condition by supplying transverse momentum transfer through a long-wavelength pseudo-gauge field, so that the OAM dichroism factorizes into a nonlocal elasto-optic tensor and the overlap of the vortex transverse phase current with the strain field. For a micron-scale Gaussian bubble, the resonant OAM-odd conductivity reaches \(\sim10^{-3}e^2/\hbar\), within reach of differential optical measurements.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes realizing multiple Majorana zero modes by coupling chiral hinge states within a higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) when placed in proximity to an s-wave superconductor. This establishes a promising platform for detecting and utilizing Majorana corner states.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete theoretical blueprint for engineering multiple, spatially separated Majorana modes using established material platforms (HOTIs), which is highly relevant for designing fault-tolerant quantum hardware architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work proposes a theoretical route to realize spatially separated Majorana zero modes (MZMs) by coupling chiral hinge states in a higher-order topological insulator (HOTI). This aims to create a platform for studying topological superconductivity.

**Main result.** By confining the system and inducing superconducting proximity effects, the model predicts the formation of four robust localized MZMs at the corners of the quasi-two-dimensional sample. These corner modes are stable against weak disorder as long as the bulk gap remains open.

**Method.** The study employs theoretical modeling using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian to analyze the superconducting proximity effect on chiral hinge states derived from a HOTI model.

**Model / system.** The system is a quasi-two-dimensional realization of a chiral HOTI proximitized by an s-wave superconductor. The physics relies on gapless hinge states along one direction, which hybridize upon finite-size confinement to form helical channels exhibiting effective p-wave pairing.

**Key observables.** Localized Majorana zero modes (MZMs) at the corners; robust zero-bias conductance peaks detectable via STM spectroscopy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The chemical potential ($\mu$) relative to the reconstructed hinge bands, and the superconducting gap amplitude ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach assumes that chiral hinge states are experimentally accessible in magnetic topological insulators and that the proximity effect induces effective p-wave pairing.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic geometry of the quasi-2D system, show energy spectra confirming gapless hinge states (Fig. 2), demonstrate the opening of a topological gap leading to localized MZMs (Figs. 3(b)-(d)), and confirm robustness against disorder (Fig. 7).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the argument by first establishing chiral hinge states in the HOTI, then incorporating s-wave pairing via the BdG Hamiltonian, demonstrating the finite-size coupling mechanism to localize MZMs, and finally verifying their topological protection against disorder.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in topological superconductors have attracted broad research interest for their potential applications in topological quantum computation. In this work, we propose a quasi-two-dimensional route to realize spatially separated MZMs in a chiral higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) proximitized by a conventional $s$-wave superconductor through a theoretical model study. In three dimensions, the chiral HOTI hosts gapless hinge states along the $z$ direction, arising from a mass term that anisotropically gaps the surface Dirac cones of a topological insulator. By confining the sample along the $x$ direction while keeping it extended along $y$ and finite along $z$, opposite $z$-directed chiral hinge states hybridize and effectively form one-dimensional helical channels. Incorporating the superconducting proximity effect into this quasi-two-dimensional system induces effective $p$-wave pairing in these helical channels, thereby opening a topological gap. A fully open-boundary sample then hosts four localized MZMs, one at each endpoint of the helical channels, realizing a second-order topological superconductor characterized by Majorana corner modes. In addition to MZMs, we also find that superconducting pairing in this model produces extended Majorana hinge modes in three dimensions. Furthermore, representative disorder calculations indicate that these Majorana corner modes are robust against weak-to-moderate disorder, provided the excitation gap remains open. These results establish finite-size-coupled chiral hinge states as a promising platform for engineering multiple MZMs via conventional superconducting proximity effect.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an advanced calibration protocol to correct systematic optical distortions in complex, custom cryo-optical setups used for localizing quantum emitters. By modeling these distortions using a Zernike vector-field approach and validating it with nanodisk arrays, the authors significantly improved absolute positioning accuracy. This method offers a practical pathway to deterministically integrating quantum light sources into scalable photonic circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to experimental quantum optics and open quantum systems as it provides a critical metrological tool necessary to translate high-precision statistical measurements into reliable absolute positioning required for building functional quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The ultimate integration yield of quantum emitters into photonic structures is limited by uncorrected systematic optical distortions inherent in custom cryo-optical setups, even when statistical localization uncertainty is low.

**Main result.** An *in situ* calibration protocol using a Zernike vector-field model reduced the residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm and improved emission polarization variance by 49% upon application to deterministic fabrication.

**Method.** The authors developed an in situ metrological calibration framework that models field-dependent coordinate offsets using a Zernike polynomial expansion, applied to lithographically defined reference arrays.

**Model / system.** The experiment uses quantum emitter localization microscopy on semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) within custom cryo-optical setups. The systematic distortions are modeled mathematically using the Zernike vector-field model for correction.

**Key observables.** Residual systematic bias (reduced to 5.3 nm), polarization variance reduction (49%), and localization repeatability ($\sigma$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Nanometer-scale accuracy, cryogenic temperature (4 K), Zernike polynomial order ($n=10$), and the use of lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays as references.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation addressed is uncorrected systematic optical distortions; one assumption involves approximating the QD emission source for simulation purposes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup schematic, performance metrics comparing localization uncertainties (QD vs. nanodisks), and validation showing the reduction of systematic offsets after applying the Zernike correction model.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of systematic distortion limiting integration yield, details the use of a Zernike vector-field model calibrated with reference arrays, presents quantitative results showing bias reduction and polarization improvement, and concludes by establishing the method's utility for scalable quantum photonic circuits.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum photonic technologies greatly benefit from quantum light emitters with high brightness, indistinguishability, and reliable polarization characteristics. Achieving optimal performance relies on the accurate localization of emitters and their deterministic integration into tailored photonic structures with nanometer-scale accuracy. Although marker-based photoluminescence imaging techniques can achieve statistical fitting uncertainties below 10 nm, the ultimate integration yield is often limited by uncorrected systematic distortions in custom cryo-optical setups that compromise metrological accuracy. Here, we present an in situ calibration protocol that uses lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays as references to calibrate optical distortions with a Zernike vector-field model. On held-out validation patterns beyond the calibration dataset, this correction reduces the residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm with a 2D scatter of 24.6 nm across the analyzed field of view. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying this correction to the deterministic fabrication of circular mesa structures around semiconductor quantum dots reduces the variance in emission polarization by 49%, indicating improved registration accuracy. This calibration strategy offers a practical route to high-yield deterministic integration of quantum emitters into scalable quantum photonic circuits.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a graph-based Kirchhoff model to simulate current flow in self-assembled nanonecklace networks exhibiting Coulomb blockade. By treating the network as a dynamic graph, the authors show that the macroscopic non-Ohmic transport behavior emerges from the collective activation of individual junctions. This establishes the framework as a powerful design tool for engineering electronic properties in disordered nanoscale devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical charge transport, the concept of percolation in disordered media, threshold switching, and emergent collective behavior is highly relevant to understanding quantum phase transitions or correlated electron dynamics in mesoscopic structures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses the poorly understood mechanisms governing the macroscopic non-Ohmic current–voltage (I–V) response in self-assembled gold nanonecklace networks.

**Main result.** The model successfully reproduces the characteristic $I \propto (V - V_T)^\zeta$ power law, showing that this behavior arises from collective, staggered activation of threshold junctions and voltage-driven percolation.

**Method.** A graph-based Kirchhoff framework is developed to solve for potentials and currents across a network modeled as a geometric graph whose conductivity changes dynamically with applied bias.

**Model / system.** The system is a synthetic random geometric graph representing nanonecklace networks. Junctions have distance-dependent tunneling resistances, and nodes possess intrinsic resistance governed by an activation voltage threshold ($R_{n,i} \propto V_{a,i}$).

**Key observables.** Non-Ohmic I–V response ($I \propto (V - V_T)^\zeta$), active nodes, conducting subgraph evolution, nodal potentials, and edge currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mean activation voltage ($\langle V_a angle$), variance of activation voltages ($\sigma_a$), network density/void fraction ($f_v$), and the applied bias $V$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The node resistance is approximated as linearly proportional to the activation voltage for computational tractability, and the global bias is used as the primary activation criterion.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the step-by-step solver process (graph formation, subgraph selection, matrix solving) and show how varying structural parameters ($\sigma_a$, $f_v$) controls the exponent $\zeta$ and threshold voltage $V_T$.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the physical problem, details the graph-based Kirchhoff methodology for solving bias-dependent conduction, presents results showing parameter control over transport exponents, and concludes by establishing the model as a design tool.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Gold nanonecklace networks are promising platforms for single-electron switching, chemical sensing, and biogating devices because of their nonlinear current--voltage ($I$--$V$) characteristics arising from collective Coulomb-blockade transport. However, the mechanisms governing this macroscopic behavior remain poorly understood because experimental measurements are generally limited to the network topology and global $I$--$V$ response. To address this, we developed a graph-based Kirchhoff framework that represents a self-assembled nanonecklace network as a graph, with nodes corresponding to junctions between necklace segments and edges to the conducting segments themselves. The solver returns the active nodes, conducting subgraph, nodal potentials, and edge currents at each applied bias, while allowing the activation-voltage statistics, network density, and structural topology to be varied independently. The model reproduces the experimentally observed non-Ohmic response, $I \propto (V-V_T)^ζ$, and shows that this behavior emerges from the collective, staggered activation of threshold junctions and voltage-driven percolation of the conducting subgraph. Independent parameter sweeps reveal that the mean activation voltage shifts the threshold $V_T$ while leaving $ζ$ nearly unchanged, increasing network density raises $ζ$ from approximately 1.9 to 3.1 and enhances current, and topology controls the response even at fixed density and node characteristics. These trends agree qualitatively with experimental observations and establish the model as a design tool for engineering collective transport in self-assembled nanonecklace devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work theoretically examines heat conduction in semiconductor nanofilms by analyzing the competition between intrinsic phonon scattering selection rules and boundary mode conversion. Using first-principles calculations, the authors show that mode conversion significantly suppresses the dominant LA phonon contribution in materials like InP at low temperatures. This effect allows for symmetry-selective engineering of thermal transport properties unattainable in bulk solids.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on phonons, the concept of non-equilibrium energy transport and symmetry-selective coupling (e.g., electron-phonon interaction) is highly relevant to open quantum systems and thermalization studies in nanoscale devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how phonon scattering selection rules compete with boundary mode conversion effects to modulate heat flow in nanoscale semiconductor films.

**Main result.** Mode conversion strongly suppresses the large intrinsic LA phonon contribution to thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) in InP nanofilms, leading to a heat current dominated by out-of-equilibrium TA modes.

**Method.** The study uses first-principles calculations solving the steady-state Peierls-Boltzmann equation (SSPBE) under the Relaxation Time Approximation (RTA).

**Model / system.** The system involves semiconductor nanofilms, specifically InP and BP, at cryogenic temperatures. The physics models phonon transport governed by intrinsic scattering rules versus extrinsic boundary reflections.

**Key observables.** Phonon mode-polarized heat currents and the thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) dependence on film thickness ($d$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cryogenic temperatures ($\le 100$ K); nanoscale dimensions; phonon branch velocities (LA vs. TA).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that boundary reflection with mode conversion dominates over intrinsic scattering at sufficiently small thicknesses, and the RTA is sufficient for the studied materials.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare $\kappa$ vs. thickness for BP and InP, showing suppression due to diffuse scattering and faster decay in InP when mode conversion occurs; spectral contributions are also analyzed.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from established knowledge of phonon selection rules in bulk solids to analyze the competition between these rules and boundary mode conversion effects in thin films using advanced computational methods.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Phonon scattering selection rules are known to control heat flow through bulk solids. Here we show that these selection rules also modulate heat flow through nanoscale semiconductor films, although through a previously-unexplored mechanism. Using first-principles calculations, we expose a competition between these selection rules and phonon mode conversion at boundaries of nanoscale films, that drives mode-polarized heat currents at cryogenic temperatures ($\le$ 100 K). This polarizing effect is stronger in materials like indium phosphide, where selection rules based on large velocity differences between phonon branches amplifies the longitudinal acoustic (LA) phonon contribution to thermal conductivity by restricting their intrinsic scattering events, while boundary mode conversion in nanoscale films suppresses it by depopulating the LA phonons. The resulting transverse-polarized non-equilibrium phonons will enable symmetry-selective engineering of phonon coupling to electrons, strains and defects in nanoscale films, that is difficult to achieve in bulk solids.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes how vacancies introduce localized topological structures into the Chern-insulating Haldane model. The key finding is that a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant, determined by sublattice imbalance, dictates whether zero-energy modes exist at the defect site. This prediction is robustly confirmed through three independent physical measurements: wavefunction geometry, fractional charge accumulation, and current flow reversal.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous demonstration of multiple, distinct physical signatures confirming a single mathematical invariant ($\mathbb{Z}_2$) provides a powerful general principle for characterizing topological defects in condensed matter systems, applicable beyond the specific Haldane model.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how local defects (vacancies) modify the topological properties of the Haldane model, specifically examining the interplay between bulk topology and defect-induced topology.

**Main result.** A $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant ($
u$) governs the presence of protected zero-energy modes at vacancies, which is confirmed by three independent experimental signatures: wavefunction dislocations, fractional charge accumulation, and opposite circulating probability currents.

**Method.** The analysis uses theoretical tools including the tenfold classification framework, Chern numbers ($C$), $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariants ($
u$), and index theorems to derive relationships between bulk and defect topology.

**Model / system.** The system is the Haldane model on a honeycomb lattice, which realizes a Chern-insulating phase. Defects studied include vacancies (bond removal) and adatoms (potential addition).

**Key observables.** Chern number ($C=\pm 1$), $\mathbb{Z}_2$ defect invariant ($
u = C \cdot m \pmod 2$), zero-energy modes, fractional charge ($e/2$), and probability current direction.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Sublattice imbalance $m = N_A - N_B$, which dictates the value of $
u$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on low-energy effective descriptions using Weyl symbols and assumes the applicability of topological invariants derived from the tenfold classification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the clean Haldane spectrum, the appearance of zero-energy modes for single vacancies ($
u=1$), mode splitting for two vacancies ($
u=0$), wavefunction dislocations tracking phase winding, and charge/current distributions confirming the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ prediction.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the bulk topology ($C$) and then introduces defects. It derives the coupling formula ($
u = C \cdot m \pmod 2$) and presents three complementary diagnostics (dislocations, fractional charge, current reversal) that all confirm this topological classification.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the interplay between local defects and topology in the Haldane model within the framework of the tenfold classification. The Haldane model realizes a Chern-insulating phase characterized by an integer topological invariant ($C=\pm 1$) and supports chiral edge states. Introducing vacancies gives rise to localized states at the defect sites, classified by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant $ν= C\cdot m,\mathrm{mod},2$, where $m=N_A-N_B$ is the net sublattice imbalance of the vacancy configuration: an odd imbalance hosts a protected zero-energy mode, whereas an even imbalance does not. We identify three independent experimental signatures that distinguish these topological defect states from trivial (adatom) defects. First, vacancy-induced states exhibit characteristic dislocations in their wavefunction profiles that track the phase winding associated with the defect. Second, a fractional charge of $e/2$ accumulates at vacancy sites, while no such charge appears at adatoms. Third, the probability current circulating around a vacancy-induced state flows in the opposite direction to that of chiral edge states, in direct analogy with the current reversal produced by a vortex in a $p$-wave superconductor. All three signatures are in quantitative agreement with the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ prediction.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper tackles the challenge of applying bulk-boundary correspondence to complex nonlinear eigenvalue problems. By developing an auxiliary system formalism, it successfully classifies these systems and demonstrates how stacking a 2D model into 3D allows for the engineering of exotic hybrid-order topological phases (first-, second-, and third-order). This highlights stacking as a powerful tool for exploring nonlinearity in topology.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the generalization of topological concepts (like BBC) from linear to nonlinear systems, which is a major frontier in condensed matter theory relevant to engineered quantum/photonic structures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The bulk-boundary correspondence (BBC) is poorly understood for nonlinear systems, especially those with multigap topologies, making topological description difficult.

**Main result.** The study establishes a multiband bulk-boundary correspondence and identifies stacking engineering as a versatile platform for realizing hybrid-order topological phases in nonlinear systems.

**Method.** An auxiliary-system formalism is developed to map the nonlinear eigenvalue problem into a formally linear pencil matrix, allowing topological classification via spectral analysis.

**Model / system.** The work analyzes a 2D spinless square-lattice model with two degrees of freedom per unit cell. This system is extended to 3D by stacking along the z-axis using SSH chain concepts.

**Key observables.** Topological invariants include Chern number ($C_1$) and mirror-graded winding number ($W_2$). State localization is diagnosed using the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Stacking parameters, such as those governing uniform vs. dimerized stacking, dictate the resulting order of the topological phase (first-, second-, or third-order).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on mapping the nonlinear problem to a formally linear auxiliary system; it extends previous work limited to single-gap topologies.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the eigenvalue spectra under OBC and PBC, demonstrating the coexistence of first-order boundary states ($\omega=0$) and second-order corner states ($\omega=-M^{-1}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the auxiliary system formalism for nonlinear BBC in 2D to analyzing how stacking this 2D structure into 3D yields distinct hybrid-order phases (e.g., uniform vs. dimerized stacking).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The bulk-boundary correspondence (BBC), which relates topological invariants to boundary modes, is well understood for linear systems but remains an open question in the presence of nonlinearity, where multigap topologies make the BBC obscure and the topological description troublesome. We address this by developing an auxiliary-system formalism that enables topological classification of nonlinear-eigenvalue systems. In the two-dimension (2D) case, we show that two fixed eigenvalues can harbor first-order gapless boundary modes and second-order corner modes. Stacking this 2D system along the third dimension (3D) reveals distinct hybrid-order realizations. Under uniform stacking, the corner states in the $xy$ plane transform into hinge states along the $z$ axis, yielding a 3D second-order phase, while the gapless boundary states become side-surface states, yielding a 3D first-order phase. For dimerized stacking, these states are further confined to the two ends of the $z$ axis, yielding a 3D third-order phase, and localized at the hinges, yielding a 3D second-order phase. Our results establish a multiband bulk-boundary correspondence and identify stacking engineering as a versatile platform for exploring hybrid-order topological phases in nonlinear systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the interaction between chiral bobbers and skyrmion strings in magnetically ordered systems exhibiting a conical phase. Using micromagnetic simulations, the authors demonstrate that this interaction is not merely distance-dependent but is fundamentally controlled by the local surface phase factor ($\phi_0$). This phase control leads to complex energy landscapes featuring distinct bonding regimes arising from structural shell reconstruction.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of phase-dependent control over magnetic interactions, where a geometric/topological parameter ($\phi_0$) dictates bonding strength rather than simple geometry ($R$), is highly relevant to understanding controlled spin dynamics in advanced spintronic devices and topological materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the interaction between a chiral bobber and a skyrmion string, focusing on how this interaction is intrinsically controlled by the local surface phase factor ($\phi_0$) within the conical magnetic phase.

**Main result.** The interaction energy landscape cannot be described by a simple distance-dependent potential; instead, it exhibits distinct regimes (repulsive, attractive, bonding) governed by $\phi_0$ due to phase-dependent reconstruction of outer distortion shells.

**Method.** Three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations were employed to compute the constrained energy landscape as a function of separation ($R$) and surface phase factor ($\phi_0$).

**Model / system.** The system models magnetic materials exhibiting bulk Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), supporting 3D topological spin textures like skyrmion strings and chiral bobbers in the conical phase.

**Key observables.** Interaction energy landscape $\Delta E(R, \phi_0)$, effective radial force $F_R$, and structural reconstruction of outer distortion shells.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Separation distance ($R$), surface phase factor ($\phi_0$), magnetic field strength ($H$), and the conical background direction.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Dipolar interactions are excluded from the minimal energy functional to isolate the core mechanism; the analysis assumes that structural reconstruction drives the bonding transitions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate contour maps of $\Delta E(R, \phi_0)$, showing distinct regimes based on $\phi_0$; real-space visualizations demonstrate shell reconstruction during bonding; and comparisons show relationships between top/bottom surface interactions via phase mapping.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical problem, details the micromagnetic simulation setup using a minimal energy functional, presents the analysis of fixed-$\phi_0$ energy cuts classifying three regimes (M, NM, Bonding), and concludes by discussing the implications of $\phi_0$ as an active degree of freedom.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Skyrmion interactions govern the formation of skyrmion lattices, clusters, and particle-like growth patterns. In contrast, the interaction between a chiral bobber and a skyrmion string remains largely unexplored, despite the role of bobbers as intermediate states in skyrmion-string formation and annihilation. Here we show that this interaction is intrinsically phase dependent in the conical phase. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we compute the locally relaxed constrained energy landscape as a function of the bobber--skyrmion separation $R$ and the surface phase factor $φ_0$. We find that changing $φ_0$ qualitatively reshapes the interaction, producing repulsive, attractive, and bonding-like regimes that cannot be reduced to a conventional distance-dependent potential. Real-space analysis shows that this behavior originates from phase-dependent reconstruction of nonaxisymmetric outer distortion shells. The phase-controlled interaction persists over a finite field range and follows the expected top--bottom phase relation of surface-sensitive conical textures. These results identify the conical phase direction, often hidden in projected or thickness-averaged descriptions, as a previously underappreciated degree of freedom in the interaction between skyrmion strings and finite-length chiral textures, as demonstrated here for chiral bobbers.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study investigates Josephson junctions formed by spin-triplet superconductors coupled via an altermagnetic material. By calculating the junction's critical current and current-phase relation using Green's functions, the authors demonstrate that these effects are highly sensitive to the direction of the superconductor's d-vector. This provides a promising, non-destructive method for characterizing intrinsic superconducting pairing symmetries.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects unconventional superconductivity (spin-triplet pairing) with emergent magnetism (altermagnetism). The sensitivity of Josephson coupling to microscopic magnetic structure provides a novel, potentially field-free diagnostic tool for fundamental superconducting properties.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a method for detecting the intrinsic direction of the d-vector in spin-triplet superconductors (STS). This is achieved by studying Josephson junctions formed between STS and altermagnets (AM).

**Main result.** The Josephson current-phase relationships are highly sensitive to the relative orientation of the superconducting d-vectors and the AM magnetization angle, allowing for a robust detection scheme.

**Method.** The study employs the Green's function method applied to the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian formalism to calculate the Josephson current across the junction.

**Model / system.** The model consists of an STS/Altermagnet/STS junction, analyzed using a total Hamiltonian composed of three parts. The AM is advantageous because it possesses zero net macroscopic magnetization while still inducing spin-dependent couplings.

**Key observables.** Josephson critical current ($I_c$) and the Current-Phase Relationship (CPR) as functions of superconducting phase difference ($\phi$), d-vector polar angle ($	heta$), and AM orientation angle ($\alpha$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key variables include the direction of the $\mathbf{d}$-vectors, the altermagnet orientation angle ($\alpha$), and the strength of magnetic coupling ($t_F$ in comparison to ferromagnets).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a lattice model for the junction structure and relies on the Green's function formalism for current calculation.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the junction setup, showing $\mathbf{d}$-vector directions relative to the AM Fermi surface. They plot CPRs versus angles and show $I_c$ dependence on these same angular parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the Hamiltonian for the three components (STS/AM/STS). It then calculates the Josephson current using Green's functions, deriving symmetries and analyzing how the resulting CPRs and critical currents depend systematically on the relative orientations of the superconducting order parameter and the magnetic substrate.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the Josephson effects in the spin-triplet superconductor/altermagnet/spin-triplet superconductor junctions using the Green's function method. It is found that the current-phase difference relationships in the junctions strongly depend on the direction of the $\bf{d}$-vectors in the spin-triplet superconductors and the orientation angle of the altermagnet. For the given orientation angle, the $0$-$π$ transition can be obtained when the $\bf{d}$-vector is rotated. The variations of the critical current of the junctions with the direction of the $\bf{d}$-vector, the orientation angle and the strength of altermagnetism are systematically investigated. These Josephson effects can provide the distinguishable information about the direction of the $\bf{d}$-vector. Compared to the existing research, the proposed altermagnetic Josephson junctions can effectively avoid the negative influence of the magnetic field on the $\bf{d}$-vector and can serve as a feasible scheme for the detection of the intrinsic $\bf{d}$-vector. The obtained $0$-$π$ transition in the junctions can also have potential applications in the design of quantum devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports the observation of a robust Nonlinear Hall effect in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, establishing them as a new platform for studying BCD-driven transport. By analyzing second-harmonic signals and confirming symmetry constraints via DFT, the authors prove that the NLHE arises from intrinsic electronic band structure asymmetry rather than extrinsic or quantum-metric effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** While primarily condensed matter physics, the study of nonlinear transport phenomena in engineered interfaces touches upon non-equilibrium quantum dynamics. The precise identification of an intrinsic electronic mechanism (BCD) provides a model for understanding how broken symmetries dictate macroscopic electrical responses in solid-state devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to observe and characterize the Nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) driven by the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) in technologically relevant magnetic multilayer platforms, extending beyond traditional van der Waals systems.

**Main result.** A robust NLHE was observed in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers persisting up to room temperature, confirming that the signal originates from an intrinsic BCD mechanism rather than quantum-metric contributions.

**Method.** The research combines transport measurements (measuring second-harmonic transverse voltage) with theoretical analysis using symmetry principles and first-principles DFT calculations.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a sputter-deposited polycrystalline magnetic multilayer heterostructure, specifically Ta/Pt/[Ir/Fe/Co/Pt]n/Pt on Si/SiO2. The theory models the NLHE via the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) mechanism in systems lacking inversion symmetry.

**Key observables.** Second-harmonic transverse voltage ($V_{xy}^{2\omega}$), second-order Hall conductivity, and the temperature dependence of resistance ($R_{xx}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range (2 K to room temperature); applied magnetic field strength ($\pm 2 	ext{ T}$); excitation frequency.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The observed signal is assumed to be dominated by the intrinsic BCD mechanism, and the polycrystalline structure's texture dictates the symmetry constraints on the response.

**Figures summary.** Figures show layer architecture, Hall bar geometry, $R_{xx}$ vs. temperature (metallic behavior), XRD patterns confirming polycrystalline growth, and plots of $V_{xy}^{2\omega}$ dependence on current, frequency, and magnetic field.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the experimental observation of NLHE in multilayers, rigorously rules out other sources (frequency/field independence, no third harmonic), uses scaling analysis to isolate the BCD term, and finally supports these findings with DFT calculations that confirm the necessary symmetry breaking for a nonzero BCD moment.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Nonlinear Hall effect(NLHE) driven principally by the Berry curvature dipole has been established in non-centrosymmetric vander Waals crystals, topological semimetals, and moiré superlattices, but its extension to technologically mature heavy-metal/ferromagnet multilayer platforms remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the observation of a robust NLHE in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, persisting from 2 K to room temperature. The second-harmonic transverse voltage is independent of both excitation frequency and applied out-of-plane magnetic field, while the vanishingly small third-harmonic response confirms that the observed signal is not dominated by a quantum-metric contribution and instead reflects a genuine second-order electronic response. A scaling analysis of the second-order Hall conductivity against the longitudinal conductivity identifies a dominant, conductivity-independent term establishing the intrinsic berry curvature dipole. Our theoretical analysis, supported by first-principles DFT calculations, further satisfies and corroborates the experimental results. These results establish sputter-deposited polycrystalline thin film as the first engineered magnetic multilayer platform for BCD-driven nonlinear Hall transport, extending the NLHE material landscape beyond van der Waals systems into scalable, industry-compatible thin-film spintronic architectures suitable for high frequency rectifications and nonlinear sensors.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates reentrant localization transitions, quantum butterfly patterns, and robust edge modes in quasiperiodic lattices.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a re-emerging delocalization phase controlled by kinetic parameters, alongside the formation of robust edge states resistant to moderate disorder.

**Method.** Analysis employs diagnostics like Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), Mean Square Displacement (MSD) scaling ($	ext{MSD} \sim t^\mu$), and multifractal analysis ($I_q$) across phase diagrams.

**Model / system.** The model is a quasi-one dimensional zig-zag ladder network governed by a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating a quasiperiodic Aubry-Andre Harper (AAH) modulation in the long-range hopping integral.

**Key observables.** Inverse Participation Ratio ($	ext{IPR}_n$), Normalized Participation Ratio ($	ext{NPR}_n$), transport exponent ($\mu$), edge probability ($P_{	ext{edge}}$), and the phase diagram parameter $\eta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the validity of multifractal scaling techniques for characterizing quantum phases in quasiperiodic systems.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate IPR intensity plots showing delocalized patches, MSD vs. time curves demonstrating different transport regimes ($\mu$), and maps correlating edge probability onto the quantum butterfly spectrum.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes localization diagnostics (IPR/NPR) to map out a reentrant phase diagram controlled by $\alpha$, followed by dynamical studies using MSD and multifractal analysis, culminating in the identification of robust edge modes via $P_{	ext{edge}}$ mapping onto the spectrum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Low dimensional tight-binding lattices in presence of quasiperiodic disorder generally exhibits localization transition. The system supports diffusive modes upto a limiting strength of disorder and all the eigenstates become localized beyond that critical strength thereby quenching the kinetic signature of the wavepacket. However, moving away from this situation, we demonstrate that with minimal long-range off-diagonal modulation, the eigenspectrum again may offer delocalization of electronic states for some subtle combination of kinetic parameters of the Hamiltonian leading to a second quantum phase change. The localization transitions are associated with the obvious presence of single-particle mobility edges. Multifractal energy landscape also shows quantum butterfly pattern with the in-gap robust edge modes. The re-emerging localization transition is manifested through the evaluation of inverse participation ratio, eigenspectrum and a pertinent quantum dynamical study.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores the coexistence of Charge Density Wave order and superconductivity in graphene under strong magnetic fields. By mapping out phase diagrams using transport measurements, the authors reveal that SC persists deep within the quantum Hall regime, suggesting a profound interplay between charge ordering and pairing mechanisms.

**Why it may be interesting.** The strong coupling between CDW formation (a charge ordering phenomenon) and superconductivity in a magnetic field provides a rich platform for studying competing orders in strongly correlated electron systems, relevant to high-Tc superconductors.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the complex interplay between Charge Density Wave (CDW) order, Superconductivity (SC), and Quantum Hall Effects (QHE) in a highly tunable electronic system.

**Main result.** The research demonstrates that SC and CDW phases coexist within the quantum Hall regime of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene, with the superconducting state persisting deep inside the QHE region.

**Method.** Transport measurements ($	ext{R}\parallel$, $	ext{R}\perp$) are used across varying carrier densities ($n$), displacement fields ($D$), and perpendicular magnetic fields ($B_\perp$).

**Model / system.** The physical platform is rhombohedral hexalayer graphene (R6G), which is tuned using a large displacement field to generate flat band edges, enabling strong Landau level mixing.

**Key observables.** Integer Quantum Hall plateaus ($\sigma_{xy}$), vanishing longitudinal/transverse resistance ($R_{\parallel}, R_{\perp}$ for SC), and pronounced thermal hysteresis associated with CDW transitions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strong magnetic fields ($B > 2	ext{T}$), flat-band edge physics, carrier density ($n$), and displacement field ($D$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on the regime where Landau level mixing is strong near the flat-band edge.

**Figures summary.** Figures map out phase diagrams in $n-D$ space showing distinct SC pockets alongside regions exhibiting Re-entrant Integer Quantum Hall (RIQH) states, with temperature dependence revealing hysteresis linked to CDW melting.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically maps the phase diagram by measuring transport properties ($\sigma_{xx}, \sigma_{xy}$) as a function of $n$ and $D$, identifying boundaries between insulating/CDW, QHE, and superconducting states. The analysis is refined using temperature sweeps and current-voltage characteristics to confirm first-order transitions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Charge density wave (CDW) and superconductivity are both common in strongly interacting electron systems. While CDW order is ubiquitous in both quantum Hall systems and unconventional superconductors, superconductivity is generally suppressed by the strong magnetic fields required for Landau quantization. Here we investigate the intertwined CDW and superconducting phases of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene (R6G) in a large displacement field, which generates tunable flat band edges, and a strong magnetic field, which generates a manifold of nearly degenerate Landau levels. CDW order is accompanied by pronounced thermal hysteresis as expected for first-order melting transitions. Surprisingly, we find a series of strong integer quantum Hall effects at magnetic fields above ~2T with Hall conductance quantum numbers that deviate strongly from nearby integer filling factors, an observation that can be explained only by CDW order that mixes many Landau levels. We also find a nearby superconducting phase that is stabilized by perpendicular magnetic fields and persists deep within the quantum Hall regime. The CDW and superconducting phases develop on comparable temperature scales and emerge from the same manifold of strongly mixed Landau levels. These observations provide new insight into the interplay between superconductivity and CDW order in R6G at zero magnetic field.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a novel, singularity-free model for black hole interiors using a scalar field described in three distinct layers: crust, transition layer, and negative energy core. It treats the entire process of BH formation and evaporation as a quasi-static thermodynamic cycle driven by the negative energy core. The work successfully unifies these disparate physical regimes within a single field theoretical framework.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on GR, the explicit use of negative temperature concepts ($eta$) to describe the core condensate and modeling BH evaporation as an 'almost adiabatic thermodynamic engine' connects directly to advanced non-equilibrium statistical mechanics principles.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To construct an effective, singularity-free model for the interior of a black hole (BH) that addresses thermodynamic issues like entropy and information loss during evaporation.

**Main result.** The BH interior is modeled as a three-layer structure (core, transition layer, crust), where Hawking evaporation can be viewed as a quasi-static cycle analogous to an adiabatic thermodynamic engine.

**Method.** Solving the static Einstein equations using an effective scalar field description and applying concepts from thermodynamics, including negative temperature notions for the core condensate.

**Model / system.** The system uses a non-linear self-interacting scalar field ($\phi$) to describe three distinct regions: a positive-energy crust of thermal excitations, a transition layer acting as a 'factory,' and an AdS-type core characterized by negative energy density. The structure is governed by matching conditions across these layers.

**Key observables.** Metric components, mass functions, energy densities ($ho$), pressures ($p$), and the two-temperature thermodynamics linking kinetic excitations to the ground state.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The Schwarzschild radius ($r=2GM_{	ext{ADM}}$), negative inverse temperature parameter ($eta$), and the quasi-particle density in each layer.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes a static configuration, uses an effective scalar field to unify core/crust descriptions, and treats BH evaporation as a reversible thermodynamic cycle.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the radial ordering of the three layers ($R_- < R^+ < R_S$) and show the potential energy landscape $V(\phi)$ defining the boundaries between these regions.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the structure by first proposing the three-layer model, then solving the static Einstein equations for each layer using quasi-particle thermodynamics (WKB approximation), establishing matching conditions at the transition layer, and finally interpreting the entire process as a thermodynamic cycle.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose an effective, singularity-free model of the black hole interior described entirely by a scalar field with a non-linear self-interaction potential. The interior consists of three layers -- a core, a transition layer, and a crust -- each fixed by the local quasi-particle density and the corresponding extremum of the potential of the field. The crust is a layer of massive, positive-energy thermal excitations above the zero-potential well, beneath a genuine Schwarzschild horizon at $r = 2GM_{\rm ADM}$. The core is an AdS-type region of negative energy density, it simulates a condensate of quasi-particles which carry zero classical kinetic energy and form a negative potential well governed by a negative inverse temperature parameter. The two regions are joined through Israel matching across the transition layer, which sits at an approximately null-gravity hypersurface of maximal regular matter density and where both the sign of the energy density and the type of thermal excitations change. Solving the static Einstein equations, we obtain the metric and mass functions of each layer, the edge equation of state of the crust, the linear stability condition of the null-gravity surface for ordinary and effectively negative mass matter, and the two-temperature thermodynamics linking the kinetic excitations to the negative temperature ground state. The framework unifies core and crust within a single field description and highlights the role of the negative energy AdS core and the associated negative temperature notion in describing black hole interior. In this picture the formation and Hawking evaporation of a black hole appear as a quasi-static cycle of an almost adiabatic thermodynamic engine, with the negative energy core as the working substance.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using an altermagnetic Josephson junction to create a parity-protected superconducting qubit. By exploiting the momentum-dependent spin splitting in the altermagnet, the system can be tuned electrically through a 0-$\pi$ transition, generating a double-well potential for robust quantum states. This approach promises scalable, all-electrical control with coherence times suitable for quantum computing applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses hardware implementation challenges in superconducting qubits by proposing a novel material platform (altermagnets) that enables all-electrical, flux-noise-free control necessary for scalable quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is developing superconducting qubits with long coherence times that avoid problematic magnetic-flux biasing.

**Main result.** The authors propose using an altermagnetic Josephson junction to create a parity-protected qubit operable entirely through gate voltages, achieving estimated coherence times of tens of milliseconds.

**Method.** Theoretical modeling involving the tight-binding Hamiltonian and Andreev level calculations are used to analyze the junction's energy spectrum as it passes through a 0-$\pi$ transition point.

**Model / system.** The system is a superconducting qubit built around an Altermagnet Josephson Junction (SC–AM–SC). The AM provides spin-dependent functionality without external fields, allowing electrical control over the junction's phase and potential.

**Key observables.** Cooper-pair parity ($\langle\hat{P}angle$), Qubit splitting ($E_{01}$), Coherence times ($T_2$, $T_\mu$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate voltages controlling chemical potential ($\mu$) and offset charge ($n_g$); Josephson energy harmonics ($E_{J,1}, E_{J,2}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on specific limits such as the 1D approximation for the AM region and assuming realistic material parameters for gate compatibility.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the physical setup and potential shape at the $0-\pi$ point; Figure 2 demonstrates how tuning $\mu$ drives the junction through a double-well landscape by suppressing the first Josephson harmonic.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, details the SC–AM–SC model using theoretical derivations (Appendix A) and numerical simulations (Appendix B), analyzes the resulting qubit Hamiltonian and control mechanisms, and concludes with performance estimates for coherence times.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Parity-protected superconducting qubits offer intrinsically long coherence, but many current implementations require magnetic-flux biasing, which introduces flux noise, control overhead, and limited scalability. Here we propose a parity-protected qubit based on a gate-tunable superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor Josephson junction. Altermagnets are compensated magnets with momentum-dependent spin splitting and zero net magnetization, providing spin-dependent functionality without external magnetic fields. In the proposed junction, the two spin sectors acquire opposite phase shifts, generating two Josephson channels whose interference is controlled electrically by the chemical potential. At the tuned $0$-$π$ transition, the first Josephson harmonic is strongly suppressed while the second harmonic dominates, yielding a double-well potential with two nearly degenerate states of opposite Cooper-pair parity. For realistic gatemon-compatible parameters, we estimate coherence times of up to tens of milliseconds while maintaining fully gate-controlled qubit operations. These results establish altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a promising route toward protected superconducting qubits with local, scalable, and all-electrical control.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work investigates how surfaces can functionalize $g$-wave altermagnets by inducing d-wave magnetic order. Using the Kubo formalism on a minimal slab model, the authors calculate a finite spin-splitter effect (SSE) originating solely from these surfaces. This suggests that thin-film engineering is a viable strategy to harness novel spintronic functionalities in complex magnetic materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of boundary states inducing novel electronic responses (like SSE) via symmetry breaking is relevant to understanding topological phenomena in engineered quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to demonstrate that surface effects can induce a spin-splitter effect (SSE) in $g$-wave altermagnets, overcoming the difficulty of finding bulk metallic d-wave AMs.

**Main result.** A finite SSE is found at the surfaces due to surface-induced d-wave altermagnetism, which is absent in the bulk. This response is linked to an accompanying weak ferromagnetism that allows for external field control.

**Method.** The spin conductivity quantifying the SSE is calculated using the Kubo formalism applied to a minimal slab model Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a $g$-wave altermagnet (AM) slab geometry, utilizing a tight-binding Hamiltonian defined on a lattice structure involving magnetic and nonmagnetic sites. The bulk order parameter ($\varphi$) dictates the surface d-wave splitting via a bulk-boundary correspondence.

**Key observables.** Spin conductivity ($\sigma_{S_z, yz}$), SSE angle ($	heta_{aa}$), and layer-resolved weak ferromagnetism ($M_y$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The calculation uses specific parameters for the hopping terms and SOC strengths within the minimal model.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on a minimal theoretical model; it assumes that surface effects dominate the SSE, as bulk contributions cancel out due to time-reversal odd nature of SSE.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic of surface d-wave splitting enabling SSE, show the crystal structure of the (210) surface, and plot the calculated spin conductivity ($\sigma_{S_z, yz}$) versus chemical potential for varying slab thicknesses.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical platform (g-wave AM surfaces), develops the theoretical framework using the Kubo formalism to calculate conductivities, derives the key results showing surface-induced effects, and concludes by discussing implications for thin-film engineering.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate surfaces of a $g$-wave altermagnet(AM) and show that they provide a platform for realizing $d$-wave altermagnetism and the associated spin-splitter functionality. Using the Kubo formalism applied to a minimal slab model, we evaluate the spin-splitter effect(SSE) by computing the spin conductivity corresponding to a transverse spin current induced by a longitudinal electric field. We find a finite SSE, absent in the bulk, that emerges from surface-induced $d$-wave altermagnetism. Strikingly, the sign pattern of the $d$-wave altermagnetism on both surfaces of the slab geometry is identical to each other, leading to additive contributions to SSE from the two surfaces, with a spin-splitter angle reaching up to 15 degrees. In addition, this response is intrinsically linked to an accompanying surface-induced weak ferromagnetism, which potentially enables control of altermagnetic domains via an external magnetic field and provides a route to optimize the SSE functionality. These results can be understood in terms of a bulk-boundary correspondence between surface states and bulk altermagnetic order parameters, where the magnetic multipolar character of the latter plays a central role. Our findings strongly suggest thin-film engineering as a viable strategy to functionalize non-$d$-wave AMs.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes a novel Janus material, $	ext{MgAlB}_2$, as an advanced anode for Li-ion batteries. By breaking structural symmetry, the material generates an intrinsic polarization that significantly enhances lithium ion transport and storage capacity. The calculations demonstrate this leads to ultra-low diffusion barriers and high theoretical energy density.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state electrochemistry, the concept of engineering intrinsic dipole moments via structural asymmetry to control charge transport barriers is analogous to designing quantum interfaces or controlling local electric fields in nanoscale devices relevant to AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research addresses the need for novel, high-performance anode materials for Li-ion batteries that overcome limitations in conventional anodes like graphite.

**Main result.** The engineered Janus $	ext{MgAlB}_2$ monolayer exhibits exceptional performance, achieving a theoretical specific capacity of $1470.24 	ext{ mAhg}^{-1}$ with an ultralow Li diffusion barrier of $17.1 	ext{ meV}$.

**Method.** The study relies heavily on first-principles calculations (DFT) to model the electronic structure, electrochemical properties, and ion transport kinetics.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a 2D Janus material, $	ext{MgAlB}_2$, created by breaking the symmetry of parent $	ext{MBenes}$ ($	ext{Mg}_2	ext{B}_2$ or $	ext{Al}_2	ext{B}_2$) to induce an intrinsic electric polarization.

**Key observables.** Li migration barrier ($17.1 	ext{ meV}$), theoretical specific capacity ($1470.24 	ext{ mAhg}^{-1}$), out-of-plane dipole moment, and electronic delocalization across the monolayer.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low diffusion barrier ($	ext{meV}$ scale); room-temperature diffusion coefficient ($3.43	imes 10^{-10} 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{s}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that engineering intrinsic polarization via Janus asymmetry can fundamentally improve both the thermodynamics (capacity) and kinetics (diffusion) of Li storage.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we propose a group II/IIIA-based Janus MBene, MgAlB_2, and investigate its electrochemical properties using first-principles calculations. The substitution of one Mg layer in Mg_2B_2 MBene by an Al layer breaks the structural symmetry and generates a permanent out-of-plane polarization, giving rise to a distinct electronic environment compared with the parent Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers. Electronic-structure analysis reveals enhanced orbital hybridization among B, Mg, and Al states near the Fermi level, resulting in improved electronic delocalization across the monolayer. The Janus MgAlB_2 monolayer is found to possess excellent dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability. Owing to its polarization-modified energy landscape, Li ions migrate with an exceptionally low diffusion barrier of 17.1 meV, corresponding to a room-temperature diffusion coefficient of 3.43x10^-10 cm^2/s. Unlike the pristine Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers, which support only a single stable adsorption layer, MgAlB_2 accommodates two complete Li layers. Detailed analysis shows that the residual polarization retained after first-layer lithiation continues to promote Li adsorption, whereas increasing Li-Li electrostatic interactions eventually limit further storage. As a result, the Janus monolayer delivers a high theoretical specific capacity of 1470.24 mAh/g together with a small volume expansion of only 3.7% during maximum lithiation. The present study demonstrates that intrinsic polarization can be utilized to regulate both the thermodynamics and kinetics of Li storage, providing a design strategy for high-rate and high-capacity two-dimensional electrode materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a systematic theory to derive nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2)}$) from general nonlocal constitutive relations, particularly for second-harmonic generation (SHG). It rigorously proves that even when bulk symmetry forbids the macroscopic SHG response, the interface itself generates a measurable signal. The core technique involves reducing complex higher-order problems to simpler effective linear ones via marginal integration.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for understanding nonlinear optics at interfaces, which is crucial for designing advanced optical devices where surface effects dominate the response despite bulk symmetry constraints. The mathematical machinery involving nonlocal kernels and distributional limits is highly technical but foundational to continuum electrodynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper systematically derives nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2)}$) from the general theory of bulk nonlocal response, specifically for second-harmonic generation (SHG). It aims to understand how interfacial effects manifest when the bulk material symmetry forbids a direct macroscopic response.

**Main result.** The complex nonlinear surface problem reduces recursively to an effective linear one via a 'marginal integration principle.' Crucially, while centrosymmetry forces the bulk $\chi^{(2)}$ to zero, it does not forbid the surface-induced SHG signal.

**Method.** The methodology combines extending distributional frameworks from linear to nonlinear response theory, employing spatial moment expansions and a distributional thin-layer limit ($\ell 	o 0$). A key mathematical tool is the 'marginal integration principle' used to simplify the higher-order boundary problem.

**Model / system.** The analysis models the nonlinear optical response of materials at interfaces, using general tensorial nonlocal constitutive relations. Examples include planar and spherical geometries analyzed with specific kernels like Gaussian or Yukawa potentials.

**Key observables.** Nonlinear surface susceptibilities ($\chi^{(2),s}_{\parallel}$ and $\chi^{(2),s}_{\perp}$), the bulk second-harmonic polarization ($P^{(2),\Omega}$), and generalized nonlinear Maxwell boundary conditions for the SH field.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The decay length scale ($\ell$), the thickness of the layer ($d$), and geometric parameters like mean curvature ($H$) and Gaussian curvature ($K$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on assuming rapid decay of the nonlocal kernel, homogeneity conditions, and utilizing the distributional thin-layer limit to isolate surface contributions.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the decomposition of polarization into different spatial cells ($\Omega	imes \Omega$, $\Omega_c$) and show how boundary conditions are derived for the second-harmonic field.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework (1D scalar case), then generalizing to the 3D tensorial case. It systematically applies symmetry arguments (centro-symmetry) to prove that bulk responses vanish while surface responses persist, culminating in generalized boundary conditions for curved interfaces.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We extend the distributional framework developed in the companion paper [Zolla, arXiv:2605.15716] to the nonlinear case, focusing on the second-order ($χ^{(2)}$) response responsible for second-harmonic generation (SHG). Starting from the most general tensorial nonlocal second-order constitutive relation and combining a spatial moment expansion with a distributional thin-layer limit, we show that the full complexity of the nonlinear interfacial response condenses, at leading order, into two scalars, the nonlinear surface susceptibilities $χ^{(2),s}_\parallel$ and $χ^{(2),s}_\perp$, associated with the tangential and normal components of the electric field, respectively. A key structural result is established: via a marginal integration over one field argument, the nonlinear surface problem reduces recursively to an effective linear one, whose surface susceptibility is determined by the bulk nonlinear kernel alone. Generalized nonlinear Maxwell boundary conditions are derived explicitly for planar and spherical interfaces, and curvature corrections are obtained systematically. The formalism is illustrated on Gaussian, Yukawa, and tensorial Lorentz kernels.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** The work bridges concepts from plasmonics and semiconductor physics by quantifying how intrinsic material properties (like the density of states in $	ext{Pt}$) can lead to measurable photoactivity far exceeding simple co-catalyst models.
